Sports.title: Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge
Sports.content:
Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez got married at their new £30million mansion near Lisbon in front of just four witnesses and their children, it emerged today.

Cristiano's doting mum Dolores Aveiro and his three siblings Hugo, Elma and Katia, were not present at the intimate civil ceremony, which took place at 1.30pm on Tuesday.

Georgina's sister Ivana, Cristiano's long-time friend Miguel Paixao and a Spanish couple named as Jose Rodriguez Sangil and his wife Monica Goncalez Martinez were the only witnesses.

Registrar Maria Manuel Ferreira de Campos Folhadela de Oliveira travelled from the northern Portuguese city of Porto to Cascais to officiate the ceremony.

And the star couple, who married exactly one year to the day after they announced their engagement on social media, have decided to keep their prenuptial assets separate despite tying the knot after a decade-long romance.

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez married with four witnesses in Cascais, Lisbon

The marriage certificate for Ronaldo and Georgina's wedding has now emerged

The couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings after the small ceremony

They signed a prenup agreement to define their property regime on August 10, a day before the ceremony, at a public notary's office in Lisbon.

Cristiano Ronaldo's representatives confirmed earlier this week the footballer and his long-time partner married on August 11 in an 'intimate' ceremony in Cascais after the couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings on social media.

It followed speculation which turned out to be false that they were due to marry at Funchal Cathedral in Cristiano's native island of Madeira on Saturday.

No details had emerged about where in Cascais they had wed or who exactly was at the ceremony apart from their children.

Overnight respected Portuguese newspaper Jornal de Noticias published a copy of the marriage certificate showing it took place at Cristiano's massive mansion in the upmarket residential area of Quinta da Marina.

And it also evidenced the fact so few people were invited there appeared to be no place for Cristiano's mum, who gave the union her blessing shortly afterwards by posting a heart emoticon on her son's Instagram in response to his wedding announcement, or the rest of his family apart from his children.

Jose Rodriguez Sangil was described as a Spanish jeweller by Portuguese press.

The marriage document listed Cristiano's full name and age of 41 as well as his birthplace and the names of his parents, including his late father Jose Dinis.

Cristiano's massive built-from-scratch mansion in Quinta da Marina was the venue

The home boats an impressive infinity pool, underground car park and a private cinema room

Ronaldo wore his wedding ring on his finger as he returned to training in Saudi Arabia

The same details were listed for 32-year-old Georgina, born in the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires, and referenced by her full name of Georgina Luisa Rodriguez Hernandez. They will both keep their pre-marriage names.

The marriage certificate was recorded as number 1,493 of this year but appears to have been listed at Porto's Registry Office instead of Cascais which is the municipality where the wedding took place.

Cristiano and Georgina are now back in Saudi Arabia where the Portuguese international plays his club football for Al Nassr ahead of the start of the new season tomorrow.

Sports.title: Farewell Jimmy Rimmer - the unassuming Aston Villa European Cup hero who never felt comfortable with being called a 'legend'
Sports.content:
Farewell Jimmy Rimmer - the unassuming Aston Villa European Cup hero who never felt comfortable with being called a 'legend'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

To the very end, Jimmy Rimmer was a picture of self-effacement and always disinclined to locate himself at the centre of a football story.

He was happy in his own company, content to enjoy a beer without others present in the corner of a pub in Swansea, the place he came to call home, and it amused to think that some of the regulars would observe of him: ‘That quiet fella in the corner used to be famous.'

He was one of the outstanding goalkeepers of his era, named by Gordon Banks as the 20th best in the world – a judgement he took as a compliment, rather than wonder how the England legend managed to put so many others ahead of him – and had fate not conspired to thwart him, his football fame would actually have been far greater than it was.

Rimmer, who has died at the age of 78, has the dubious distinction of being the only English player to win the European Cup with two different club without being on the pitch when either final finished. The first came early, when a role in Manchester United’s Youth Cup winning team of 1964 earned him a place among the club’s substitutes in the 1968 European Cup final at Wembley. Though the 20-year-old looked on as Sir Matt Busby’s side sweep away Benfica, with Alex Stepney nowhere near being dislodged, Rimmer would reflect on the privilege of being around George Best, Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and others.

It was always enough for him that he had the memory of a United first team debut, a few months before the final, when Stepney was injured for an Easter Monday match against Fulham at Old Trafford. There was 64,000 people inside, another 10,000 locked outside and Rimmer did his job, making one save and handling a few crosses in a 3-0 win.

Former Aston Villa and Man United goalkeeper Jimmy Rimmer has died aged 78

Rimmer famously had to come off through injury in Aston Villa's 1982 European Cup final triumph over Bayern Munich

But after his football journey had taken him on loan to Swansea and then to Bertie Mee’s Arsenal, where he was a mainstay in the mid-1970s, European Cup glory beckoned once more, after his Aston Villa side reached the 1982 final against Bayern Munich. The game was five days away when he collided with Swansea’s Bob Latchford in a league game, crashing down onto his neck and finding himself in agony.

The physios did what they could for him and generous quantities of cortisone were applied to his shoulder and neck on the night of the final, but nine minutes into the game, he knew it was a lost cause and signalled that he would be unable to play on. He sat in the Villa dressing room and wept, as Nigel Spink ran on in his place for what would be a career-defining role. Rimmer had previously missed just one match in five years for Villa.

The many sports journalists who ventured to ask Rimmer had he regretted that decision to depart the scene were always cut short by him. ‘You can't do that,’ he’d always say. ‘We got to the final as a team. I couldn't be the Jimmy Rimmer people would expect me to be.’

That ‘Jimmy Rimmer’ was a quite exceptional player, a graduate of United’s Busby school who took every word the old man instilled in him to heart. ‘He treated you like a man,’ Rimmer said of Sir Matt in later life. ‘You knew not to do silly things because if you did that with him, you were going upstairs for a chat in the office.’

But it was Harry Gregg, the former Manchester United goalkeeper and reluctant hero of the Munich disaster who, as a goalkeeping coach, had imbued him with the wisdom which served him best. 'Catch the ball. Get some shape in your hands. Cover your near post. They're not so good at the near post these days.' It was also Gregg who talked a 23-year-old Rimmer into a loan move at Fourth Division Swansea, then told Arsenal scout Gordon Clark to sign him in April 1974.

Rimmer proved a fine successor to Bob Wilson, who retired at the end of that season and, once elevated to No1, missed only three Arsenal games in three years – a period in which he secured his solitary England cap, against Italy in 1976. Rimmer had Ray Clemence and Peter Shilton ahead of him in the order: more evidence of an absence of serendipity in his long football career.

In a wonderful interview with Daily Mail Sport’s Matt Barlow two years ago, Rimmer delighted in telling against himself a story about his arrival as an unsophisticate at Arsenal in 1974. After his debut in a 1-0 win at Liverpool, he thought he was on the receiving end of a wind-up when offered prawn cocktail or smoked salmon on the bus home. ‘At United, the bus driver would go and get fish and chips, and now there's two fellas asking me what starter I'd like, whether I want steak or chicken and red or white wine,’ he said. ‘That's why they're called the Arsenal. It's nothing but the best and I'd come from Man United.'

The goalkeeper started his career at Manchester United after joining the club as just a boy

He’d make occasional mistakes, like any keeper, though it was perhaps the nature of the man that he tended to internalise them more than most. ‘I'd go into my own world when I made a mistake,’ he reflected. ‘I used to hold them in and think about them for too long. Harry Gregg would say, "Oh, you're the only one who ever made a mistake, are you?" But you can't go around telling people about all the great saves you made.’

For all that, he was an adventurer, spending three years coaching goalkeepers in China, after finishing his playing days at Swansea, whom he managed twice as caretaker. He lived rent-free in a suite of the Shangri-La in Beijing and had only planned to go for three months but loved the culture there and respected it, which always said that was why he lasted there so long. Rimmer being Rimmer, he didn’t put it down to his technical capabilities.

After suffering a heart attack which left him a coma for 11 days, 18 years ago, while living in Vancouver, he returned to South Wales to be closer to his son David, one of his three children. He followed Swansea City, was an occasional speaker in their matchday lounges and when extending a hand of friendship would apologise for no longer possessing him a firm grip, explaining that several artificial joints were the penalty for his career between the posts.

Rimmer would not have had the game’s slings and arrows any other way. He always liked to reflect that he’d played for the biggest clubs in North West England, London the Midlands and Wales. ‘People call me a legend but I don't see it like that,’ he said in later years. ‘I played with legends though - that's for sure.’

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca tells his old club Chelsea he WON'T meet their 5pm deadline for £120m Enzo Fernandez transfer today as Man City saga threatens to turn sour
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca tells his old club Chelsea he WON'T meet their 5pm deadline for £120m Enzo Fernandez transfer today as Man City saga threatens to turn sour

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester City will not meet Chelsea’s 5pm deadline to bid £120million for Enzo Fernandez.

New boss Enzo Maresca insisted that City will not be doing any incoming business before the close of play, while Rodri returned to the training ground for pre-season testing after back surgery.

Barcelona are attempting to thrash out a transfer worth more than £60million for the Spain captain, who held talks with his manager on Friday.

Fernandez wants a move to the Etihad Stadium this month, with Chelsea insistent that his future will be resolved before the weekend.

‘Not today to be honest, I don’t think we’re going to do something today,’ Maresca said, while opening the door to more big-name departures out of City this month.

Tijjani Reijnders is putting the finishing touches to a £52m switch to Al Qadsiah in Saudi Arabia, while Savinho wants to join Tottenham.

Enzo Maresca has said he won't adhere to Chelsea's deadline over a move for Enzo Fernandez

Maresca is overseeing a midfield rebuild at City after replacing Pep Guardiola this summer

Maresca – who heads into his first competitive fixture with the club in Sunday’s Community Shield against Arsenal – has suggested that there could be further outgoings in the coming weeks.

‘We’ll see what happens with some more, there is a change in this moment,’ the Italian said. ‘We are in a moment where players that were here many years have already left or [others who] probably can leave.

‘And that means there is a change. We're going to try to do our best. At the moment the transfer window closes, we need to be good enough to find as soon as possible solutions for the team.’

The 46-year-old refused to discuss players from other clubs, adding that ‘I don’t think it’s good when people from other clubs speak about our players’ after a summer of discussion around Rodri in Spain.

Reijnders had decided to pursue other opportunities after a lack of starts last season and Maresca believes there are others in the same boat.

‘They all work every day, they all do sessions every day and at the end of the week they all want to play a game,’ he said.

‘When they don’t play, they struggle to understand or they struggle to see the reason why and I can understand that after one season some of them would like to play a little bit more.

‘It’s a bit difficult to convince players when they are already convinced. You need to change their thoughts, that is not always easy.

‘Tijjani’s situation is like James Trafford’s situation and some more players but I think when the club, the player, the manager, they all think the same way, that probably the best decision for a player is to go, you have to go.’

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez is the face of the ugly game and Enzo Maresca should run a mile from him. Replacing Pep Guardiola at Man City is already the hardest job in football without once again indulging Argentine's graceless, brainless behaviour
Sports.content:
Enzo Fernandez is the face of the ugly game and Enzo Maresca should run a mile from him. Replacing Pep Guardiola at Man City is already the hardest job in football without once again indulging Argentine's graceless, brainless behaviour

Read Oliver Holt's column every Monday with a DailyMail+ subscription - and unlock access to the best exclusives, interviews and analysis

It is not a surprise that Manchester City appear to be pursuing Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez, a player who has come to symbolise much that is ugly about the beautiful game.

City's new manager, Enzo Maresca, has got form for indulging and rewarding the graceless and base antics of the Argentina midfielder that goes back to his time in charge at Stamford Bridge.

Two years ago, Maresca was forced to defend his decision to select Fernandez as Chelsea captain in their opening game of the 2024-25 season, against City, just a month after Fernandez posted a video of him and other Argentina players mocking the racial heritage of the France team.

Chelsea team-mate Wesley Fofana branded the video, uploaded by Fernandez after Argentina's victory over Colombia in that summer's Copa America final, as 'uninhibited racism'. Fernandez apologised. And in the absence of Reece James, Maresca made him skipper.

What Fernandez did was brainless as well as offensive. This is a player, don't forget, who was suspended by his own club at the end of last season after he flirted publicly with Real Madrid. This is a player who helped to get Liam Rosenior the sack at Chelsea when his performances dipped noticeably.

This is a man who is up there with the worst in the league in his attempts to pressure referees with his antics. This is a player who was sent off in the World Cup final and whose thuggish, unpunished behaviour in the semi-final against England prompted widespread disgust.

It is not a surprise that Manchester City appear to be pursuing Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez, who in the last couple of years has come to symbolise much that is ugly about the beautiful game

City's new manager Enzo Maresca has got form for indulging the graceless and base antics of the Argentina midfielder that goes back to his time in charge at Stamford Bridge

In those circumstances, and given Chelsea set an asking price of £120million, it was predictable that Madrid did not want to go anywhere near him. It was less predictable that they would take the unusual step of stating publicly they were not interested in buying him.

'The club wishes to state,' read the Madrid communique at the beginning of July, 'that it has not made any efforts, either directly or indirectly, aimed at signing the aforementioned player and, furthermore, has no intention of pursuing such an operation.'

But now, a couple of months into the job, Maresca is already risking the reputation City built in their Pep Guardiola years, for being a side that was widely admired for the quality, style and attitude with which it went about dominating the Premier League.

Chelsea have set a deadline of 5pm on Friday for City to make a bid for Fernandez and meet their asking price but it is possible the story will bleed further towards the transfer deadline of September 1.

City under Guardiola were the team of gifted stars like Kevin De Bruyne and Bernardo Silva. They were the team of Rodri and Ilkay Gundogan, Jack Grealish and Erling Haaland. They were a team that put a smile on the face of any neutral that watched them.

The purchase of Fernandez, if it happens, will change that. Fernandez is a fine player but his quality comes at a high cost in terms of the image of the team he plays for. The wisest managers buy character as well as quality.

The truth is that if City buy Fernandez, it will represent not just a downgrade on Rodri but a reversal of much that the club stood for under Guardiola. It will represent an embrace of the ugly side of the game. It will be a transfer that stands for cynicism. It will be a move that says City are swapping beauty for the game's dark arts.

The truth is also that Chelsea overpaid for Fernandez when they agreed to give Benfica £106.8million for him in the aftermath of the 2022 World Cup. He has not been as big a failure as some of the BlueCo signings but he has mixed some outstanding performances with periods of near anonymity.

The truth is that if City buy Fernandez (right), it will represent not just a downgrade on Rodri (left) but a reversal of much that the club stood for under Pep Guardiola

It will represent an embrace of the ugly side of the game. It will be a transfer that stands for cynicism. It will be a move that says City are swapping beauty for the game's dark arts

He is supposed to be one of the leaders of the team but there were spells last season when he looked nothing like a leader. Leaders don't flirt with other teams. Leaders don't get suspended by their own club. Leaders don't allow mediocrity to flourish all around them.

Chelsea finished tenth in the Premier League last season, 33 points adrift of champions Arsenal and Fernandez was part of that surrender. If Chelsea do sell him to City and somehow manage to recoup the money they paid for him, it should be cause for a huge celebration on the King's Road.

There are early signs, in fact, that Chelsea, under their own new manager Xabi Alonso, are starting to pursue a more coherent transfer policy and achieve a better balance in their playing staff. If Fernandez leaves, it will be another step in the right direction.

For City, it would be the opposite. Maresca already has the most difficult job in English football in attempting to replace Guardiola. If he signs Fernandez, that job will get a whole lot harder.

Sports.title: 'We've seen the script written for us but we're here to prove them wrong': Lincoln's coaching double act Tom Shaw and Chris Cohen on sharing the 'chaos' together, why they know their dynamic works and the Imps' transfer plans
Sports.content:
'We've seen the script written for us but we're here to prove them wrong': Lincoln's coaching double act Tom Shaw and Chris Cohen on sharing the 'chaos' together, why they know their dynamic works and the Imps' transfer plans

Unlock more of the best of our football coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

When Michael Skubala left Lincoln City for Bristol City in June, the club had a decision to make.

Skubala had overseen an incredible two-and-a-half years at the ProAmpac Stadium, guiding the Imps to the League One title with 103 points last season and promotion to the second tier for the first time in 65 years.

But Lincoln’s rise from the National League to the Championship has been built around a unified, club-wide strategy that is bigger than any one person - in an environment where staff are given the opportunity to develop.

So, while interviews took place with outside candidates, Lincoln took the bold step of promoting Tom Shaw and Chris Cohen to joint-head coaches.

Shaw joined Lincoln's academy in 2018 and had a seven-game spell as caretaker boss before Skubala’s arrival in 2023. Cohen, in his third spell with the club, had been joint-assistant head coach alongside Shaw since November 2024.

Both had significant responsibility under Skubala, regularly taking training sessions, leading meetings and helping to develop Lincoln’s game model.

Lincoln City appointed Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw as joint-head coaches earlier this summer

The unique and bold move came after boss Michael Skubala left the club to join Bristol City

A single head coach was considered, but the club felt the partnership best suited their collaborative approach. More importantly, they believed it offered the best way to preserve the structure behind such a special campaign.

‘There are a few more things like this to do,’ Shaw tells Daily Mail Sport about his newfound media responsibilities. 'It’s been very similar on the pitch, but a few more roles off it, which have been really good challenges.’

Ironically, the idea of becoming joint-head coaches was one Shaw and Cohen had already discussed in the event Skubala left, but the club beat them to it.

‘They'd thought of it first,’ Cohen says. ‘So we never had to ask for it. They came to us and said, "This is the way we see it happening if you two are both happy to do it that way”.

‘And I couldn't think of a better person to be sharing the chaos of being a manager in the Championship with.’

The appointment has inevitably sparked debate. Peterborough owner Darragh MacAnthony this week said he ‘hated’ the idea of joint-managers, insisting there ‘can only be one’ and argued the model is ‘problematic’.

‘We appreciate the question marks because it's not the norm,’ Shaw says. ‘But this is a way of working that we've been doing for a number of years that has brought big success.

‘Everybody in the building knows how it works, why it works, and we'll be continuing that. We’ll share duties between us, and, over time, figure out who's better at each of them.

‘But we've known each other for a long time, and we've earned this opportunity to do it together.’

Lincoln won the League One title with 103 points after an incredible unbeaten run last season

They are sticking with the players who won them promotion, meaning stars like Reeco Hackett (pictured) will get a chance to thrive in the Championship

Managing in tandem remains unusual, and critics will point to the infamous failed experiment when Liverpool paired Gerard Houllier with Roy Evans in the 1990s.

But Cohen and Shaw insist their arrangement is fundamentally different. And, listening to the pair explain their relationship, it is easy to see why Lincoln believe the model can work.

‘For the last three seasons, we've been designing a game plan throughout the week,’ Cohen says. ‘We would then go to Michael with it, and he had the final say.

‘By the time we went into the room, we were united. We got there through a load of disagreements and debates, but the main thing was we would live by it on a Saturday. By the time we’d leave the analysis room, we’d be completely convinced.'

Their relationship goes beyond the training ground, too.

Shaw, who has driven in with Cohen for the past three years, says: 'We've grown to love each other's company and there is massive respect.

‘I watched Chris play back in the day so I have huge respect for him as a football man and just as a bloke in general.

‘We’ve got a really nice relationship, and our families know each other now too, which is another lovely thing.’

Cohen and Shaw were key cogs in Skubala's coaching team, and they are relishing the step up

The Imps are back in the second tier of English football for the first time in 65 years

The appointment also provides continuity after a campaign that ended with Lincoln on a club-record 29-match unbeaten run. That became 30 with Saturday’s 2-1 Carabao Cup victory over Derby.

Several members of the promotion-winning squad have signed new deals and, while key man Jack Moylan moved to Cardiff City, five players have come through the door, including highly rated Tottenham forward Mason Melia, who had been the subject of 30 loan enquiries.

‘We don't want to be one of these clubs that moves up a division and clears the decks to try and get players they think are going to be better,’ Cohen says.

‘These players are capable in the Championship. They got 103 points last year, which should give them an incredible amount of confidence.

‘There's some big names in the division, some experienced managers we've got to go toe-to-toe with, but we feel prepared. The players deserve to go and push themselves and see how they can do at this level too.

‘There will be some tough weekends but our job is to keep the belief in this group because we know they’re good enough.’

Lincoln had the 17th biggest budget in League One last season and are likely to be among the Championship’s smallest spenders. Yet they are prepared to be ambitious in the transfer market.

The Imps have already broken their transfer record for Romanian defender Andrei Coubis and are likely to do so again before the window closes.

They remain the overwhelming bookies’ favourites for relegation, but Shaw and Cohen are relishing the opportunity to silence the doubters.

‘We've seen the script that's written for Lincoln City in the Championship,’ Shaw says. ‘That’s a massive motivation for our lads.

‘We're here to prove people wrong every week and this club has done pretty well as the underdog in recent seasons.’

Lincoln extended their club-record unbeaten run to 30 games with a 2-1 victory over Derby

Cohen and Shaw celebrate after the impressive season-opening win in the Carabao Cup

Whatever happens, it will be a journey for the thousands of Lincoln fans who will follow their team around the country and watch them face sides they could have previously only dreamed of meeting in a league match.

It starts with Middlesbrough on Saturday.

‘We’re hopefully going to win lots of games, but we’ll also lose and draw lots,’ Cohen concludes. ‘But at the end of every game we have to make sure we've put in a performance that everyone can be proud of.

‘If we walk off the pitch feeling that it is a team we can be proud of, that will be enough. There will be days where the ball wazzes in the top corner a couple of times, and there's not much we can do. But if it's something within our control, and we do it incredibly well, we're going to overachieve again.’

Shaw adds: ‘We've got some trips to some big names and stadiums, which will feel very different, but we have no fear.

‘We want to go and have a real ding-dong at some of these ex-Premier League and big football clubs.’

Sports.title: 'I want to be an extension of his legacy': New Salford City boss Peter Cklamovski on making Ange Postecoglou 'proud', leading David Beckham's club-wide reboot - and the League Two promotion race
Sports.content:
To most English football fans, Peter Cklamovski is a name that needs some introduction.

The highly rated Australian coach took over as Salford City boss this summer after building an impressive career across continents and in some hugely demanding environments.

He was a long-term assistant to Ange Postecoglou in Australia, Japan and Greece, before striking out on his own, winning plaudits for his attacking, high-energy football and work with young players at Shimizu S-Pulse, Montedio Yamagata and FC Tokyo in Japan. He also impressed with the Malaysia national team.

Now, at 47, he has arrived in League Two as one of the most intriguing EFL appointments in recent years, and with a clear objective – to get Salford promoted after seven seasons in the division.

‘I’ve loved English football from afar and now I’m in the middle of it,’ Cklamovski tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘I’m honoured and privileged to be here, and it’s been fantastic so far.’

His relationship with Postecoglou naturally attracts plenty of interest. The pair spent 15 years working together, including a spell in the lower divisions in Greece as the former Tottenham boss built his managerial career.

Salford City appointed Australian coach Peter Cklamovski as their new manager this summer

Cklamovski was a long-term assistant to former Tottenham boss Ange Postecoglou

Together, they won the AFC Asian Cup with Australia and took the Socceroos to the 2014 World Cup. Their partnership was credited with helping reshape coaching standards, methodology and tactical identity in Australia and Asia, and only ended when Cklamovski took the managerial job at Shimizu in 2020.

The pair remain in constant contact, with Postecoglou acting as a mentor and ‘sounding board’ while Cklamovski was applying for the Salford job.

‘Fifteen years with Ange… it’s a long time with anybody,’ says Cklamovski. ‘We’ve got a special connection and synergy. I take a lot from him, and I can't speak highly enough of him.

‘Whatever I’ve done in my career over the last eight years, and however long I've got left, I want it to be an extension of his legacy. That's how much he means to me.

'If we're successful, I know that's going to make him very proud sitting in Saudi Arabia, and hopefully he can do the same in 12 months.’

Cklamovski certainly shares some similarities with his former boss, particularly in his mannerisms and the way he communicates. But his route to English football has been distinctly his own.

‘Mate, this is going to get deep, but for a long time I didn’t really have that aim to get to England as a manager,’ he says. ‘Ange had a motivation to get to English football so as a loyal soldier to him, I pushed hard for that.

‘When I went out on my own, my ambition was to be a dominant manager in Asia. But in the last couple of months, the ambition for me personally, the fire and flame of English football just switched. And here I am.

‘The timing of it was natural. Trust the universe. I’ve got a really strong motivation to do something special with a football club that has great people and an inspiring mentality in the playing group.’

Cklamovski gained rave reviews for his work as a manager in Japan and with Malaysia

He has taken over a Salford side desperate to get promoted from League Two this year

How Cklamovski ended up in the English fourth tier, at a club whose ownership group includes David Beckham and Gary Neville and where Paul Scholes serves as the chief football adviser, is an interesting story.

Its origins date back eight years, when he was working alongside Postecoglou at Yokohama F Marinos, part of the City Football Group.

Salford CEO Gavin Fleig spent 17 years with CFG, including seven as director of talent management, and came across Cklamovski during his time in the Far East.

The pair met up earlier this summer - with Salford’s process of looking for a new manager coinciding with the end of Cklamovski’s family holiday in the UK.

This was no favour to an old colleague, however. Cklamovski – who didn’t speak to Beckham or Neville during the process – emerged as the outstanding candidate after impressing across various data metrics and during the interview process.

‘The aim is to chase promotions and that resonates with me,’ he says. ‘I'm not afraid of that. I have a strong belief we can achieve it with special people and play a brand of football that's going to entertain our fans and bring pride and excitement to the Salford community.’

Scholes had to Google Cklamovski as he didn’t know who he was, but was particularly impressed, although Salford’s decision to appoint a manager with no experience of English football is undoubtedly a risk.

That move came after the club sacked Karl Robinson despite only missing out on automatic promotion on the final day of last season, before they lost to Notts County in the play-off final.

The hierarchy admitted the decision to part company with Robinson was a difficult one. But with Salford’s budget understood to have increased this season, the club are determined to finally make the step up to League One.

Cklamovski intends to build on Robinson's work, rather than rip everything up and start again.

‘Whatever sort of team you take over, you can’t stand still,’ he says. ‘We've got the benefit of the work done over the years, especially last year, and we’ve used that as a foundation. But you’ve got to go to another level. We’ll use the heartache from last year as motivation as well.’

Salford missed out on automatic promotion last season before losing in the play-off final

Salford, whose ownership group includes Gary Neville and David Beckham, have reverted to their traditional orange colours ahead of a big season for the club

His arrival at Moor Lane coincides with a significant season of change for Salford.

The club have increased their playing budget, reverted to their traditional orange colours as part of a rebrand in which Beckham played a key role, improved their Man United-owned Littleton Road training ground and overhauled their medical department.

There have also been statement signings, including Millwall striker Macaulay Langstaff, the League Two Golden Boot winner in 2023-24, and Doncaster Rovers winger Luke Molyneux, who was named in the division’s Team of the Season in 2024-25.

‘It’s a sign of the club’s ambition,’ Cklamovski says. ‘But it also shows the commitment to building something special long-term. We’ve made some great signings but there's a super core group here as well, and that's exciting.’

Salford begin their league campaign at Barnet on Saturday after losing on penalties to Shrewsbury in the EFL Cup last week.

It promises to be the first proper acid test of Cklamovski’s reign – and whether his aggressive style can translate into the results and entertainment he has promised supporters.

‘We want to play a brand of football that's going to make every Salford fan and everyone at the club proud and excited,’ he says. 'We want to have a goalscoring mentality, but we'll also have a real strong mentality to roll our sleeves up and keep clean sheets.

‘We've got to stay humble, work hard, and commit to that. Some really good work has started, but there's a lot more work to do.’

Sports.title: Why Arsenal insiders believe this is the season Max Dowman will vault into superstardom: Breaking Lamine Yamal's records, bulking up to shrug off defenders twice his age and a golden chance for club and country
Sports.content:
Long before Max Dowman began making headlines, the warnings started to come from within Arsenal’s senior ranks.

In May 2024 this baby-faced prospect, then just 14, was invited to join Mikel Arteta’s first-team training and, so the whispers went, was someone we would be hearing a whole lot more about for years to come.

Such claims around young talent can often be taken with a pinch of salt. As Arsene Wenger would often say when he was in Arteta’s shoes, you don’t know who a player really is until they’re 24, and for Dowman that was still a decade away.

But with Dowman, it’s different. Very, very different. Close to Lamine Yamal territory. Yes, really. The numbers don’t usually lie, and the very early milestones Dowman has already beaten the Spaniard to suggest a similar trajectory.

The Barcelona star made his league debut against Real Betis on April 29, 2023, aged 15 years and 290 days. Dowman did so against Leeds on August 23, 2025, aged 15 years and 235 days – 55 days fewer. Yamal made his first senior start against Cadiz on August 20, 2023, aged 16 years and 38 days. Dowman achieved the same feat against Brighton in the Carabao Cup on October 29, 2025, aged 15 years and 302 days – 101 days fewer.

But now, the 16-year-old attacker is no longer Arsenal’s best-kept secret. He enters the new season with expectations rising rapidly – for club and country – after a series of eye-catching first-team performances at the back end of last season, which have continued in this pre-season.

The Gunners have long believed Dowman possesses something extraordinary. Now, they are preparing to find out just how far he really can go.

Max Dowman is no longer Arsenal’s best-kept secret. He enters the new season with expectations rising rapidly – for club and country

The Gunners have long believed he possesses something extraordinary. Now, they are preparing to find out just how far he really can go

In July 2025, Arsenal began stepping up their efforts to prepare the then 15-year-old and his camp for the spotlight that was about to land on him.

There were flashes through the early months of the season – winning a penalty in that debut against Leeds, becoming Arsenal’s youngest ever starter against Brighton and then the Champions League’s youngest player a month later – but the hype machine did not hit overdrive until March 14, at home to Everton in the Premier League.

Brought on at 0-0 in the midst of a nerve-jangling title race, Dowman’s cross created Viktor Gyokeres’ 89th-minute goal to break the deadlock before he scored perhaps the most cathartic goal of Arsenal’s title win, streaking clear of an Everton defence from a corner that Jordan Pickford had gone up for, and tapping into an empty net. Now he was the Premier League’s youngest ever goalscorer, and there were even calls for him to be a bolter in Thomas Tuchel’s England World Cup squad.

And all this while having GCSEs to sit just a couple of months later (he gets his results on Thursday, the day before Arsenal’s Premier League campaign starts at home to Coventry City). Sources say that Dowman would sometimes feel stretched having had to juggle schoolwork alongside first-team football, sometimes on the bench for a late kick-off and then up early for school in the morning. That is no longer the case. It’s understood Dowman will not be doing higher education such as A-levels so he can fully focus on football.

With that, there is hope internally that he can really push on this season, at the age that Yamal also announced himself as arguably the world’s most-promising footballing talent.

At 16, the Spaniard made 22 league starts, and a barely believable Euros campaign followed in the summer of 2024, where Yamal became the youngest player to both appear and score at the tournament, before providing an assist to help Spain beat England in the final, the day after his 17th birthday.

It would be difficult to expect the same from Dowman, but having edged Yamal on the earlier records, the coming season could well be ground-breaking for the Englishman.

He has the required temperament, a player who is said to be highly critical of himself, and has had to adapt in an Arteta setup where standards are sky-high and demands unrelenting. ‘You could say, “Great performance” and he’ll be like, “Nah I could’ve done this more, this more”,’ a source said.

Dowman streaks clear of the Everton defence to become the Premier League's youngest ever goalscorer and seal a crucial victory in last season's title race

It’s understood Dowman will not be doing higher education such as A-levels so he can fully focus on football

He has been one of Arsenal's best players in pre-season, starting all five friendlies and scoring a low drive against Girona

The pre-season camp has emboldened the hype around the forward. Dowman has started all five friendlies and been one of Arsenal’s most dangerous attacking players in all of them.

From kick-off against Girona, Dowman pressed hard from the front, an aspect of the game that he struggled with last season. His flank would often be exposed on defensive transitions, but he’s worked on improving his work rate off the ball.

In the match against Borussia Dortmund, Dowman groaned in frustration when Gyokeres mistimed a shot. There’s a confidence now, a sense of belonging for this child among a group of men.

Yet, it’s Dowman's desire to drive at opposition backlines which has been consistent across the matches. His willingness to take players on and bounce back when things don’t go to plan has earned the respect of his peers.

In Dublin, in a 3-1 defeat by Real Betis, Dowman was the bright spark. His tight dribbling style, at speed, is hard to contain. Girona felt the same too, as he weaved his way around the opposition. He assisted Kai Havertz with a sublime through-ball and then in the second half a trademark dribble drove him to the edge of the box, where he fired into the bottom corner. Sandwiched between these two moments were a series of dribbles forward and threatening passes.

With Bukayo Saka recovering from a tough period with injuries and Noni Madueke having failed to nail down the right-wing spot, Dowman has a chance to stake his claim in the first month of the season.

If he were to start against Man City on Sunday and grasp his moment, Madueke could find it tricky to reclaim his spot.

Last season, Arsenal were very careful around the need to balance Dowman's exposure, and consider the welfare of a minor. This time around, the handbrake looks set to be lifted. There is a belief that Dowman is ready to take the next step, aided by the players around him.

With Bukayo Saka recovering from a tough period with injuries and Noni Madueke having failed to nail down the right-wing spot, Dowman has a chance to stake his claim for a starting role

He’s developing quickly physically. He is able to shrug off players much older than himself, which has impressed staff in matches and training

If Dowman can translate his remarkable early promise into consistent Premier League impact, the coming months could mark the beginning of something truly extraordinary

Martin Odegaard, who had the world’s attention on him as a 15-year-old kid from Norway joining Real Madrid, is well placed to understand the peculiar pressures that come with being labelled a prodigy before you are old enough to drive. Saka has helped Dowman settle in the first team, aware of what it’s like to be a Hale End kid thrust into the limelight and carrying the weight of expectation.

Declan Rice has been another reassuring presence, spending time with Dowman off the pitch and even supporting him around academy games last season. It is these seniors who can make a 16-year-old feel he belongs in a dressing room that he still isn’t allowed to get changed in until he turns 18.

He’s developing quickly physically, too. His frame is said to have got stronger over the summer, an essential for first-team football at Premier League level. He is able to shrug off players much older than himself which has impressed staff in matches and training.

For now, the comparisons with Yamal remain just that. But if Dowman can translate his remarkable early promise into consistent Premier League impact, the coming months could mark the beginning of something truly extraordinary.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Play-off Path A:
