Under the 2017 Provisional Development Order, multi-family developments are only permitted if the land exceeds 0.5 acres, unless compelling reasons are shown. The 2 Broadway Close site is exactly 0.5 acres, a fact that should have triggered additional scrutiny,” the residents claimed.

They further argued that with Broadway Close being a dead-end street, a five-storey, multi-family development will generate significant vehicular traffic that must enter and exit through a single point.

“The KSAMC is required to assess access and traffic flow as mandatory planning criteria. Emergency vehicles — fire trucks and ambulances — require adequate turning radius and access. The Jamaica Fire Brigade is a mandatory referral agency that must approve such developments. Residents are demanding that a traffic impact assessment be conducted and made public before any permit is granted,” argued the residents.

They added: “The certificate of title for 2 Broadway Close contains restrictive covenants that are binding on the land and its owners. No building other than that used for the purposes of a private dwelling house with appropriate outbuildings appurtenant thereto shall be erected on the said land or any part thereof. Restrictive covenants are contractual obligations imposed on purchasers by the original vendor, intended to limit the purchaser’s use of the land for the benefit of all land owners in the subdivision.

“They run with the land, meaning successive owners are bound by the same covenants. A covenant that precludes subdivision would limit the owner’s ability to legally construct an apartment complex.”

World.title: It’s an event scene!
World.content:
DJ Zacky (left) and his MC, Flex Supreme.

In recent years, a new generation of event promoters have emerged on the party scene, adding to night-time entertainment offerings.

But even though some of these promoters have been hosting successful events, there are some challenges that come with the territory.

Kyle Chin said securing dates and identifying an appropriate venue remain challenges.

“I got into event promotion as a youth, just by helping my older cousins promote their event in St Elizabeth about ten years ago. Officially, I have been doing my own events for the past three years,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Known for Socaverse and B43, he added: “The cost of getting the permits to actually keep the event is also of concern as well as the high taxes that promoters face.”

Chin’s events target the 18 and older demographic. Socaverse is a soca/EDM music event and is held twice annually while B43 is held monthly.

“What sets us apart and what we are bringing to nightlife is the experience. We cater to individuals with the different genres that are played and the type of setup we use,” said Chin who works as a corporate broker.

Popular teenage disc jock DJ Zacky, who hosts the bi-weekly SATDEHZ, which is held at Oceano, says he would like to see more support from corporate Jamaica for promoters.

“…I’d like to see more support for young promoters through sponsorship opportunities, easier access to venues, and stronger partnerships… I believe that there can be more collaboration within the entertainment industry. Better regulation and security support would also help events operate more efficiently,” said DJ Zacky.

“[P]eople don’t always take you seriously until you’ve built a name for yourself. But as our events continue to prove themselves, and our attendance keeps growing, you can see people starting to view us differently and put more respect on our name. That journey has motivated us to keep raising the standard with every event,” DJ Zacky shared.

He revealed that his passion for entertainment and creating memorable experiences were what drew him to event promotion.

“I saw an opportunity to bring people together through well-organised events… Event promotion allows me to combine creativity, business, and networking into something I genuinely enjoy,” DJ Zacky, who has been involved in event promotion for over a year, said.

SATDEHZ, a drink-inclusive event that offers patrons a premium nightlife experience, targets the 18-35 age demographic.

“We cater to university students, young professionals, and anyone looking for a quality entertainment experience. We’re focused on creating a premium yet accessible experience. Through strong branding, creative marketing, quality DJs, and engaging social media campaigns, we want every event to feel unique and memorable,” the business Administration student at the University of Technology, Jamaica shared.

On his way to The University of the West Indies (UWI), Mona, where he will be pursuing a degree in management studies, DJ Kovert, a popular disc jock, is the co-promoter for FWD, a bi-weekly event held at Dulce Lounge in Barbican.

Dominic Bartley is his business partner in this series which wrapped up on July 29.

“I decided to get involved in event promotion because I’ve always had a passion for music and creating experiences where people can take a break from their everyday lives and truly enjoy themselves. As a DJ, I realised there was an opportunity to create events that reflected the energy and atmosphere that I wanted to experience in Kingston, especially for my generation,” says DJ Kovert.

“While I’ve been promoting public events for a little over a month, my experience actually started before that. During my time at Ardenne High School, I helped curate and organise several school socials and events, which gave me valuable hands-on experience in planning, marketing, and understanding what it takes to have a successful party. Those experiences built the foundation and confidence that encouraged me to step into the entertainment industry and begin promoting my own events.”

FWD primarily caters to the 18-30 demographic.

“Each FWD staging is designed to have its own identity, with different themes, concepts, and elements that keep the experience fresh for patrons… As a younger promoter, we also bring a fresh perspective on how events are marketed and how audiences connect with entertainment,” DJ Kovert shared.

He spoke with Splash on the improvements he would like to see in the sector.

“I would like to have more support and opportunities created for promoters, especially young promoters who are trying to build sustainable events. This includes stronger partnerships with sponsors, more collaboration between promoters, venues, artists, and other stakeholders, as well as more accessible resources to help events grow. The entertainment industry is a major part of Jamaica’s culture and economy, and creating a better support system for promoters would allow more creativity, innovation, and quality experiences to thrive.”

Lemar Smith, who is from Trelawny, is the new kid on the block as far as event promotion is concerned. His weekly Saturday night event is called Sapphire Saturdays and is held at Vuebar in Liguanea.

“I started promoting Sapphire Saturdays in May this year… Although I’m still relatively new to the industry, the experience has taught me a lot,” said The UWI student, adding, “Whether you’re a university student, young professional, entrepreneur, or simply someone looking for a great Saturday night out, Sapphire is designed to bring people together in a fun and vibrant environment… We also place a strong emphasis on high-quality photography, videography, and social media content so people don’t just attend the event they become part of the Sapphire experience. It’s about creating a lifestyle and a community, not just another party.”

Smith would like the entertainment sector to become more diverse.

“I’d like to see more promoters take chances on concepts that feature house music, Afro House, Amapiano, R&B, throwback nights, and other unique experiences. Giving people more variety not only benefits patrons but also creates opportunities for DJs, artistes, promoters, and creatives to showcase different styles. I believe diversity will help Jamaica continue growing as one of the Caribbean’s top entertainment destinations.”

World.title: TWIN PEAKS: YEARS AWAY
World.content:
JAMAICA’S planned overhaul of financial regulation is likely to take years more to complete, outgoing Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) Governor Richard Byles has said, putting the Twin Peaks reform beyond both its original 18-to-24-month timetable and the Government’s subsequent 2026 target.

Byles, who is scheduled to demit office on August 18, said the BOJ and Financial Services Commission (FSC) were close to submitting the proposed architecture to Cabinet.

“Having brought it to Cabinet, remember now, really still we are at the beginning of the process,” Byles told the Jamaica Observer in an exit interview.

“The laws now have to be drafted… and the two Houses [of Parliament] have to debate it before it becomes law, so we do still have years of discussion and work to do on Twin Peaks, even when it goes to Cabinet and even if Cabinet says yes.”

Twin Peaks was announced in January 2023, shortly after disclosures of an alleged fraud at investment firm Stocks and Securities Limited intensified scrutiny of Jamaica’s regulatory system. The Government said the new structure would be implemented within 18 to 24 months, pointing to a transition between approximately July 2024 and January 2025.

That deadline passed.

In June 2024, then Finance Minister Dr Nigel Clarke told Parliament that implementation was expected in 2026. He said a concept paper prepared by the BOJ-FSC Twin Peaks Steering Committee had been approved and the Cabinet submission was in its “final stages”, after which drafting instructions would be issued.

More than two years later, Cabinet approval has not been publicly announced. BOJ said in June that the architecture would “soon” be ready for Cabinet; its latest Financial Policy Committee statement said only that progress continued.

It remains unclear how the concept paper approved by the then finance minister differs from the architecture Byles said was still being readied for Cabinet in 2026.

Byles hoped the submission could reach Cabinet before its August break. He said much of the time had been spent obtaining comments from the agencies involved.

“Any institution, not just the Bank of Jamaica, who has had to get legislation passed has found that that process is very cumbersome. It is onerous,” he said.

Although Byles described the difficulty broadly as part of the legislative process, Twin Peaks had not yet reached formal drafting or parliamentary debate. Most of the delay so far occurred while the architecture, inter-agency comments and Cabinet submission were being prepared.

MORE THAN MOVING REGULATORS

The significance of the delay extends beyond a missed deadline. Until the laws change, Jamaica must continue regulating institutions largely by sector even though many operate in groups spanning banking, insurance and securities. BOJ supervises deposit-taking institutions, while the FSC oversees securities dealers, insurers and pension funds.

Twin Peaks would divide the work by purpose. BOJ would supervise the financial soundness of institutions across the system. The FSC, or a proposed successor known as the Financial Services Conduct Authority, would oversee how firms treat customers, sell products, disclose fees and risks and handle complaints.

A bank would therefore answer to BOJ for its financial health and to the conduct regulator for its treatment of customers. The same division would apply across the sector.

The challenge is not simply transferring employees. The legislation must determine where one regulator’s authority ends and the other’s begins, what information they must share and how they will handle problems involving both financial safety and customer treatment. Poorly drawn boundaries could replace the gaps in the current system with either new gaps or duplicated regulation.

The public documents reviewed by BusinessWeek identify neither a final list of laws to be changed nor a consolidated schedule assigning responsibility for each stage and setting consultation, parliamentary and legal-cutover targets.

Jamaica is not starting from nothing. BOJ’s 2025 annual report identifies seven work areas covering supervision, consumer protection, legislation, staffing, technology, funding and Twin Peaks Practice. The regulators have trained employees and tested the approach across banking, insurance and securities within their existing powers.

Operational preparation can reduce disruption, but it cannot substitute for law: Only Parliament can transfer the responsibilities and make the new system enforceable.

One concern among non-bank institutions is whether BOJ would apply rules designed for banks. Byles said supervision would instead reflect each institution’s size, complexity and risk.

“It’s not that we will supervise the non-banks in the same way we do banks, because the non-banks are a different animal and we have a concept that says ‘proportionality’,” he said.

Proportionality would not exempt small firms. It would match scrutiny to the risks an institution presents and the wider damage its failure could cause.

THE INTERNATIONAL LESSON

South Africa’s experience shows why Byles’s warning should be taken seriously—and why long transitions still require clear deadlines.

Its regulatory review began in 2007 and widened after the global financial crisis. Twin Peaks was formally proposed in 2011, followed by a draft Bill in 2013. The Bill was tabled in 2015, enacted in 2017 and the regulators opened in April 2018.

The core transition took seven years from the formal proposal, or 11 from the initial review. Even then, the legal overhaul was incomplete. Cabinet approved a unified conduct Bill for submission to Parliament only in 2026-15 years after Twin Peaks was proposed.

That history does not make Jamaica’s delay unavoidable. Its lesson is that South Africa managed a long process through a published roadmap, successive drafts, consultations and phased implementation.

The United Kingdom moved faster, announcing its overhaul in 2010 and launching its regulators in 2013. There is no standard timetable, but reform is more measurable when divided into stages with clear responsibility.

For Byles, Twin Peaks remains his most important unfinished reform. He expects it to continue because it is Government policy rather than a BOJ initiative dependent on his leadership.

The next measurable step is Cabinet approval, which would allow formal drafting instructions to be issued. Legislation, consultation, parliamentary debate and legal commencement would follow.

More than three and a half years after Twin Peaks was announced, Jamaica has begun practising the system but has not legally entered it. Cabinet approval would advance the reform. Byles’s warning is that it would also expose how much of the journey remains.

World.title: Douglas hard on self despite three-medal haul
World.content:
Shanoya Douglas celebrates one of her two silver medals after winning the women’s 100m and 200m at the 21st World Athletics Under-20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday. Douglas won three medals — gold in the women’s 4x100m and silver in the 100m and 200m — to take her total to five after winning gold and bronze two years ago in Lima, Peru. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Shanoya Douglas may have left the 21st staging of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships with three medals, but the highly rated sprinter believes she could have performed much better at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday.

Douglas, who entered the five-day championships as the World Under-20 leader in both the 100m in 10.98 seconds and 200m in 22.11, won gold as the anchor on Jamaica’s women’s 4x100m relay team and silver in both individual events.

The Jamaican women’s relay team won in a World Under-20 leading 42.89 seconds, the fourth-fastest time, ever, but Douglas said she was disappointed with her overall performance.

“I have mixed feelings in this championship. Normally, I always get gold individual medals but I got two silver this time,” she told the Jamaica Observer. “The gold in the relay means a lot for me because I wanted to continue our streak and it means a lot to be able to continue that streak, especially knowing that I’d broken it in the 100 metres.”

The result means Douglas has won five medals at the last two World Under-20 Championships, including another relay gold and a bronze in the 200m at the 2024 championships in Lima, Peru.

The haul puts her among Jamaica’s most successful performers at the championships, a distinction that appears to surprise her.

“You know I never realised that I had that many,” she said, while admitting that she expected more from herself in Eugene.

Douglas won the 100m and 200m doubles at both the Intersecondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA)GraceKennedy Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships and the Carifta Games this year. She is also tied for third all-time with American sprint legend Allyson Felix in the World U-20 200m rankings and is 10th all-time in the 100m, also at the World U-20 level.

Her two silver medals in Eugene, both behind American Mia Maxwell, have given her a different perspective.

“This championship has taught me a lot, knowing that it’s not always things gonna go your way, and I was saying that sometimes it’s good to control the controllable, but this time I was having difficulties controlling the controllables,” she said. “And I’ve been hard on myself this championship, and I was like, ‘Let’s come out here, put everything aside, and deliver for my country.’”

Jamaican women had won the previous four World Under-20 200m titles through Briana Williams in Tampere, Finland, in 2018; Tina Clayton in Nairobi, Kenya, in 2021; Alana Reid in Cali, Colombia, in 2022; and Reid again in Lima, Peru, in 2024.

Douglas was particularly hard on herself when asked to grade her performance on a scale of one to 10.

“A five,” was her instant response.

She said members of the Jamaican coaching staff told her she was being too hard on herself, but she explained that the standards she sets for herself are what drive her.

“When you have a standard for yourself and not been able to reach that standard that you set for yourself, it’s like a different mental struggle,” she said. “And it’s just I’ve not met my standard and the standard that I had for myself going to this championship.”

Despite her disappointment, Douglas believes the experience will benefit her as she begins her professional career. She will forgo another year in high school after signing a professional contract the week before travelling to Eugene.

“I’m still having hope. I have great faith in myself that in the future I will be able to perform way better going into the other championships, and this has taught me a lot,” she said.

Douglas also pointed to the championship format, which required the sprinters to run the first two rounds of their events on the opening day before returning for the final the following day.

“This has set me up for what is to come in the professional setting where facing difficulties will be a reality every day. So yes, it has taught me a lot,” she said.

She said she was able to rebound from what she considered below-par performances in Eugene and resisted the temptation to dwell too long on the moments when she performed well.

Douglas said the experience had reinforced an important lesson about the difference between expectations and performance on the day.

“This championship probably taught me that because you have the fastest time on paper, it’s who show up on the day. And it’s not that I didn’t show up on the day, it’s just that circumstances didn’t make me perform how I wanted to. And regardless of that or not, I’m trying to see the positive in it because I was able to leave the championship with a medal, three medals,” she said.

World.title: 2026 MG ZS: Luxury on a budget
World.content:
The 2026 MG ZS in luxury trim offers premium features at a very competitive price point. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Sports car brands that make SUVs have it tough with the car-buying public. The fact that MG, one of the most-storied British auto makers and a cornerstone of the quintessential English roadster, has given in to the SUV-pocalypse must have the faithful spitting their afternoon tea across their crumpet-laden tables. Still, history has proven them more wrong than right, as these companies with sporting intention are able to infuse the mundane family hauler with their original ethos. MG has done just that with the ZS.

EXTERIOR

SUVs tend to stay on the conservative side of things, whereas the ZS has adopted a previous trend held by the premium brands: Russian Dolling, the act of simply scaling corporate design up or down a specific model. Yes, there is the usual Grilleus Maximus styling across the MG family present on the ZS; however, it has only been possible with the updates made to its larger sibling, the HS, to tell them apart. Otherwise, the ZS is inoffensive, clean, and modern-looking with a bit of sporting purpose due to the standard 18-inch wheels on the luxury trim.

Adding to its visual appeal is its availability in a wider colour palette than many of the sub-compact SUV class rivals. Push past the black, white, silver, and grey to the Brighton Blue Metallic on Auto’s review unit, or the Emerald Green Metallic that instantly brings forth similar tones to the iconic British Racing Green.

INTERIOR

The ZS is feature-rich given its class and price point. Keyless entry gets one into a cabin similar to the exterior. It’s a clear, modern design, highlighted by soft-touch materials across the main contact surfaces. Drop into the 6-way powered driver’s seat for an ergonomic experience.

Button clutter is a thing of the past, as there are hard buttons for the most accessible functions, and the other controls are tucked away in the 12.1-inch infotainment touchscreen. Some functions can even be assigned to steering wheel-mounted buttons. These few physical controls available operate with assuredness.

Luxury trim buyers will enjoy a bit more digital instrumentation via their 7-inch gauge cluster. The system works smoothly, has a logical layout, and all the connectivity modern passengers want.

While the ZS is the smaller MG SUV, the cabin space is more than sufficient for all occupants, and the sense of space is enhanced by the glass-to-body ratio and the sunroof. Even with the large greenhouse, the cabin retains a low-noise quotient for further comfort. Storage, including trunk space, is more than sufficient for family treks.

Combine this with a number of automated or powered convenience features and the ZS is a very nice place to be.

ON THE ROAD

For many class rivals, it would just fall apart right here, falling into either the ‘too soft, I don’t want to drive it fast’ category, or the ‘too stiff, my passengers are going to throw up and complain’ side of the graph. Then there are those soft, yet unable to provide comfort; and hard, yet unable to provide any actual vehicular control. This is where the sports car legacy kicks in.

The real beauty of the ZS is its driving dynamics, clearly inherited from MG’s performance car know-how. The suspension is compliant, but firm enough to be sporty. At the first corner, at speed, there’s magically precious little body roll, instilling confidence to drive with some enthusiasm. Even better, the rest of the car can keep up, as the steering is direct in tracing the given driving line, and the brakes assure constant speed reduction. The 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder is more than willing to respond in unison with the transmission for rapid increases in velocity as demanded by the accelerator pedal. Even on the broken surfaces that make up the Jamaican internal road network, the ZS quickly makes one forget that it’s an SUV, taking on a car-like feel and making as much use of its front-wheels as possible.

For those that are more measured in their pace, the ZS can handle precious human cargo with the abundance of equipped safety systems, passive, and active for urban operations. Things are a breeze in stop-and-go traffic due to the auto hold function on the luxury trim.

Then there is the MG Pilot Driver Assistance suite. Put together, they keep the vehicle in check and the driver alert for potential accidents, while allowing the vehicle to be operated for short periods with minimal driver intervention.

VERDICT

With its size, price, comfort, and feature set, the 2026 ZS Luxury is already a top contender in the cut-throat sub-compact SUV segment. And while the brand faithful may scoff at it, or others mislabel it as another small SUV, MG did take time to work their magic. This is a brand known for driving excellence, and the ZS is a pleasure to be behind the wheel, packed to the gills with the family, or alone on a B-road. If that last part is important, then the 2026 ZS MG Luxury should be at the top of your list.

World.title: Help delivered, but…
World.content:
Tents, provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management, erected in the area of Coopers Pen, Trelawny, where 20 houses were demolished on Tuesday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Even as the Government mobilised multi-agency help for about 40 families whose houses were demolished a day earlier, a group of irate residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny staged a peaceful protest Wednesday, demanding more. The residents said they want to be relocated, after their houses were demolished allegedly by the owner of land some of them have occupied for decades.

The protesters insisted that the Government, or the landowner, must provide them with alternative accommodation. They said the temporary tents provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), in which some of them spent Tuesday night, are not enough.

“We get tent last night, so we can lay a head for the night. What about today? What is going to happen? We want to know where we are going to relocate to. What is going to happen to the people them that their house push down?” asked demonstrator Jessica Haye.

In a Wednesday afternoon release, while emphasising that the demolition arose from a long-standing private matter, and that the Government of Jamaica was not a party to the underlying private dispute, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) said a number of State agencies had been deployed “to address the immediate humanitarian and social welfare needs of affected families”. The Ministry of Labour and Social Security, ODPEM, Child Protection and Family Services Agency, Poor Relief Department within the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, and the Social Development Commission are among agencies involved. OPM said teams worked well past midnight, Tuesday, to help those who lost their homes.

“Assistance provided included food supplies, bottled water, toiletries, temporary shelter supplies, tents and lighting equipment. As part of the emergency response, ODPEM mobilised and transported relief supplies directly to affected families, including 40 family-size tents, cots, foam pads, solar lights, care packages, cases of bottled water and sanitary products. The Ministry of Labour will return on Friday, August 14, to provide additional support,” said OPM.

But while grateful for the help, residents said they expect more, and they laid out their demands during Wednesday’s protest.

“There is no way you can demolish a house like this, and no notification. No notification. We need justice,” said Haye, who stressed that many of them had not yet recovered from the devastation caused by last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“We are not going to stop this [protest] until the prime minister [Dr Andrew Holness] hear. We naw stop. We go come out here day by day because we want justice. It must be a relocation!” she insisted.

Another demonstrator, Sylvia Fisher, said while they understood that the residents could not remain on privately owned property indefinitely, they should have been given notice and assistance to relocate.

“You can’t run in pon people so. And run pon people goods… and then now put you under tent! You have pickney to go back to school. It cannot work,” she said.

She said she has lived in the community for 32 years, while her father lived there for more than 50.

Fisher is adamant that the government has a responsibility to assist affected residents whom, she said, voted them into office.

“The government need to come see this cause a we the people make the government, and is we the people put politicians in power, and a we the people have power. So they must consider poor people. A no rich man, a poor people put them in a power,” she argued.

“We know we have to go, but please relocate we, relocate we. We live pon the land 20, 30, 40 years you just come pitch we off so. No! Find somewhere and put we. The private man who them say claims to own the land, him fi find somewhere and put we. A him come mash we up,” Fisher alleged.

Even as those who have lost their homes agitate, there are fears that the wrecking crew will return. Among the worried is 69-year-old Stanley Hill, who said he has lived on the property for 51 years.

He said a marker has been placed at the doorway of the small concrete house he has occupied for decades, indicating that it is earmarked for demolition.

“Now to the age a me now, me soon 70, me a 69-year-old. And me live there from me a little boy. Where me going go now as an old man? Me can’t make house again,” said Hill.

“I need somebody to talk to me so me know where me stand. Because me can’t come sleep under tree. And me don’t have no money. Me don’t have no bank account,” he added.

The OPM has given a commitment to keep an eye on what is happening in the community and “coordinate additional interventions”. It said it is aware that those affected include senior citizens such as Hill, children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable individuals.

Said the media release issued Wednesday: “The Poor Relief Department of the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, along with the Social Development Commission, will undertake further assessments of affected residents and households. Assistance will be provided through the applicable government programmes and support frameworks. Furthermore, the Ministry of Local Government has indicated that drop-in shelters will be available to meet the needs of residents.

“The Government of Jamaica’s response is being coordinated across the relevant social protection, disaster management, child protection, local government and community development agencies, with the immediate priority being to ensure that vulnerable residents have access to essential assistance while individual and household circumstances are properly assessed.”

World.title: ‘My soul is hurting’
World.content:
A screen grab of Opposition spokesperson on Youth and Human Rights Isat Buchanan making a plea for children found with firearms to have greater access to diversion. He was speaking during a sitting of the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act on Wednesday at Gordon House.

APPEALING not just as a legislator, but also from his own experience with past convictions, Opposition Spokesperson on Youth and Human Rights Isat Buchanan has urged the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act to make simple possession of a firearm or ammunition an offence that can be referred to child diversion, rather than leaving it solely to a judge’s discretion under Section 37 of the Act.

He argued that children caught in possession should be given a chance to avoid a lifelong criminal record.

But the proposal drew resistance from committee chairman Delroy Chuck and other members, who warned that making simple firearm possession a scheduled diversion offence could remove judicial discretion and allow criminals to exploit children as gun carriers, knowing they could be sent to diversion if caught.

The emotional exchange unfolded on Wednesday as the committee continued reviewing the matrices and submissions on the Child Diversion Act, 2018.

During the sitting, Buchanan repeatedly pressed his colleagues to consider what may have happened before a firearm ended up in a child’s hands.

“We are well aware that there are adults who are using children, even children below the age of criminal responsibility, to lock firearms, let’s call it that, and to carry. So if we are going to be in the business of being able to pull these children and divert them from this deviant behaviour, possession simpliciter has to be a space that we can divert them and put them in programmes. If we leave it to the discretion under section 37 in that contemplation, I’m afraid that there will be children who won’t be able to benefit,” he said.

Possession simpliciter, in this debate, means the simple fact of being found in possession of a firearm or ammunition, without necessarily alleging that the child used the weapon in another offence.

Buchanan wants that form of possession added to the First Schedule of the Child Diversion Act, which sets out offences that qualify as diversion offences. His argument is not that children should automatically be diverted in every firearm case. Rather, he wants firearm or ammunition possession placed among the offences that can be dealt with through the diversion framework, instead of relying solely on the separate discretion currently available to judges.

That distinction became the heart of the disagreement.

Section 37(2)of the Act already gives a court a route to diversion even when an offence is not listed in the First Schedule, providing that a court may make a child diversion referral order for any other offence where it is in the interest of justice.

This formed the basis of Chuck’s opposition to Buchanan’s plea.

He argued that this existing discretion is important because it allows the court to examine why the child had the gun, how the child came into possession of it, and whether the child was being used by someone else before deciding whether diversion is appropriate.

“The child may well, deliberately want to control a gun. A 16-year-old may well, deliberately want to control a gun, and having been found with the gun, he says, ‘put me on child diversion’, or automatically it has to go to child diversion, and my answer is that may not be an appropriate case for child diversion,” he argued.

He also warned that criminals could exploit diversion by using children as gun carriers, knowing they might avoid conviction.

However, Buchanan maintained that the possibility of coercion is precisely why simple possession should be included. His argument became increasingly personal as the discussion continued.

“At 47, chairman, I am still dealing with the past of convictions that have nothing to do with firearms. If you want this version of a Jamaican child to be better than me, if at all, if there’s any good in me, and you see, chairman, I’ve interfaced with you many times…all I’m asking is to empower the Jamaica Constabulary Force to drape up a boy, take the gun from him and let the don realise that you can’t buy enough guns that we can’t confiscate,” he said.

Buchanan was himself convicted in Jamaica in 1997, when he was 17, of possession of cocaine, dealing in cocaine and taking steps to export cocaine. He served 21 days in prison and paid a fine. In 2000, he was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to import cocaine and was sentenced to 10 years in prison, serving about eight and a half years. The Jamaican conviction was later expunged from his police record in 2014. The General Legal Council subsequently approved his application to practise law after considering his convictions, rehabilitation and character references.

Using his circumstance as an example, Buchanan reiterated that the purpose of child diversion was to give children another chance, not simply to punish them for behaviour that may have been shaped by their environment.

He eventually yielded the floor, visibly frustrated by the resistance to his proposal.

“If the Parliament doesn’t want to, or this committee doesn’t want to agree with me and we don’t want to put it to a vote and we don’t want to be brave enough to protect our children.. I will yield, chairman, but I’m hurt by this. I must tell you my soul is hurting,” he said.

Buchanan’s proposal did not face opposition only from Government members.

Opposition Senator Donna Scott Mottley said she had long had concerns about aspects of the Firearms Act but was uncomfortable supporting the change without evidence showing how children charged with firearm possession are currently being treated in the courts.

“I do agree that there should be some guidance to the judiciary. Whether or not it should be a part of the schedule is what concerns me. Because our discussion does disclose that the judges have discretion. And I wonder if it is not more that the judges should be aware of the policy of the administration as it pertains to children rather than for us to have it in the schedule,” she said.

She also warned that the proposal required more analysis, particularly because of the possibility that it could be abused by people with influence.

State minister in the ministry of National Security and Peace Juliet Cuthbert Flynn was more firmly opposed to including firearm possession in the Child Diversion Act’s First Schedule.

“We do have a gun problem in Jamaica, and so with this proliferation of guns, and, you know, just our culture, I think a standard has to be set. And these children, they might be young, but I think they all know right from wrong,” she said.

By the end of the exchange, the committee had not reached a consensus on Buchanan’s proposal.

Chuck suggested that the committee could record itself as divided rather than take a formal vote, while maintaining that the existing Section 37 mechanism could still protect children in appropriate firearm cases.

World.title: Le Conseil Constitutionnel censure la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs
World.content:
France's President Emmanuel Macron speaks to the press after a visit to the departmental fire and rescue operational center (CODIS) in Bordeaux. | Pool photo by Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS – Le Conseil Constitutionnel a rendu ce vendredi sa décision sur la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs et a annoncé censurer son article 1er, qui acte ladite interdiction pour les moins de 15 ans.

De fait, la décision rend caduque le principal objet de cette loi portée depuis plusieurs années par le président de la République.

Dans sa décision, les Sages estiment en effet que cet article, en instituant une interdiction "de portée générale" des réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans, porte "une atteinte disproportionnée à la liberté d'expression et de communication" qui n’est pas "adaptée, nécessaire et proportionnée à l’objectif poursuivi" : celui de protéger les mineurs en ligne.

World.title: French court shoots down social media ban for under 15s
World.content:
France's President Emmanuel Macron speaks to the press after a visit to the departmental fire and rescue operational center (CODIS) in Bordeaux. | Pool photo by Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images

A Constitutional court in France on Friday rejected a bill that would ban access to social media for minors under 15 years old in a major blow to French President Emmanuel Macron.

The Council of State, the top administrative court that advises the French government, said the restrictions in the bill disproportionately infringe on minors’ right to freedom of expression and communication. The bill also fails to put in place adequate protections for privacy, the court said.

Macron had made Europe’s would-be first social media ban a flagship policy of his second and final term, aiming to push the new restrictions to the top of the agenda of the European Union. Macron had hoped to implement a ban in September in time for an expected announcement by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen of EU-wide measures.

The government bill had passed through the legislative procedure after a lengthy back-and-forth earlier this summer. It was set to bring forward Europe's first social media age restrictions with Greece and Denmark following suit.

But Article 1 of the French bill essentially rendered it a blanket ban, not distinguishing enough between the risks of each social media platform nor the differences in vulnerability of minors themselves, the court said. It would also apply to online platforms that have not been proven to have risks to the health and safety of minors, said the court.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's military warned that similar incidents may happen again in the future. "While the Russian aggression in Ukraine is ongoing, the recurrence of such cases when a foreign unmanned aircraft enters or approaches Latvian airspace is possible," it said.

An air raid alert was declared in four eastern Latvian municipalities at around 4 a.m. local time. The military urged people to stay indoors and away from exterior walls.

After the drone was downed, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugāji village administration, told the Latvian Information Agency that the incident “caused no casualties,” as the drone wreckage fell in a “wooded area.”

There has been an uptick in similar incidents over recent months in countries close to the war-zone. A week ago, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Ukrainian-made drone crossed Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam.

World.title: Spain and Morocco reinforce border amid fears of fresh Ceuta migrant surge
World.content:
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers.

“We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.”

The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies.

Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

World.title: Farage’s victory over Binface won’t silence his critics
World.content:
But second-placed this time was Count Binface, a comedian with a trash can on his head who secured — by many thousands — his highest ever vote count in a palpable protest against Farage. None of Britain’s mainstream parties took part in the contest, branding it a circus.

The Reform UK leader’s refusal to turn up at the count to hear the result Friday — a move that would have seen him pictured alongside a cast of comedy characters — underlined the struggle for him to get back on the front foot he is used to contesting politics from.

More significantly, Farage’s triumph means that parliamentary investigations into his financial affairs will now resume. That could lead to another by-election — one in which serious rivals are far less likely to stand aside to allow Farage to face-off against a long list of no-hopers.

Count Binface waits with other candidates for the declaration of the winner of the Clacton by-election at Clacton Leisure Centre, eastern England, on Aug. 14, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

Labour MPs switched out their own leader in part because of Farage’s storming success at local elections in May, but the focus on this contest has also made it harder for Farage to land blows on Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

This week, Labour overtook Reform in POLITICO’s Poll of Polls after months on the back-foot for the governing party.

Snubbing the count

Clacton is Farage’s fiefdom. It was one of the most Brexit-voting constituencies in the country and was the place that first sent him to the Commons on his eighth time of trying.

World.title: Farage probe resumes after he wins Clacton by-election
World.content:
The by-election was called by Farage himself amid mounting scrutiny of his finances.

The right-wing populist has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, received before he became Clacton’s member of parliament in 2024, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

Farage has given varying explanations for the support, and billed this election — called at a dramatic press conference railing against the mainstream parties — as a “people versus the establishment” chance for Clacton’s voters to be his judge.

On Friday, the website of Parliament’s standards commissioner was updated to make clear that a paused probe into the Harborne donation has now been resumed.

That tees up the prospect of a further electoral test for Farage in Clacton if he is found to have broken the rules. The Conservatives, likely to be the most competitive challengers, have made clear that they would stand in such a contest.

Farage on Friday broke with tradition by declining to attend the result declaration at Clacton Leisure Centre.

World.title: Machthaber: Wolodymyr Selenskyj
World.content:
Wer regiert die Welt – und was treibt sie an? In unserem regelmäßigen Machthaber-Spezial geht es um die mächtigsten und umstrittensten Politikerinnen und Politiker unserer Zeit. Wir zeigen, wie sie denken, entscheiden – und was das für uns bedeutet. Eine Politikerin oder Politiker, ein Blick hinter die Kulissen der Macht.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Gordon Repinski und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig. This week and next, the Brussels Playbook Week Ender podcast is away for the summer holiday.
