World.title: Popular Lebanese restaurant Al Beiruti to open in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Al Beiruti, a popular Lebanese restaurant, is set to build its first Iraqi branch in Iraq Mall in Baghdad, adding another significant regional dining name to the capital’s growing restaurant scene.

The Baghdad inauguration will be the next chapter of Al Beiruti’s regional development, after previous launches in Jordan and Qatar, as well as its established presence in the UAE.

The restaurant announced that its Iraq Mall restaurant is about to open, with a local franchise arrangement handling the expansion.

Al Beiruti has become a renowned location for Lebanese food in the Middle East, providing both classic dishes and a more modern restaurant experience.

The menu includes Lebanese favorites, including manakish, fattoush, hummus, baba ghanouj, and grilled halloumi, as well as shawarma, wraps, and mixed grills. Larger meals include steak, chicken escalope, and grilled salmon.

Al Beiruti joins a growing number of international and regional food and beverage companies in Baghdad, as new malls and commercial expansions change the city’s retail and entertainment markets.

Iraq Mall has emerged as a focal point of that expansion, drawing new restaurants, boutiques, and entertainment ideas as consumer spending and private-sector investment continue to rise in the capital.

World.title: Baghdad and Erbil agree on unified digital customs system across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Baghdad and Erbil have agreed to fully adopt the digital ASYCUDA customs system across border crossings, with non-oil border earnings shared equally by the federal and Kurdistan regional governments.

The deal is a significant step toward standardizing customs processes across Iraq and addressing long-standing disagreements over border revenues and claimed import quantities.

ASYCUDA, designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), digitizes customs declarations, payments, and clearing processes, allowing authorities to better monitor products entering the nation and the income they earn.

Linking customs operations to Iraq’s banking and electronic payment systems may help limit the potential for underreporting, revenue leakage, and corruption at border crossings.

The deal comes as Iraq’s Finance Ministry and Central Bank work to digitize customs, payments, and government financial data in collaboration with UNCTAD.

A combined computerized customs system for Baghdad and Erbil might give more accurate revenue data while resolving one of the two governments’ ongoing financial issues.

The change is also significant for Iraq’s overall economy.

More open and uniform customs processes might facilitate cross-border commerce, boost governmental revenues, and enhance the business climate as Iraq pursues more foreign investment and closer integration with international markets.

World.title: Iraq’s Chief Justice Faiq Zidan meets Syrian President Al-Sharaa in Damascus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus on Thursday, marking another high-level Iraqi outreach to a neighboring Arab state as Baghdad seeks to bolster regional relations under rising security problems.

Al-Sharaa welcomed Zidan and an Iraqi delegation to the People’s Palace, which also included Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais.

According to the Syrian president, the talks focused on extending judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Syria, as well as resolving mutual concerns.

The visit also resulted in more practical conversations among the two nations’ judicial officials. Iraqi and Syrian authorities agreed to set up joint judicial committees to continue working on cases involving Syrian prisoners and other cross-border legal issues.

Zidan’s visit is crucial as he is one of the most prominent persons in Iraq’s state institutions, and it coincides with Baghdad’s increased diplomatic, security, and judicial interaction with its neighbors.

The Damascus meetings come after a separate Iraqi security group visited Riyadh, where senior military official Abdul Amir al-Shammari met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman.

Zidan had also just visited Ankara as part of a larger Iraqi effort to build ties with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Turkey.

That approach has become more urgent in light of the regional escalation involving Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

In late July, the United States and Saudi Arabia conducted synchronized attacks against locations used by Iran-aligned organizations in Iraq, after Riyadh accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones against Saudi energy infrastructure.

The incident put Baghdad under strong pressure to prevent armed organizations from exploiting Iraqi territory to launch assaults on neighboring nations and also highlighted the potential that militia activity may harm Iraq’s improved ties with Arab governments.

Against this setting, Zidan’s encounter with Al-Sharaa is significant beyond regular court cooperation.

Iraq and Syria share a long border and confront shared concerns such as terrorism, organized crime, prisoners, and cross-border security. Baghdad also has a strategic interest in preserving stable ties with Damascus, as Iraq strives to boost regional connections and prevent unrest from spilling over its borders.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s administration sees recent diplomatic efforts as part of a larger effort to strengthen Iraq’s ties with its neighbors while keeping the nation out of the developing conflict between Iran and its regional adversaries.

Baghdad has increasingly emphasized that choices on security, armament, and relations with neighboring governments must be made by Iraqi official authorities rather than armed groupings.

The travels to Damascus and Riyadh therefore convey an essential message: although Iran-aligned militias have exacerbated tensions between Iraq and certain of its neighbors, Iraqi official institutions are working directly with those nations to restore cooperation and avoid further escalation.

Strengthening judicial, diplomatic, and security ties with Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey might serve as an essential regional buffer for Iraq as it seeks to safeguard its sovereignty, control armed groups, and avoid being drawn further into the region’s crises.

World.title: Iraq’s Al-Shammari visits Riyadh to meet Saudi Defense Minister
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A top Iraqi security team has traveled to Riyadh for meetings with Saudi Arabia’s leadership, as Baghdad and the Kingdom work to improve security and military cooperation after weeks of heightened tensions in Iraq involving Iran-backed militias.

First Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman on Thursday to discuss military cooperation, regional developments, and increased coordination between the two nations.

According to reports from the visit, the conversations included cross-border drone concerns, air defense, and intelligence collaboration.

The conference is especially significant in light of the combined US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in Iraq on July 29.

Washington and Riyadh said the operation targeted Iran-backed terrorists’ weapons and logistical facilities in response to a series of drone assaults on Saudi oil installations that they said originated in Iraqi territory.

The strikes drastically escalated tensions between Baghdad and Riyadh, highlighting the Iraqi government’s problems in preventing armed groups from exploiting its territory to target neighboring nations.

Thursday’s visit indicates that both parties are now attempting to move beyond that conflict via direct military and intelligence collaboration.

Prince Khalid underlined Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Iraq’s security, stability, and economic growth, identifying it as an essential neighbor with whom the Kingdom has strong political and social relations.

The meetings in Riyadh follow Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali al-Humaidan’s visit to Baghdad last week, during which he met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and reiterated an offer for the Iraqi leader to visit Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

Al-Zaidi has frequently said that Iraqi soil should not be used to attack other nations and has stepped up efforts for weaponry to be put solely under state control.

The most recent Iraqi trip to Riyadh symbolizes more than just normal defense diplomacy. It is part of a joint effort by Baghdad and Saudi Arabia to restore security trust after the July escalation and prevent militia activities from dragging the two neighboring nations into conflict.

World.title: Rare blind fish found in underground river in Iraq’s Anbar desert
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security and environmental teams have discovered a fascinating underground water system deep under the dry Anbar desert, where rare eyeless fish thrive in total darkness.

The location is in the Al-Khasfa region near Haditha, and crews traveled through a remote desert cave and sinkhole system to access running groundwater hundreds of meters under the surface.

The expedition’s footage shows little, pale fish moving in the subterranean water in the lack of sunshine.

The fish have evolved to live in darkness by losing their eyes and pigmentation, giving them a characteristic white-to-pink look.

The crew traveled more than 500 meters into the cave system despite challenging terrain and low oxygen levels.

The difference between above- and underground has piqued interest: underneath what seems to be an isolated and very arid stretch of western Iraqi desert, there is flowing freshwater and a specialized ecology.

Initial investigations have also suggested a link between the subterranean water system and the Euphrates basin, with the watercourse possibly running for a long distance under the desert.

However, environmental experts have highlighted that the blind fish themselves are not a novel finding.

Qais Najeh, the chairman of the Anbar Environment Directorate, stated that experts first confirmed the occurrence of eyeless fish in Al-Khasfa in 2010.

Similar fish have also been discovered in subterranean water near the Sheik Hadid mausoleum in Haditha district.

According to experts, the fish may grow to be roughly 49 millimeters long and survive in rather steady groundwater temperatures ranging from 20 to 22 degrees Celsius.

Their lack of vision and pigmentation are adaptations to generations of living in perpetually dark subterranean habitats.

The recent mission is nonetheless noteworthy because it has refocused attention on one of Iraq’s least-known natural ecosystems, perhaps allowing scientists to better research the subterranean water network, its geology, and the creatures that rely on it.

The fish’s severely limited environment renders it vulnerable.

Changes in groundwater levels, pollution, or human intervention might endanger a population that has acclimated to highly particular subsurface circumstances.

The Al-Khasfa location offers a unique dimension to Anbar, a region best known for its wide western desert and the Euphrates.

Hidden under that terrain lies an environment few Iraqis have ever seen: flowing subterranean water that feeds fish who have evolved to survive their entire lives without sunshine.

World.title: Israel reopens once-closed West Bank settlement
World.content:
GANIM – Israel officially reopened the West Bank settlement of Ganim on Thursday, more than 20 years after it withdrew from the community, in a move emblematic of the current government’s policy of rapid settlement expansion.

The smell of freshly-poured asphalt hung in the air above Ganim’s new and only street, where future residents and their families — who had come to help with the move — smiled at the sight of their pre-fabricated homes.

“A month ago there was nothing here. A rocky mountain, barely any trees, barely any shade. We’re arriving now,” new resident Reut Baran, 35, told AFP in front of her new home.

In a nearby truck, dozens of brand new air conditioning units still in their boxes were waiting to be installed.

Matan Berkovitch, a 25-year-old who moved into the new settlement with his wife and child, said he was satisfied with the government’s policy towards settlements as he looked around a brand new home just connected to the electric grid.

“I’m happy to be part of a time like this where there are ministers in the government who support and guide us in the right direction and know how to get things done properly,” he said.

Berkovitch’s mother Carmit, who came from Jerusalem to move him in, said another one of her sons would soon study at the religious school in the settlement, and expressed pride at their active part in the settler movement.

“Here, this is the Land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said at the ceremony, after arriving by helicopter.

Ganim is one of four Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank that Israel evacuated under former prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan in 2005.

The move came partly because of their isolated location in the north of the territory among many Palestinian cities and villages.

Under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, settlement construction and expansion have soared, including with the official re-establishment of three of the four evacuated communities — Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh.

In Ganim, about two dozen pre-fabricated homes have already been installed, while steamrollers and other construction machinery busily created new space for future houses on the hillside on Thursday.

About a hundred people from Israel and other West Bank settlements attended the ceremony, including Katz and Yossi Dagan, head of the Israeli authority in charge of settlements in the northern West Bank.

“The era of evacuation is over — from here, we only build,” Dagan said.

In the valley below, Palestinians who spoke to AFP feared Ganim’s construction would make their lives harder, or even mean eventual displacement.

On both sides of the road leading to the settlement from Israel, the army has demolished stores in recent days and blocked several dirt roads to Palestinian communities with piles of rubble.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.

Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.

World.title: Carrick urges Man Utd to push for more signings to boost title bid
World.content:
London – Michael Carrick has urged Manchester United to splash the cash to keep pace with their Premier League title rivals.

United have spent around £85 million ($114 million) on Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Karl Darlow since the end of last season.

But that outlay pales in comparison to some of United’s fellow title contenders, with Manchester City, Arsenal and Chelsea all paying huge fees for high-profile signings.

Carrick knows United need more quality and depth if they are to challenge for a first English title since 2013, while also competing in the Champions League.

Remarkably, United have never spent more than £89.5 million on a single player — the fee paid for Paul Pogba in 2016.

And ahead of his first season as permanent United boss after a successful interim spell last term, Carrick called on the club’s hierarchy to push for more new recruits.

“I think we’ve done really good business and we’ve got really some top, top, top players,” Carrick told reporters on Thursday.

“We’re delighted with that. We always want to improve. We want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that. That never stops.”

Carrick led United to a third-place finish in the Premier League after he replaced the sacked Ruben Amorim.

But with United so far spending less than promoted sides Coventry and Ipswich, some fans are becoming restless as their Premier League opener at Hull on August 22 looms into view.

“Money’s money, I get that. It’s still about the football, and that’s where the competition lies,” Carrick said.

“Certainly the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever. For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, but we’ve got to keep pushing and push everything and every boundary that we can to be able to win again.”

Asked why United were not spending on the level of other clubs, Carrick added: “To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it.”

Having spent last season on loan with Barcelona, Marcus Rashford is back at United this week after returning from the World Cup.

Barcelona declined their option to buy the 28-year-old England forward and questions remain over his United future.

“He’s our player, and he’s a good player and he gives us something a little bit different in the group,” he said.

“Marcus can offer us so much. He has done, and he can do again, so in that respect it’s quite exciting.”

Several United players have backed the team to dethrone Arsenal as champions and the understated Carrick wouldn’t rule out a title push.

“We’ve definitely got the potential to achieve something really special,” he said.

“I’m not hiding from the fact, and we should aim to do that, but I can’t give you a definite answer on that.

“It’s certainly what we’re pushing to do because we have to, because that’s the club we are.”

World.title: Leicester’s Thai owners put troubled club up for sale: reports
World.content:
London – Former Premier League champions Leicester have been put up for sale by the club’s Thai owners, according to reports on Thursday.

Just 10 years after their fairytale Premier League title triumph, Leicester will play in English football’s third tier for only the second time in their history this season.

The Foxes, who won their first FA Cup in 2021, have endured a dire period featuring successive relegations from the Premier League in 2025 and the Championship in 2026.

Last season, they were docked six points after breaching the Football League’s profit and sustainability rules, sparking their slump into League One.

A BBC report on Thursday said Leicester’s Thai owners King Power — run by the Srivaddhanaprabha family — have commissioned a leading US investment bank to help find a buyer, with the club’s assets said to be listed at more than £200 million ($269 million).

King Power bought Leicester in a £35 million deal in 2010.

Aiyawatt Srivaddhanaprabha took over as Leicester chairman following the death of his father Vichai in a helicopter crash outside the club’s King Power stadium in 2019.

Following last season’s relegation, Aiyawatt said he should shoulder the “blame” for the club’s predicament but also stressed the “structure will change”.

Russell Martin’s side kick off their promotion bid with a trip to Notts County on Saturday.

World.title: 'Greatest threat': How India, Pakistan view each other; data lays bare deep animosity
World.content:
Nearly eight decades after the 1947 Partition of British India gave birth to two independent nations, deep-seated historical trauma, and territorial disputes that have led to multiple military confrontations continue to shape the mindset of citizens on both sides of the border.

As the two countries celebrate their independence, a major survey by the Pew Research Center reveals that an overwhelming majority of adults in both nuclear-armed rivals view the other as their single greatest geopolitical threat.

Conducted across South Asia between February and May 2026, the findings highlight a persistent, deep-rooted mutual hostility that shows little sign of thawing. These sentiments reflect not merely political disagreements, but deeply entrenched unfavourable opinions among general populations, extending into perceptions of global superpowers, regional allies, and the long-term prospects for bilateral peace.

' Greatest threat ': India and Pakistan point at each other

The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.

In India, 54% of respondents named Pakistan as the greatest threat to their country.

Conversely, 43% of Pakistanis identified India as their primary security threat.

The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.

For Indians, China is the next most cited threat at 21%. For Pakistanis, Israel and the US each register at 24% as major threats â though still far below India.

These threat perceptions align closely with how each public judges the otherâs commitment to peace.





Most Indians believe their own government and people are committed to good bilateral relations, but a majority say Pakistanâs government and people are not.

Pakistanis mirror this: they express confidence in their own sideâs commitment but doubt Indiaâs.

Mutual hostility runs deep

The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.

Nearly nine in 10 Pakistanis have an unfavourable view of India, with 73% describing their opinion as 'very unfavourable'.

The sentiment cuts across demographic groups, suggesting that hostility toward India is not confined to any particular section of Pakistani society.

The picture in India is similarly bleak. As many as 78% of Indians have an unfavourable view of Pakistan, including 65% who hold a very unfavourable opinion. There is, however, a notable internal divide in India. Indian Muslims are somewhat more favorable toward Pakistan (21%) than Indian Hindus (6%), and they are also less likely to name Pakistan as their top threat (34% vs 57% among Hindus).

The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.

Pew's polling also shows that this is not a temporary shift in sentiment.

Indian views of Pakistan have remained overwhelmingly negative for more than a decade, with the share expressing a favourable opinion never rising above 20% since 2013.

Historical Pew surveys also show that Pakistanis have long held predominantly negative views of India. Pakistani respondents expressing favourable views of India have generally ranged from single digits to around one-third.

Lack of trust

The survey further suggests that hostility is not simply about how Indians and Pakistanis perceive each other. It also extends to whether they believe the other side genuinely wants better relations.

A clear pattern emerges: people tend to believe that their own government and population are committed to good bilateral relations, while doubting the intentions of the other side.

When asked whether the Indian and Pakistani governments and people are committed to good relations with each other, the clear pattern is that people only have faith in their own country Pew Research report

A majority of Indians believe both the Indian government and Indian people are committed to maintaining good relations with Pakistan.

But a majority of Pakistanis reject that assessment, saying the Indian government and people are not committed to good relations.

The mirror image appears in Pakistan.

Beneath the geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.

A majority of Pakistanis say their government and people want good relations with India.

Most Indians, however, believe Pakistan's government and people are not committed to improving ties. About a quarter of Indian respondents were unsure.

This mutual lack of trust creates a difficult cycle: each side sees itself as willing to improve relations while viewing the other as unwilling to reciprocate.

Indian Muslims again stand apart to some degree. Around a third say the Pakistani government and people are committed to good relations, significantly higher than the corresponding share among Indian Hindus.

How Bangladesh, Sri Lanka view the rivals

The Pew findings become even more revealing when India and Pakistan are placed alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

Of the four South Asian countries surveyed, Sri Lanka is the only country that receives more positive than negative ratings from respondents in all three of the others.

The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations.

India, meanwhile, has the widest range of perceptions.

Sri Lankans are overwhelmingly positive toward India, with 79% expressing a favourable opinion. In Bangladesh, 42% view India favourably. In Pakistan, however, the figure plunges to just 7%.

India is also seen as Sri Lanka's most important ally by a clear majority: 63% of Sri Lankan respondents name India.

The picture is very different in Bangladesh and Pakistan, where India is most often identified as the greatest threat.

Views of Prime Minister Narendra Modi follow a broadly similar pattern. Seventy percent of Sri Lankans express confidence in PM Modi to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 42% in Bangladesh and 4% in Pakistan.

The survey also finds that Pakistan is not universally viewed negatively across South Asia.

Fifty-seven percent of Sri Lankans and 54% of Bangladeshis have a favourable opinion of Pakistan, compared with only 8% of Indians.

Bangladesh itself receives broadly positive views in Pakistan and Sri Lanka: 66% of Pakistanis and 56% of Sri Lankans express favourable opinions of Bangladesh. Only about a quarter of Indians do so.

Sri Lanka emerges as the region's relative outlier. Around half or more of respondents in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh view the island nation positively, while significantly fewer hold negative views.

Divergent worldviews

The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations to the way each country views the global order.

For Indians, Russia remains a particularly important and popular partner. Thirty-six percent identify Russia as India's most important ally, while 16% name the United States.

Russia's favourable image in India is particularly striking. Fifty-eight percent of Indians have a favourable opinion of Russia, while 51% express confidence in Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Pakistanis are considerably less positive: 39% have a favourable view of Russia and only 32% express confidence in Putin.

India's relationship with the United States is also reflected in public opinion. Indians are substantially more favourable toward the US than Pakistanis are and are more likely to express confidence in US President Donald Trump.

The picture is almost completely reversed when it comes to China.

An overwhelming 90% of Pakistanis have a favourable view of China, while 83% express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Three-quarters of Pakistanis identify China as their country's most important ally.

Saudi Arabia is a distant second, named by 12%.

In India, however, only around a quarter of respondents view China or Xi positively. Even Indian Muslims, who are more favourable toward China than Indian Hindus, remain negative toward both China and its president on balance.

Two countries, two very different worlds

Nearly 80 years after Partition, the survey suggests that the India-Pakistan rivalry remains deeply embedded not only in government policy and military strategy, but also in public perceptions.

The most striking finding may therefore not be that Indians and Pakistanis dislike each other. It is that both overwhelmingly believe the other side sees them as the problem.

That mutual conviction â reinforced by decades of conflict, competing national narratives and geopolitical rivalry â remains one of the biggest barriers to changing the relationship between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.

Yet beneath these geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.

Both populations believe their own side is committed to better relations, while doubting the intentions of the other.

World.title: 'Cannot imagine': Rajnath Singh's sharp 'Gandhi surname' attack on Rahul Gandhi over PM hug jibe
World.content:
Defence minister

has hit back at Congress leader

over his remarks on Prime Minister

and the government's foreign policy, calling them âpetty and condemnableâ and warning that such language could damage democratic discourse.

Singh said he was particularly upset that the comments came from the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. He accused Gandhi of lowering the dignity associated with the post and questioned whether such conduct was appropriate for someone holding a key constitutional position.

"The remarks made by LoP Rahul Gandhi on PM Narendra Modi and India's foreign policy yesterday are petty and condemnable. It is painful for me personally, too.

In my long political life, I had never seen such indecent and unimaginable conduct from any LoP. Such conduct is a grave sign of a threat to a healthy democracy," Singh said.

The defence minister also defended Modi's record as Prime Minister and his standing abroad, while arguing that political differences should not lead to what he described as disrespectful remarks.

"Rahul Gandhi might have frustration with PM in his mind, but such indecent remarks are unacceptable, especially when PM Modi has been a Prime Minister who has brought prestige to India nationally and internationally, and paved the way for Viksit Bharat. "

"In 12 years, working with full dedication, he did not take any leave.





Such indecent remarks against such a PM pain every Indian," he said.

Singh then turned his criticism towards the Congress, questioning whether the party could continue to claim the legacy of several of India's prominent leaders after Gandhi's remarks.

"I would also like to humbly tell the

Congress party

that after such language and conduct, can they have any claim over the legacy of Lal-Bal-Pal and Gandhi, Patel and Nehru, from Subhas Babu to Rajendra Babu and Shastri ji and Narasimha Rao ji to Pranab Mukherjee?" Rajnath Singh said.

He further accused Gandhi of not only targeting Modi but also damaging India's image and the dignity of the Leader of Opposition's office.

"With this conduct, Rahul Gandhi has not only insulted PM Narendra Modi but also the international prestige of India. He has shredded the dignity of the post of Lok Sabha LoP. I cannot even imagine that someone with the Gandhi surname can make such a shameful remark."

The exchange followed remarks made by Gandhi at the Congress's Rachnatmak Congress National Convention in New Delhi on Thursday.

Gandhi criticised the government's approach to foreign policy and argued that India's international relations should be driven by national interest rather than personal relationships between political leaders.

"I don't know where it came from; this idea got into their heads. I don't know who put it there or where it came from, the idea that foreign policy means hugging politicians. I was young. We went to America.

Since we're talking about expressions, I'll share this. We went to America. I was twelve years old. Priyanka, myself, my mother, and my grandmother - my grandmother was the Prime Minister. There was a state dinner - an official dinner.

My grandmother and mother went to the official dinner," he said.

He added, "You aren't just visiting a friend's house. In this role, the Prime Minister of India doesn't engage in mere friendship.

They have no interest in friendship; their job is to protect the country."

Gandhi also accused the Modi government of damaging India's foreign policy, using the ongoing conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel as an example.

"War broke out in Iran. For India - had it recognised its own strength and had its leader been someone like Indira Gandhi--this presented the greatest opportunity in the world. What kind of opportunity? Iran was our old friend, America was our friend, and Russia was our friend.

We could have stepped up, become relevant, and leveraged these friendships. But what actually happened? Nothing of the sort. Instead, Pakistan stepped in and took our place; Pakistan became the mediator, while India and Modi-ji simply looked on," he said.

Rahul Gandhi claimed he receives "information directly from Modi ji's office these days; there is a full-blown revolt going on inside".He also referred to certain claims in videos on social media about China's actions concerning patrolling along the LAC in a border area of Arunachal Pradesh.

He also raised allegations concerning Chinese activity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and accused the government of pressuring the media not to report certain claims.

"In our patrolling areas--specifically in Arunachal--China blocked us from patrolling. They essentially said, 'Look, all that is fine--it is indeed your land--but you cannot patrol here.' Rajnath Singh, Amit Shah, and Narendra Modi have been completely deflated.

They are calling up all the media editors, telling them, 'Don't publish this in your newspapers; suppress the story.' They are causing direct harm to the country without a second thought," he said.

Gandhi also revisited the dispute over India's handling of the border situation with China following the Galwan clash.

In his message to soldiers on the eve of Independence Day, Rajnath said India had reduced its dependence on defence imports while strengthening indigenous manufacturing under the

The union minister further highlighted recent tests and developments in indigenous defence technology, including the MIRV-equipped Advanced Agni missile, Rudram-II air-to-surface missile, Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile and Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket.

91% indegenisation in Army ammunitions

World.title: Gandhi's letter to India, as told through TOI
World.content:
A fast unto death announced by

in Puneâs Yerawada jail in 1932 was to change the course of Indiaâs political history. Imprisoned for the Civil Disobedience Movement, Gandhi announced the fast in a Sept 13 letter to British PM Ramsay MacDonald that was shared with the press.

His aim was to oppose a separate electorate for Dalits, proposed under the Communal Award of August 1932.

âI have to resist your decision with my life,â Gandhi wrote, saying his fast would begin on Sept 20. âAs a man of religion that I hold myself to be, I have no other course left open to me.â

The award classified Dalits as a minority whose representatives would be elected only by Dalit voters, just as Muslims, Christians and Sikhs would elect their own representatives. Gandhi believed this would divide Hindu society; BR Ambedkar supported it as a safeguard for Dalit political representation

Gandhi acknowledged that he might be wrong. If his judgement was âwarpedâ, he wrote, his death would be âa penance for my errorâ and would lift the burden from those who had âchild-like faithâ in his wisdom.

His week-long fast led to the Poona Pact, negotiated by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Ambedkar and accepted by Gandhi. It abandoned a separate electorate but reserved seats for Dalits within the general electorate, becoming a milestone in Dalit representation and a precursor to reservations for SCs and STs in independent India.

Suspending Satyagraha

Gandhi also used a letter to the press to announce the suspension of Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act.





Writing on July 21, 1919, he asked satyagrahis to âswallow the bitter pillâ and halt their campaign after protests had turned violent.

The act allowed the colonial government to detain political prisoners for two years without trial. Gandhiâs campaign against it, launched in March 1919, was his first nationwide political mobilisation after returning from South Africa. Despite his appeals for peaceful hartals, fasts and prayers, violence erupted in several places.

Gandhi was prevented from entering Punjab and arrested; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on April 13 made the situation explosive.

Attacks on police stations and railway property, and deadly clashes between protesters and authorities, led him to pause civil disobedience.

For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Boseâs different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941

In the July letter, published under the headline âSATYAGRAHA. Civil Resistance Suspendedâ, Gandhi disclosed that the governor of Bombay had conveyed âa grave warningâ from the Government of India that renewed civil disobedience could threaten public security.

Writing from Mani Bhavan in Bombay, Gandhi conceded that the suspension was painful. Yet he remained unyielding on the law: âSatyagrahi will pay for its removal with their lives if it cannot be removed by lesser means.â He also warned the Raj: âIf my occasional Civil Resistance be a lighted match, Rowlatt legislationâ¦is a thousand matches scattered throughout India.â

For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Boseâs different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941: âWith me, no doubt non-violence is an end in itself, though it is also a means for the attainment of the freedom of the country.â

A year earlier, he had underlined its voluntary nature: âNon-violence cannot be imposed upon anyone. It has to come from within.

â

The South Africa Years

Gandhiâs letters to the editor predated his emergence as a leader of Indiaâs freedom struggle. During his 21 years in South Africa, where he first used Satyagraha as a method of resistance, he repeatedly drew attention to discriminatory laws against Indians

In a Dec 19, 1901 letter, he described the restrictions in the Transvaal, where Indians could not hold land, were required to live and trade only in designated areas, and were barred from footpaths.

In the Orange River Colony, he wrote, an Indian could not even enter without special permission, except as a domestic servant or labourer.

After returning to India, he continued to write about the poor conditions of Indians legally settled in South Africa. In an Aug 29, 1919 letter, he blamed the âgreedy Europeans of Natalâ for importing Indian indentured labour at miserably low wages while ignoring local Zulu workers, all in pursuit of âenormous profitsâ.

Cow Slaughter And Eid

Gandhiâs correspondence also addressed social fractures, particularly Hindu-Muslim relations. In a 1919 letter written around Bakrid, he recounted a conversation with Maulana Abdul Bari of Lucknowâs Firangi Mahal, a prominent supporter of the Khilafat Movement.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Gandhi quoted the Maulana as saying: âIslam will fall to pieces if it ever takes and never givesâ¦. If we take from you, we must give to you.â Abdul Bari had urged his followers to abstain from cow slaughter.

On Bakrid, he sent Gandhi a telegram: âIn celebration of Hindu-Muslim unity, no cow sacrifices in Firangi-Mahal this Bakri-Id.â

More than a century later, these letters are more than historical records. They reveal Gandhi not only as a politician confronting colonial power but as a public figure wrestling with representation, violence, communal division and moral responsibility. Through TOIâs pages, his words travelled beyond the immediate battles of the freedom struggle, leaving an intimate record of how he tried to shape public opinion â and India itself.

World.title: GOBARdhan scheme: How India plans to turn cattle dung, crop waste and garbage into fuel
World.content:
For years, India has spoken about the enormous amount of energy locked inside its agricultural residue, cattle dung and organic waste. The challenge has been turning that potential into a commercially viable industry.

Now, the government is making one of its most serious attempts yet.

The Union Cabinet on August 6 approved GOBARdhan, the National Circular Bioenergy Scheme, with a total outlay of Rs 23,731 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36. The scheme has set a target of ten-fold increase in domestic production of Compressed Biogas (CBG) and brings together everything from assured demand and pricing to capital assistance, pipelines and credit under a single framework.

The idea sounds simple: take waste that would otherwise be burnt, dumped or left to decompose, and process it in a biogas plant and turn it into fuel that can be used much like natural gas.

The initiative aims to increase nation's CBG production

But the government's ambition goes much further.

It wants villages to become centres of energy production, farmers to become suppliers to the energy industry and organic waste to become an economic resource rather than a disposal problem.





The question is whether the new scheme can solve the problems that have held back India's CBG industry for years.

What exactly is GOBARdhan?

GOBARdhan is not an entirely new idea.

The initiative was originally launched in 2018 under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen as a waste-management programme. Its focus was on converting cattle dung, kitchen waste, crop residue and other organic material into biogas and bio-slurry, helping villages manage waste while generating useful products.

The 2026 version is much broader.

The government has now positioned GOBARdhan as a national framework for the Compressed Biogas industry, bringing several existing measures under one umbrella and placing the scheme under the ministry of petroleum and natural gas.

These include the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) initiative, the Market Development Assistance scheme for organic manure, the Biomass Aggregation Machinery scheme, pipeline infrastructure support and central financial assistance for CBG plants.

In simple terms, the government is moving from âhow do we manage organic waste?â to âhow do we build an industry around it?â

How does waste become fuel?

The process begins with organic material such as cattle dung, agricultural residue, press mud from sugar mills and municipal organic waste.

This material is fed into an anaerobic digester, where microorganisms break it down in the absence of oxygen and produce biogas. The raw biogas contains methane along with carbon dioxide and other impurities.

The gas is then purified to remove these impurities and compressed.

Production process of CBG

The resulting Compressed Biogas, or CBG, has properties comparable to natural gas and can be used within the existing gas ecosystem. This is one of its biggest advantages: India does not necessarily need to create an entirely separate fuel infrastructure for it.

The process also produces organic material that can be processed into fertiliser.

That means one plant can potentially create several economic outputs:

Waste â CBG + organic manure + rural jobs + additional income opportunities

This is the circular economy the government is trying to build.

Why does India need CBG?

The biggest reason is energy security.

India currently imports nearly 50% of its natural gas requirement, according to the government's latest GOBARdhan backgrounder. That leaves the country exposed to international gas prices, shipping disruptions and geopolitical shocks.

Domestic CBG offers a way to produce a portion of that gas from resources that India already has in abundance.

Importance of CBG for India

The government estimates that lower dependence on imported fossil fuels under GOBARdhan could eventually save more than Rs 40,000 crore in foreign exchange.

That is a government projection rather than a guaranteed saving, but it illustrates the scale of the ambition.

There is also an environmental argument.

Agricultural residue that is not economically used can become a waste-disposal problem, while organic waste dumped in landfills can generate methane and other emissions. Converting such material into fuel gives it an economic value while potentially reducing waste-related emissions.

For farmers, the attraction is an additional market for residue and dung.

For energy companies, it is another source of domestic gas.

For the government, it is a way of connecting waste management, rural development and energy security.

India has tried CBG before. So what went wrong?

This is where the GOBARdhan story becomes more complicated.

India's push for CBG production predates the new scheme by several years.

The government launched SATAT in October 2018, with an ambitious target of establishing 5,000 CBG plants producing 15 million tonnes a year.

But the industry struggled to scale at the pace initially envisaged.

A 2022 review by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas found that against the target of 5,000 plants by 2023-24, only 40 had been set up at that point. The committee also highlighted problems with financing, multiple approvals, pricing and feedstock availability.

One of the biggest problems was that a CBG plant needs much more than a piece of land and a digester.

It needs a reliable supply of biomass, equipment to collect and transport that biomass, storage facilities, technology, financing and, crucially, a buyer for the gas.

One big complication with agricultural residue is that it is seasonal.

Crop waste may be available in large quantities for only a few months of the year, forcing plants to invest in storage and logistics if they want to operate throughout the year. The parliamentary committee specifically flagged this issue.

Bansal estimates that India generates around 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue annually, suggesting that the problem is not a shortage of biomass but the difficulty of turning dispersed and seasonal supplies into a reliable, year-round feedstock chain.

GOBARdhan's focus on biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure and district-level planning is therefore critical to making plants operate at high utilisation.

There was also a financing problem.

Banks and investors were wary of projects whose revenues depended on uncertain feedstock supplies and evolving CBG prices. The committee noted concerns over the low internal rate of return of plants and called for more remunerative pricing.

This is the gap GOBARdhan is now attempting to close.

Kapil Bansal, partner, energy transition and decarbonization at EY-Parthenon India, told TOI that the biggest change is that GOBARdhan tackles the entire CBG value chain rather than individual bottlenecks.

Earlier measures addressed issues such as biomass aggregation, organic manure, pipelines and financial assistance separately, but developers continued to face uncertainty around demand, pricing and financing.

âThe sector is moving from a project-led approach to a market-led approach, where demand, pricing and financing visibility are available before developers invest,â Bansal said.

The combination of assured offtake, a ten-year pricing framework, capital assistance, pipeline connectivity and credit guarantees, he said, should improve project bankability and give investors greater confidence.

What changes under the Rs 23,731-crore scheme?

The government has structured GOBARdhan around six major components, each designed to address a different weakness in the existing CBG ecosystem.

New changes introduced in the upgraded scheme

1. Assured demand for CBG

Perhaps the biggest change is that producers will have greater certainty that someone will buy their gas.

City Gas Distribution companies will procure CBG in line with a notified obligation that rises from 3% in FY 2026-27 to 4% in FY 2027-28 and 5% from FY 2028-29 onwards for the CNG transport and PNG domestic segments.

This creates a predictable demand signal.

For investors, that matters because a plant is much easier to finance when there is greater clarity about who will buy its output.

2. A stable price

GOBARdhan introduces a government-backed CBG price of Rs 2,110 per MMBTU, with a minimum ten-year framework.

The objective is to give producers greater revenue visibility and make projects more attractive to investors and lenders.

This directly addresses one of the problems identified in the earlier CBG ecosystem: uncertainty over whether the economics of a plant would work after it was built.

3. Capital assistance

Eligible greenfield CBG projects will receive capital assistance of up to Rs 2 crore for every tonne per day (TPD) of installed capacity.

Importantly, the support is not restricted to the core plant.

It can also cover critical assets linked to feedstock aggregation, organic manure processing and value addition. Brownfield projects expanding existing capacity will also be eligible.

That matters because the economics of CBG depend on the entire supply chain, not just the digester.

4. Pipelines to connect plants with buyers

A CBG plant cannot be commercially successful if its gas cannot reach the market.

GOBARdhan therefore provides for cluster-based and standalone pipeline infrastructure connecting plants with trunk pipelines and City Gas Distribution networks.

The aim is to reduce evacuation costs, improve reliability and expand the market available to producers.

5. Credit guarantees

The scheme also attempts to solve the financing problem through a dedicated credit guarantee mechanism.

By sharing part of the lending risk, the government hopes banks will be more willing to finance MSME-based CBG projects.

This could bring smaller companies, cooperatives, women entrepreneurs and first-time developers into an industry that has so far been dominated by larger players and institutional initiatives.

6. A district-level ecosystem fund

The final component focuses on the problem that often receives the least attention: where will the feedstock come from?

The CBG Ecosystem Challenge Fund will support biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure, district-level development plans, technology adoption, process improvements and organic manure value addition.

The objective is to build the local ecosystem around each plant rather than treating the plant as an isolated piece of infrastructure.

What does this mean for farmers?

The government's larger pitch is that farmers should become participants in India's energy economy.

Crop residue and cattle dung can become feedstock for CBG plants, creating potential additional income for farmers and local aggregators.

The benefit does not stop with the gas.

Scheme to empower the farmers

The material left after the biogas production process can be processed into organic fertilisers such as Fermented Organic Manure and Liquid Fermented Organic Manure.

This creates a second revenue stream while returning nutrients to agriculture.

The government has already been supporting this side of the industry through the Market Development Assistance scheme. Together, these measures are intended to create a cycle in which agricultural and livestock waste becomes an input for both energy and agriculture.

That is why GOBARdhan is being presented as more than an energy scheme.

It is also a rural infrastructure and waste-management programme.

How big is India's CBG industry today?

This is perhaps the most revealing part of the government's latest numbers.

As of August 6, the GOBARdhan Unified Registration Portal had recorded 1,908 registered CBG/Bio-CNG plants. Of these, 217 had been commissioned, while another 339 were under construction, according to the government.

The numbers show both the opportunity and the problem.

Current capacity of CBG in the country

There is considerable interest in building CBG capacity, but the number of plants actually operating remains far below the number registered.

The government says the various initiatives introduced over recent years have helped commission more than 200 CBG plants and establish the initial production and offtake ecosystem. GOBARdhan is now intended to take that foundation to a national scale.

In other words, the new scheme is not starting from zero.

It is an attempt to make the existing pipeline of projects commercially viable and scalable.

Can GOBARdhan finally make CBG commercially viable?

That remains the biggest question.

Government support can reduce the initial cost of a plant and create a market for its gas. But it cannot eliminate the fundamental logistical challenge of collecting biomass.

Bansal cautioned that commercial viability will still vary from project to project because feedstock costs, transportation distances, plant utilisation and financing costs will continue to determine returns.

âA project with reliable access to high-quality feedstock can achieve significantly better plant efficiency and returns than a project relying on dispersed or lower-yield biomass resources,â he said.

A plant located far from its feedstock source may face high transportation costs. Agricultural residue is seasonal. Competing uses for biomass can raise prices. Plants also need to maintain reliable operations and consistent gas quality.

These problems were highlighted by the Parliamentary Standing Committee even before the latest scheme was announced. It pointed to the uneven availability of feedstock, the need for storage and the importance of synchronising CBG production with the national gas grid.

This is why the six components of GOBARdhan matter together.

A subsidy without a buyer does not solve the problem.

A buyer without a pipeline does not solve the problem.

A pipeline without reliable feedstock does not solve the problem.

And a plant with all three still needs affordable financing and efficient operations.

GOBARdhan is effectively trying to solve all of these problems at the same time.

What could India get by 2035-36?

The government has set an ambitious ten-year vision.

It expects GOBARdhan to deliver nearly ten-fold growth in domestic CBG production, attract large private investment, create rural employment and expand the organic fertiliser economy.

It also projects lower fossil-fuel use and significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

These are targets and government projections, not guaranteed outcomes.

The more important test will be whether the number of operating plants grows alongside registrations, whether plants remain viable after initial assistance and whether farmers and local businesses actually benefit from the new demand for biomass.

If that happens, GOBARdhan could change the economics of waste in India.

Instead of paying to collect, transport and dispose of organic waste, communities could potentially build local industries around it.

The bigger picture

India's CBG journey has already shown that having abundant biomass is not enough.

The country had an ambitious 5,000-plant target under SATAT, but financing constraints, feedstock logistics, approvals, pricing uncertainty and weak project economics slowed the industry's development.

GOBARdhan is the government's attempt to address those weaknesses through one national framework.

At Rs 23,731 crore over ten years, the bet is substantial.

But the real significance of the scheme is not the size of the allocation. It is the attempt to connect India's farms, villages, waste streams and gas networks into one economic system.

If the model works, cattle dung and crop residue will no longer be treated merely as waste.

They could become feedstock for a domestic fuel industry, while the by-products return to farms as organic fertiliser.

That would turn the government's âwaste-to-wealthâ slogan into a functioning business model.

The challenge is making sure the economics work beyond the subsidy period.

For GOBARdhan, success will therefore not be measured simply by how much money is spent or how many plants are registered. It will be measured by how many plants actually operate, how much CBG they produce, whether farmers earn from supplying biomass and whether India's dependence on imported gas falls.

India has plenty of waste. GOBARdhan now has to prove that it can turn that waste into a dependable source of energy, income and economic value.

World.title: Independence Day: Minister Bindu Krishna to hoist national flag in Kozhikode
World.content:
Minister for Labour, Animal Husbandry, and Women and Child Development, Bindu Krishna, will hoist the national flag at the district-level Independence Day celebrations at Captain Vikram Ground in West Hill in Kozhikode city on Saturday (August 15).

Officials said preparations across Kozhikode district were now complete for the event. ​The official proceedings will commence at 8.40 a.m. when the platoons assemble at the parade baseline. The Parade Commander will take charge at 8.45 a.m., followed by the arrival of the District Police Chief (Kozhikode City) at 8:50 a.m. to receive the parade salute.

At 8.53 a.m., the Deputy Inspector General of Police and the District Police Chief (Kozhikode Rural) will arrive, followed by the District Collector at 8.55 a.m.

​Ms. Krishna is scheduled to arrive at 8:58 a.m., where she will be formally received by the District Collector along with the City and Rural Police Chiefs. The parade will then present a general salute before the Minister hoists the national flag at 9 a.m.

​A total of 22 platoons will take part in the parade, featuring personnel from the police, Excise, Fire and Rescue Services, Forest department, National Cadet Corps, Scouts and Guides, and Student Police Cadets.

​At 9.02 a.m., accompanied by the Parade Commander, the Minister will inspect the parade. Following her official Independence Day address, Ms. Krishna will present awards to the best-performing platoons.

​The ceremonial parade will conclude with the National Anthem, paving the way for a series of cultural programmes performed by local school students.

(The writer, Aleesha V. Joseph, is an intern with The Hindu)

World.title: HSBC India opens new branch in Thiruvananthapuram
World.content:
HSBC India opened its new branch in the capital city on Thursday. This will be the second branch for the bank in Kerala after its branch in Kochi. Although the bank earlier had a branch located at Vellayambalam, it was closed down some years ago. At an interaction with mediapersons after the inauguration, Sandeep Batra, Head of Wealth and Premier Banking, HSBC India, said that Kerala has a strong base of globally connected families and entrepreneurs backed by one of India’s most significant NRI communities.

He said that the branch in the city is part of 20 new branches that it has opened across the country after securing approval from the RBI in January 2025. “Kerala’s economy is poised for significant transformation and banks are expected to play a key role in supporting growth through active participation in developmental initiatives and financing of large-scale infrastructure,” he said.

World.title: Headmaster transferred, inquiry ordered after video of school students consuming alcohol surfaces
World.content:
The Headmaster of a government school in Kanniyakumari district has been transferred and departmental inquiry has been initiated following the circulation of video on social media purportedly showing school students allegedly consuming alcohol on the school premises.

Kanniyakumari District Collector M. Prathap told The Hindu that the headmaster of the school had been transferred and a departmental inquiry had been initiated. He added that the incident was reported to have occurred a few weeks ago after a half-day special class.

Mr. Prathap further noted that officials from the health department, counsellors and others have visited the school on Friday and checked with the students. He added that the person who had provided alcohol to the students had been identified and would be remanded shortly.

According to police, Thuckalay police has registered a case against the individual who had provided alcohol to the students. The case was registered under Section 77 of Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act and Section 123 of BNS Act.

World.title: Experts seek time-bound plan for all-round development of Kalyana Karnataka
World.content:
A round-table conference of experts, academics, development activists, and representatives from the seven districts of Kalyana Karnataka has unanimously called for a scientific and time-bound action plan for the comprehensive development of the region, with a long-term vision of five to 10 years.

The conference, organised by the Kalyana Karnataka Horata Samiti at Sharnbasva University in Kalaburagi on Friday, discussed the region’s present development status in light of the Govindrao Committee report on regional imbalance and deliberated on the measures required to accelerate its development. It was chaired by Basavaraj Deshmukh, honorary president of the Samiti, while its founder-president Lakshman Dasti coordinated the proceedings.

Experts and development activists from Bidar, Kalaburagi, Raichur, Yadgir, Ballari, Koppal, and Vijayanagara districts examined the development indicators and recommendations of the Govindrao Committee and compared them with the parameters adopted in the earlier Nanjundappa Committee report.

Speakers expressed concern over what they described as the lack of clarity in the Govindrao Committee report for formulating development programmes. Raichur-based development activist Razak Ustad said the provision of ₹42,000 crore for the development of 172 backward taluks did not appear to provide a clear scientific basis for prioritising development interventions in the region. He urged the government to formulate a time-bound action plan based on clear development indicators.

Basavaraj Kalasa, president of the Raichur AIIMS Struggle Committee, called for a united effort by political leaders and development organisations across the seven districts to put pressure on the government for a comprehensive and long-term development plan.

Educationist Dhanraj of Gangavathi stressed the need to improve the quality of primary education in Kalyana Karnataka through planning and implementation at the grassroots level. Former HKCCI president Umakant Nigudagi called for the effective implementation of the special status granted to the region and sought a separate industrial policy to generate employment.

The conference resolved that the government should prepare a scientific five- to 10-year action plan for the overall development of Kalyana Karnataka. The Kalyana Karnataka Region Development Board should, apart from the routine budgetary schemes of the government, give special attention to neglected sectors, villages, and taluks and prepare a separate five-year action plan for measurable and time-bound progress.

The participants also decided to seek an early meeting with the Chief Minister through a delegation comprising representatives from the seven districts and Ministers from the region to press for comprehensive development measures.

The conference called for measures to create employment opportunities in both agricultural and non-agricultural sectors to prevent migration from the region. It also sought separate industrial, agricultural, and education policies for Kalyana Karnataka.

The participants extended support to the ongoing demand for an AIIMS in Raichur and resolved to urge Ministers and legislators from the seven districts to demonstrate collective political will and lead an all-party delegation to the Centre. They also decided to support the demand for adequate compensation to the Karanja project-affected people in Bidar.

The conference further called for development programmes to be taken up in accordance with the indicators suggested by the Govindrao Committee, with emphasis on human development, education, agriculture, and non-agricultural sectors. It also sought pressure on the Union government to establish a railway divisional headquarters in Kalaburagi.

Mr. Dasti said the region needed a clear development roadmap rather than isolated schemes. “The development of Kalyana Karnataka has to be taken up through a time-bound and scientific action plan covering all seven districts. The seven districts must come together and place their demands before the government with a united voice,” he said.

World.title: Government taking comprehensive reforms to curb exam paper leaks, protect youths’ future: President on the eve of 80th Independence Day
World.content:
President Droupadi Murmu addressed the nation on August 14, 2026, on the eve of the 80th Independence Day. The National Song Vande Mataram was played before and after the speech along with the National Anthem.

Underlining that students are the “architects of India’s future,” President Droupadi Murmu on Friday (August 14, 2026) said the government is taking comprehensive steps to reform public examinations to completely curb paper leaks and unfair means, making the system transparent, secure, and trustworthy.

In her address to the nation, the President stressed that just as government and society remain united to ensure national security, everyone must contribute through joint and concerted efforts to safeguard the present and future of students.

“Public examinations become gateways to opportunities for our students. The government is undertaking comprehensive steps to reform these examinations. The objectives of these reforms are to completely curb the use of unfair means in public examinations and make the examination system more transparent, more secure, and more trustworthy for the youth,” she said.

Her remarks assume significance in the backdrop of recent nationwide Gen Z and student-led protests demanding systemic overhauls, fast-track investigations, and stringent legal action following high-profile paper leak irregularities in competitive examinations.

Highlighting the spirit of enterprise among young citizens, she said youths are increasingly embracing a culture of job creation rather than job seeking.

“Many of our youth are embracing the culture of job creation as they pursue the path of self-employment. The participation of young entrepreneurs has led to the creation of a strong start-up ecosystem in our country. Major global enterprises are impressed by the talent and dedication of Indian youth and entrust them with leadership roles,” she added.

The President said such achievers have enhanced the reputation of India’s youth power globally and reaffirmed her faith in the country’s bright future.

Turning to holistic development, the President said that the physical and mental well-being of the youth forms the cornerstone of the nation’s future, adding that families and society share the collective responsibility to motivate them.

She highlighted sports as a key vehicle for youth development and nation-building under the flagship ‘Khelo India’ programme.

“Under the Khelo India programme, a sports ecosystem is being developed across the country, from the grassroots to the national level. The government is making unprecedented investments to promote sports, yielding remarkable leaps in the achievements of our sportspersons in international tournaments,” she said.

President Murmu also lauded the “unmatched valour” of the Indian Armed Forces, saying Operation Sindoor demonstrated the country’s capability to execute precision counter-terror operations and sent a firm message that terror elements and their backers will face consequences regardless of where they hide.

She recalled the anniversary of the military action alongside historic observances like Kargil Vijay Diwas, reaffirming India’s tradition of overcoming forces hostile to humanity.

“On the 26th of July, we observed Kargil Vijay Diwas. Earlier, on the 7th of May, we commemorated the completion of one year since the launch of Operation Sindoor. We remembered the unmatched valour of our Armed Forces. That historic operation against terrorism demonstrated the capability of the Indian Armed Forces to act with precision,” she said.

She said the operation delivered an unequivocal warning to enemies. “It sent a clear and firm message to terrorists and those who support them that no matter where they hide, they will have to face the consequences of their actions.” The President also highlighted the strategic measures accompanying the counter-terror posture, describing the decision to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty with the nation harbouring terror networks as a “decisive step in the interest of our nation, especially the farmers.” On internal security, she termed the eradication of Maoism a monumental achievement for the country after decades of struggle.

“For decades, Naxalism posed a serious challenge to the nation. Making India Naxal free is a major achievement. Today, enthusiasm prevails in the areas once affected by Naxalism,” she said, pointing to all-inclusive development efforts and active local participation in initiatives like the Bastar Olympics and the Bastar Pandum festival.

Highlighting the nation’s civilisational heritage, the President said that Sarnath, the site of Lord Buddha’s first sermon, was included in the UNESCO World Heritage List this year, following the listing of 12 Maratha military forts last year.

She stated that India proudly balances monuments of deep spirituality with historic symbols of military strength and resilience.

Addressing foreign policy, she reiterated that peace, dialogue, cooperation, and the ideal of ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’ (the world is one family) remain the bedrock of India’s international relations.

“We believe in a rules-based international order. Our endeavour is to ensure that the global community receives appropriate representation in the United Nations and other multilateral organisations,” she stated, noting India’s growing stature among Global South nations.

The President also touched upon senior care, pointing out that alongside the world’s largest young population, India is also seeing a rise in senior citizens and noted that about six crore senior citizens aged 70 and above can now avail of free healthcare services up to Rs 5 lakh per year under government initiatives, urging society to remain sensitive and uphold their dignity.

She said the country is moving steadily towards building a ‘Viksit Bharat’ by 2047, driven by economic resilience, massive digital infrastructure, and empowered youth and women.

She stressed that guided by the spirit of ‘Antyodaya’, the core resolve of the nation remains ensuring the fruits of development reach every individual, even as global warfare and instability present severe economic headwinds worldwide.

“Even in such trying circumstances, our economy is moving ahead as the fastest-growing major economy in the world. According to economic projections, the growth rate of the Indian economy is expected to be more than twice the average global growth rate. Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan’ has further strengthened the foundation of our economic progress and national security,” she said.

Highlighting internal welfare milestones over the past decade, the President said that more than 25 crore people have been lifted out of poverty and added that nearly 59 crore account holders have joined the banking system under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, with over 32 crore of these account holders being women, while food security has been ensured for over 80 crore people through free rations.

Underlining India’s technological leap, she pointed out that the country has developed the world’s largest and best digital infrastructure, accounting for more than half of global real-time digital transactions.

Highlighting the demographic dividend, the President said that 65 per cent of the country’s population is below the age of 35, describing the youth as India’s “most valuable asset.” She commended young entrepreneurs for driving a robust startup ecosystem and lauded young innovators, citing a recent space exploration milestone led by a team with an average age of just 28 years.

Women’s empowerment remained a central theme of her address. Celebrating achievements ranging from rural self-help groups to high-altitude defence, she said that the initial target of creating three crore ‘Lakhpati Didis’ has been achieved, with the government now pushing towards a goal of creating three crore more.

“Our girls are performing exceptionally well in education and diverse sectors, from the Drone Didi enhancing agricultural productivity to the Fighter Combat Leader in the Air Force. In the recently concluded Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, women won 8 out of India’s total tally of 13 gold medals,” she said.

The President also highlighted political inclusion, pointing out that the enactment of the ‘Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam’ in 2023, which reserves 33 per cent of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies, will make Indian democracy more inclusive.

Speaking on sustainable development, she asserted that India is playing a leading role globally in protecting the environment, having achieved several Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030 ahead of schedule.

Reciting a Santali language poem penned by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, she urged citizens to remain committed to preserving nature and human values, linking individual action to national initiatives such as ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ and ‘Lifestyle for Environment’ (LiFE).

The President also paid homage to freedom fighters, Mahatma Gandhi, B. R. Ambedkar and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel for integrating over 550 princely states. She also solemnly remembered those who lost their lives or faced displacement during partition, observed on August 14 as ‘Vibhajan Vibheeshika Smriti Divas’.

She invoked Telugu writer Gurajada Apparao’s lines, “A nation is not just its land, a nation is all its people,” urging every citizen to contribute wholeheartedly to transforming independent India into a fully developed nation by 2047.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: Partition Horrors Remembrance Day observed at Mysuru railway station
World.content:
Mysuru division of South Western Railway observed Partition Horrors Remembrance Day at Mysuru Railway Station on Friday, recalling the immense suffering, displacement and loss of lives endured by millions during the Partition of India.

The programme paid tribute to those who faced the hardships of Partition and highlighted the importance of remembering its human cost. On the occasion, Divisional Railway Manager Mudit Mittal honoured retired Railway employee Nagaraj K.S. in recognition of his valuable contribution and dedicated service to the Railways.

A photo exhibition featuring archival photographs related to Partition was also inaugurated. The exhibition depicted the experiences of people affected by Partition, including their displacement, hardships, courage and resilience. The photographs offered visitors an opportunity to reflect on the difficult chapter in the nation’s history and the spirit of unity with which the country overcame the challenges.

ADRM Shammas Hameed, branch officers, railway employees and passengers were present.

Participants said the observance was not merely an occasion to remember the past but also an opportunity to reaffirm the values of unity, peace, harmony and social cohesion. Remembering the sacrifices and suffering of the past, they said, would help strengthen the collective resolve to build a more united and harmonious society.

World.title: Roads worth ₹182.74 crore constructed in undivided Kadapa district, say officials
World.content:
The officials on Friday (August 14, 2026) said that roads measuring 586 km in length and valued at ₹182.74 crore have been constructed in the undivided Kadapa district by the State government.

At a meeting in Pulivendula to review the progress of road projects across the district, Minister of Roads and Buildings B.C. Janardhan Reddy and district in-charge Minister S. Savitha directed the officials to expedite the land acquisition process for the national highways criss-crossing the district.

In spite of the fund crunch, Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu has accorded top priority to laying of roads across the State, Mr. Janardhan Reddy stated, while instructing the officials to match the speed.

The Ministers questioned the officials about the hiccups, if any, faced in executing the road projects in the district. Of the 93 works taken up in Kadapa district, 29 have been completed, while 58 are in various stages of progress and six are in the tenders stage, the officials informed the Ministers.

In Pulivendula constituency, represented by former Chief Minister Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy, the government has taken up a whopping nine projects worth ₹10.55 crore. “Five of them have been completed and even brought to use, while the remaining are in progress,” Mr. Janardhan Reddy said.

World.title: T.N. govt. has formed committee to look at anomalies in guideline values: Minister
World.content:
The Tamil Nadu government has formed a committee to study the anomalies in guideline values, Minister for Registration and Commercial Taxes D. Lokesh Tamilselvan said on Friday (August 14, 2026).

“There is no request for increasing the guideline values. But there are anomalies. Hence, we have formed a committee, and we will take action based on the report of the committee. We will get into this after the Assembly session gets over,” he told The Hindu here on Friday.

The Minister took part in the inauguration of a workshop in Coimbatore for document writers, realtors, developers, and promoters on the ‘presence-less’ registration that will be mandatory from August 17 across the State.

Those registering first sale of plot or apartment units can do so from the office of the promoter or seller and need not visit the sub-registrar office. The registration will be done almost immediately. “Requirement of many documents will not be necessary since these are first time sales,” the Minister said.

Mr. Tamilselvan said the ‘presence-less’ registration will bring in transparency and remove middlemen. Workshops were held in Chennai, Madurai, Tiruchi, and Coimbatore on this system. Call centres that will function 24x7 have been set up to assist public with the registration, he added.

Minister for Backward Classes V. Sampathkumar said the ‘presence-less’ registration is part of the efforts of the government to take its schemes and welfare measures directly to the public.

According to the Inspector General of Registration G. K. Arun Sundar Thayalan, registration of a document involves three processes – execution, presentation, and registration. When a sale is executed, the documents can be presented from anywhere through this system.

World.title: PM Shehbaz briefs President Zardari on Pak-Saudi-Turkiye defence pact
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called on President Asif Ali Zardari in Islamabad on Friday and briefed him on a recently signed defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, according to a statement issued by the Presidency.

For his part, President Zardari “expressed his best wishes for the effective implementation of the tripartite agreement with regard to defence cooperation, regional peace and stability and promotion of the security of the Muslim ummah”, the Presidency’s statement on its X account said.
