World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.title: ‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.content:
Yan Bowen’s only attempt to get a credit card came during her first year at university. The bank rejected her because she had no income, reinforcing her belief that cards were meant for “people with stable incomes.”

Then, at 22, she found herself in debt anyway.

Last October, she realized she owed around 3,000 yuan ($400) — more than her entire monthly student allowance. With the debt weighing on her, she cut daily expenses, took on part-time work, and borrowed from friends to pay it down.

The debt had built up through apps she used every day to order takeout, buy groceries, and shop online, each offering the option to pay later or split purchases into installments.

Even so, Yan sees the relatively low limits on app-based credit as a safeguard against getting in too deep. “It keeps the risk manageable, nothing big enough to shock my parents,” she said. “A credit card would just mean higher risk.”

That wariness extends well beyond Yan. By the end of March 2026, China had about 687 million credit and combo cards in circulation, down roughly 120 million from their 2022 peak, according to central bank data.

Yan is one of 12 people aged 20 to 26, including students, job seekers, and office workers, whom Sixth Tone interviewed in July. Of them, nine had never owned a credit card. Many knew little about how cards worked and worried most about missing repayments. The few who did use cards tended to do so for specific reasons, such as overseas travel or managing cash flow.

More than 60 credit card subcenters closed across China in 2025, according to state-run People’s Daily, while some banks folded their card businesses and standalone apps into broader retail operations.

Yet outstanding balances on bank cards have remained relatively stable, said Jiang Jiajun, an associate professor at Fudan University’s School of Economics, in Shanghai. That suggests many of the cards being canceled were dormant rather than evidence that consumers had stopped borrowing. Even so, he said, “at least from the data, there is a clear trend of people avoiding credit cards.”

The traditional selling points — higher limits, longer interest-free periods, and richer rewards — may simply matter less to younger consumers. Those perks “are not necessarily what Gen Z cares most about,” Jiang said.

Yan’s first encounter with borrowing came through a food-delivery coupon. During her sophomore year, Chinese delivery app Meituan offered her a discount worth less than 1 yuan, but only if she activated its pay-later service. She did.

Before long, she had signed up for Huabei, a credit service inside Ant Group’s Alipay payment app, and Baitiao, a similar product from e-commerce giant JD.com. “They’re just so easy,” Yan said. “Even when traveling, hotels let you stay first and pay later.”

Even with enough money in the bank, Yan sometimes chose to pay later or in installments rather than watch her balance fall. Small debts piled up across different apps, and she often did not know the total until the monthly bill came due.

Her biggest current debt comes from a 6,500-yuan laptop. To be eligible for a student discount, Yan had to pay through Baitiao, so she split the cost into six monthly installments of more than 1,000 yuan. As of Aug. 5, she still owed more than 5,600 yuan.

Unlike credit cards, which require a separate application, app-based credit is built directly into services young consumers already use, often with lower limits and fewer steps between browsing and borrowing.

Jiang said the difference comes down partly to “mental accounting” — the way people sort spending into different mental buckets. Small, frequent purchases through apps like Huabei can feel like part of a “convenient lifestyle” rather than “financial debt.” Credit cards, by contrast, make the borrowing harder to ignore.

“They make users acutely aware that they are borrowing money, which naturally triggers resistance,” Jiang said. “These two things sit in completely different mental accounts for young people.”

For some young consumers, credit cards begin to look more useful as purchases get bigger and finances more secure.

Wang Xuanren, 23, works in finance in the eastern city of Nanjing and applied for her first and only credit card in 2024 ahead of an overseas trip. She already had more than 500,000 yuan in a fixed-term deposit at the bank, helping her secure approval the same day; the card arrived five days later.

She now saves it largely for electronics and luxury goods. For big-ticket purchases, Wang said installments can turn a 40,000- or 50,000-yuan expense into much smaller monthly payments, automatically deducted from her debit account.

“I keep a lot of cash on hand,” she said. “Using a credit card interest-free is basically borrowing someone else’s money and paying it back later.”

Zheng Yuxin, a 21-year-old university student in Shanghai, is far less comfortable with that bargain. She has no plans to apply for a credit card or use app-based credit anytime soon. “Nothing in life is free,” she said.

Even generous sign-up bonuses make her wary. Credit cards feel “very distant and risky,” she said. “I worry about falling for a scam because I can’t tell what’s real.”

In 2023, Zheng activated Huabei after agreeing to an authorization screen and completing facial verification. It then became her default payment method, allowing later purchases to be charged through the service without her actively choosing it each time.

She realized what had happened only when roughly 100 yuan was deducted from her bank account on repayment day. “Seeing unexpected money disappear gave me this empty, unsettled feeling,” she said. Since then, she has stuck to a simpler rule: buy only when she already has the money.

From Sept. 30, China will require a clearer separation between paying and borrowing online. Non-bank payment providers will no longer be allowed to present loans as payment options or market lending products through their payment services, with companies required to adjust their practices before the rules take effect.

Jiang said such rules should make borrowing more transparent and give users clearer warnings before they take on debt. The goal, he said, is not to eliminate app-based credit, but to make sure consumers know when an ordinary purchase has become a loan. “This protects consumers and helps platforms earn long-term trust,” he said.

Those preferences may change with age. Higher incomes, more travel, and larger spending needs could eventually make the higher limits and longer interest-free periods of credit cards more useful. “The same group of people might develop completely different habits 10 years from now,” said Jiang.

Zhang Xinyun, 24 and from the northeastern city of Harbin, is currently unemployed and remains deeply wary of credit cards after watching a relative struggle with card debt when she was a teenager. “Spending ahead always comes with bad temptations,” she said. High limits look more like added risk than freedom, and sign-up gifts do little to reassure her.

But Zhang can imagine her needs changing. Once she starts working or running a business, she said, a card could become useful for managing cash flow or traveling overseas.

Jiang underscores that banks cannot rely on that change happening on its own. “They need to improve convenience, embrace fintech, and create use cases that resonate with younger consumers.”

At the bank where Zhao Wei works in the northeastern city of Shenyang, signing up new credit card users is part of the job. She is expected to bring in dozens each year and, last year, even opened her own first card partly to help meet the target.

Many customers worry about missing repayments and damaging their credit records, Zhao said. Others simply see little need for a card when mobile payments and app-based credit are already woven into daily spending through digital services such as WeChat Pay, Alipay, and Huabei.

Banks have responded with incentives. Zhao’s gives new cardholders 150 yuan in spending credits, along with gifts ranging from rice and cooking oil to household appliances. Elsewhere, welcome offers can include health checkups, airport lounge access, fuel vouchers, coffee coupons, and cash back on purchases.

Zhao is blunt about how far such incentives can go. “People who are put off by credit cards won’t open one just for that,” she said.

More recently, her bank began offering customized cards printed with customers’ pet photos, along with discounts on pet supplies.

Even that has not made Zhao optimistic. “Credit cards are being squeezed by more convenient products,” she said. “If they can’t build stronger ties to daily life, becoming obsolete is not impossible.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.title: Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.content:
A Chinese county known as the home of over 400 temple murals dating back to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) is facing a heritage restoration crisis, with many of its murals stolen, destroyed, or marred by thieves.

In an investigation published Wednesday, Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper visited 16 fortified villages in Yu County in the northern Hebei province and found that many of the area’s temple murals had been stolen, destroyed during temple collapse, or weathered beyond recognition. Remaining fragments often bore looters’ cut marks.

A major cultural relic hub, the county served as a military and commercial crossroads during the Ming and Qing dynasties (1644–1911) and is home to more than 1,600 registered cultural heritage locations, including numerous fortified villages. The accompanying temples feature murals depicting Taoist, Buddhist, and folk religious elements.

Danhou Village — inscribed on China’s official list of traditional villages in 2016 — is one of the county’s most popular tourist destinations. The village’s Guandi Temple was once home to extensive murals, but only fragments remain today.

When The Paper visited, the temple was under renovation for leaking roofs, missing wooden components, and cracked walls after years of neglect. Work began in April and is projected to be completed by the end of the year.

Of the 16 villages The Paper visited, only those officially considered “traditional villages” or protected sites received restoration and care. The report noted that overall neglect of the fortified villages stems from their abandonment, as villagers have mostly lived outside the sites since the 1980s, leaving the buildings to decay.

A member of the county’s cultural relics management office told The Paper that he recently inspected a temple on a visit to his hometown.

“I went there around noon, and the wall was still standing,” he said. “But at around 2 p.m., I got a call saying the western wall of that temple had collapsed. If I had gone any later, I might have been buried under it.”

Another obstacle to upkeep is funding. Under China’s cultural relics law, their owners or users must preserve them, with government subsidies provided where possible. But in Yu County, most low-level relics are owned by villages that can’t afford maintenance, placing the burden on the county.

The cultural relics worker described how every village has an appointed relic steward, but with no subsidy budget, the role falls to village cadres as an additional duty. With heavy workloads and no stipends, protection relies on individual goodwill.

Yet government investment has been considerable. Over a decade ago, Yu County built a 12,000-square-meter museum for 10,000-plus movable relics, free to the public, costing the county nearly 4 million yuan ($600,000) annually. In 2023, state and provincial funds for restoration projects totaled 14.6 million yuan.

Despite the investment, Yu County’s neglected relics expose gaps in China’s heritage architecture protection, a problem that it has been working to solve in recent years.

In July 2024, the Finance Ministry created a lottery-funded program for unlisted ancient buildings. Upon submitting a proposal, local authorities whose heritage architecture and restoration projects are deemed to serve the public good are given priority. The program will run through 2027.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Murals at an ancient temple in Yu County, Hebei province, June 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.title: The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.content:
During the opening decades of the 15th century, a eunuch from China’s imperial court led seven epic voyages across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, pushing westward as far as the Red Sea and the shores of East Africa.

The expeditions were astonishing feats of engineering and navigation. Setting sail decades before Christopher Columbus or Vasco da Gama, Zheng spent years crossing the oceans at the head of a vast fleet of 200 ships. Some of the vessels measured up to 70 meters long — three times the size of Columbus’ ships.

For many, Zheng deserves to rank among history’s greatest explorers. Yet, much about the voyages — and Zheng himself — remains shrouded in mystery. He barely features in the official records left by China’s Ming dynasty (1368–1644), with court historians dismissing his expeditions as impressive, but ruinously expensive. Even the place and date of Zheng’s death are unknown.

The Ming court’s assessment still colors views of Zheng centuries later. Today, the great admiral is well known in China, with generations of schoolchildren learning about his amazing treasure ships that brought giraffes, lions, zebras, and other exotic beasts back from Africa. But the voyages tend to be presented as a historical curiosity that had little lasting impact.

Zou Zhenhuan is on a mission to change that. The 69-year-old — now a distinguished professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University — has spent decades studying Zheng He, and his research has played a significant role in shifting perceptions of the explorer and his legacy. His latest book, “Monsoon Asia and Africa: Cultural Exchange and Zheng He’s Voyages,” is his most comprehensive look at the subject yet.

For Zou, Zheng’s voyages were far more influential than often assumed. Far from a flash in the pan, they opened up a new era of maritime trade between Asia and Africa, as merchants took advantage of the navigational technologies and sea routes pioneered by Zheng. He even believes they helped pave the way for the European Age of Discovery that followed.

In this interview, Zou, who is also a research fellow at the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History, explains why Zheng He is often so misunderstood — and why his voyages should be seen as a harbinger of globalization. The text has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: You have studied Zheng He for more than 20 years. What drew you to this subject in the beginning?

Zou: My interest in Zheng He began in my boyhood. What captivated me most was his extraordinary perseverance — seven voyages spanning more than two decades. Such marvelous experiences are enough to stir the imagination. As the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões wrote in “Os Lusíadas,” the true and marvelous deeds of brave men surpass all fantasy and legend. I was a sickly boy, but I harbored an intense hero complex, and Zheng He’s exploits answered it perfectly.

It was this interest that led me to study Zheng He once I became a historian, and it is this same interest that has sustained my research for so many years.

Sixth Tone: After all these years of research, what kind of person is Zheng He in your mind?

Zou: As my research has deepened, the image of Zheng He in my mind has grown ever richer. Take his religious faith, for example. Many people might assume Zheng He was simply a Muslim. He was indeed born into a Muslim family; his grandfather and father both made the hajj to Mecca. But he was also a devout Buddhist who was accepted as a disciple by an eminent monk, receiving the Dharma name “Fushan,” and supervising the construction of the Great Bao’en Temple in Nanjing. At the same time, Zheng He was also an adherent of Confucianism. Historical records describe him as “endowed with the talent to govern and versed in the teachings of Confucius and Mencius.”

The most famous material testimony to Zheng He’s plural faith is the trilingual stele he erected in the kingdom of Ceylon (present-day Sri Lanka) during his second voyage in 1409. The stele, commonly known as the Galle Trilingual Inscription, is carved in three scripts: the Chinese text praises the Buddha and records a list of offerings; the Tamil text glorifies the Hindu god Shiva; and the Persian text extols Allah. Paying tribute to the deities of three great religions on a single stone tablet is, in my view, the most vivid expression of Zheng He’s cosmopolitan, all-embracing spirit.

Sixth Tone: It seems “plurality” is a keyword when it comes to Zheng He.

Zou: Exactly. Zheng He was a man of all-around talent. To begin with, he possessed exceptional organizational and managerial abilities — commanding a fleet of more than 27,000 men was in itself an enormously complex feat of systems engineering.

He also had the metaphysical learning of a Confucian scholar and was equally adept at practical, technical matters: during the voyages he spread the Chinese calendar, rituals, weights and measures, and architectural techniques to other countries, and with superb diplomatic skill he mediated disputes between Siam and Malacca, and between Annam and Champa.

Plus, he even displayed outstanding military talent: on his very first voyage he defeated Chen Zuyi, a pirate chief who commanded tens of thousands of followers in the Strait of Malacca, wiping out more than 5,000 pirates.

Sixth Tone: When I was reading your book, what impressed me most was Zheng He’s nautical technology — especially his precise understanding and ingenious use of the Indian Ocean monsoons.

Zou: That’s right. The fleet’s seven expeditions were deeply embedded in the monsoon, which is the main reason I titled the book “Monsoon Asia and Africa.”

The regions the fleet traversed — East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Indian Ocean — are among the areas of the world where the monsoon phenomenon is most pronounced. And in an era without modern propulsion, the monsoon was the “engine” that drove this enormous armada on its long voyages.

The fleet usually departed China in winter, between October and March, riding the northeast monsoon southward. By the time it reached the Indian Ocean, the summer southwest monsoon would be blowing, allowing a smooth voyage home. The whole round trip took about a year and a half.

To visit more places efficiently, Zheng He would dispatch detached squadrons along the way; after completing their missions, these squadrons would regroup at designated rendezvous points in accordance with the monsoon patterns.

But here’s the thing: the monsoon and the compass could carry the fleet forward, but they could not tell the crew exactly where they were on the open sea. To do this, the fleet mastered a refined technique known as “guoyang qianxing,” or star-observation navigation, using an instrument called the “qianxing,” or star-measuring, board to determine a ship’s latitude according to stars’ altitude above the horizon. Zheng He’s fleets also compiled these observations into dedicated star charts, creating a reusable navigational database.

One could say that Zheng He’s fleet fused three techniques — the monsoon patterns, star-observation navigation, and the magnetic compass — into a single, world-leading navigational system for its time. I believe these sea routes, nautical technology, and geographical knowledge helped lay the intellectual and technical foundations for the arrival of European explorers more than half a century later. However, this topic needs further research.

Sixth Tone: Since you mention the European explorers who came later, I have to raise a common critique: that unlike the explorers who launched Europe’s Age of Discovery, Zheng He’s expeditions — for all their grandeur — were a mere flash in the pan that left no lasting imprint. How do you see it?

Zou: This view is indeed very common. I would point out that Zheng He’s seven voyages were not merely official acts of diplomacy by the Ming court; they also facilitated exchanges of goods, species, and technologies between Asia and Africa on an unprecedented scale.

The exotic animals the fleet brought back from foreign lands — giraffes, lions, ostriches, zebras — and the rare plants and fruits such as pepper, sappanwood, and durian greatly enriched China’s native stock of species. Wherever it went, the fleet shared nautical and astronomical knowledge with local peoples, deepening mutual learning among the civilizations of Asia and Africa.

The most representative example of all this is blue-and-white porcelain. Zheng He’s fleet carried large quantities of porcelain into the Islamic world, while the cobalt pigment needed to produce blue-and-white ware, known as “Sumali blue,” originally came from Persia. This pattern of “bringing finished products out and importing raw materials in” was itself a cross-cultural dialogue of technology and aesthetics.

As the Ming dynasty’s most sought-after export in overseas markets, blue-and-white porcelain was among the important gifts carried on every mission. Pieces dating from the period of Zheng He’s voyages have been unearthed at Fustat in Egypt, at Aydhab in Sudan, at Aden on the Arabian Peninsula, and elsewhere.

The huge overseas demand, in turn, stimulated a massive increase in early Ming porcelain production: according to historical records, in 1433 alone the court ordered the firing of 443,500 pieces in a single decree.

What does this tell us? It shows that nearly a century before Columbus set sail, Zheng He’s fleet had already opened up the east-west sea routes of the Indian Ocean and built a regional network of trade and cultural exchange. I call this the “Zheng He exchange.”

Sixth Tone: That concept readily brings to mind the “Columbian exchange” — the massive exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that opened up after Columbus’ voyages.

Zou: I did indeed borrow the theoretical framework of the “Columbian exchange,” but my concept points to an earlier wave of civilizational interaction — one that unfolded between Asia and Africa. In many respects, Zheng He was a key catalyst on the eve of globalization.

Of course, while the “Zheng He exchange” and the “Columbian exchange” share many similarities, their purposes were fundamentally different. Zheng He’s voyages never established colonies overseas, and they were extremely restrained in their use of force.

As you mentioned, many Chinese people feel rather regretful about this, believing it caused China to miss a golden opportunity to dominate the globe. Liu Cixin’s short science-fiction story “Xiyang” (“The Western Ocean”) expresses exactly this sentiment through an alternate-history framework: in the story, Zheng He’s fleet sails farther west from the East African coast, rounds the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually reaches Europe, defeats the combined Anglo-French forces, and conquers the European continent, turning China into an empire on which the sun never sets.

But in my view, Zheng He radiates the light of pacifism and cultural pluralism — and that is precisely where his example can offer inspiration for our own time.

(Header image: A statue of Zheng He in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, 2024. 500px Essential)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.title: An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.content:
“My contact lenses are comfortable even after wearing them all day. Do you want to try them?”

So says a young woman in glasses with transparent lenses, in response to a friend who says her contacts are painful. She then takes a contact box out of a black handbag, offers it, and says, “You can blink without worry.”

The endorsement seems genuine enough — except neither woman is real.

This , featuring the popular AI actress Fang Taozi endorsing colored contacts, has recently sparked controversy in China over whether an AI character can vouch for a product’s quality.

Released in late July on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by domestic contact lens brand Nutnutlook, the ad was taken down without comment last week.

In response, Chinese netizens criticized the  for using an AI avatar instead of a human actress. “What makes me uncomfortable is that someone without eyes now has the right to speak about eyes,” one user commented.

“AI doesn’t even know what it feels like to actually wear the product,” another wrote.

Neither the company behind the AI actress, Guangzhou-based World Media Film and TV Culture, nor the contacts brand has responded to the controversy.

The fictional 20-year-old Fang Taozi was unveiled in the AI short drama “The Laid-off Girl” in June this year. The series, which tells the story of a small-town girl moving to a fictional city to pursue a modeling career, has been viewed more than 320 million times on Douyin.

In the months following the series’ release, directed by popular content creator Fei Feifei, Fang’s personal Douyin account — created by companies to boost AI actors’popularity — gained more than 470,000 followers. Her account posts content ranging from so-called “behind-the-scenes” footage during the show’s production to snippets of her supposed daily life, such as making breakfast.

Fang has been lauded by fans for having, unlike many AI characters, moles and blemishes, giving her an imperfect and realistic appearance. In “The Laid-off Girl,” she struggles with relatable Chinese workplace challenges, such as pressure to attend business dinners and getting bullied by her colleagues.

Domestic media reported that on Juliang Xingtu, Douyin’s influencer marketing platform, Fang Taozi’s advertising rates are 168,000 yuan ($24,900) per video for clips under 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan for videos between 21 and 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan for videos over 60 seconds — significantly higher than ad rates charged by most human influencers.

Ma Lihong, a senior partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, told domestic media that, despite AI avatars not being considered people under Chinese law and therefore not legally considered  endorsers, the video could still constitute false advertising.

Ma added that advertisers are responsible for the truthfulness of their content and that by making a first-person claim about experiencing a product, the AI character could be seen as fabricating user experience. As such, the brand and the ’s producer could potentially be in violation of the law.

Compounding the severity of the issue, colored contact lenses are classified as Class III medical devices under China’s regulatory system, reserved for items that pose the highest risk to consumers. Actors are prohibited from recommending such products in s, a rule aimed at preventing brands from misleading consumers.

This is not the first time Chinese brands have experimented with AI-generated figures in advertising. Major bottled water company Nongfu Spring made headlines last year for using AI-generated images in promotional posters, while companies ranging from yogurt brands to office chair suppliers have collaborated with various AI-generated actors to endorse products and use slogans. Tutorials on using AI-generated videos for livestream commerce have also become common.

Entertainment law expert Qiu Zhimiao said AI-powered endorsements will become increasingly common, and regulating them is a new frontier. As s endorsed by virtual influencers exist in a legal gray area, he said, there is a need for clearer regulations.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of the AI actress Fang Taozi in the  promoting colored contact lenses. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.title: 1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.content:
On a rain-washed weekend morning, mist clings to the peaks surrounding Ze’e Village in the southwestern Sichuan province. Over the sound of a rushing mountain stream, 24-year-old Jifu Lama leads a procession of children in matching kits. They navigate through rice paddies, along irrigation canals and over earthen mounds until they reach their destination: a soccer pitch carved out of a former cornfield.

Perched halfway up a mountain at an altitude of 1,300 meters, Lama’s pitch looks like a vibrant green terraced field folded into the sweeping landscape of Sichuan’s Daliangshan region. Standing in the center circle, the young coach directs his players — mostly children aged 6 to 13 from six neighboring Yi ethnic villages — to lace up their boots, arrange the cones and begin their warm-ups.

Ze’e Village is remote, accessible only by winding mountain roads, but the children’s imaginations stretch far beyond the peaks. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, the young athletes devoured match highlights on smartphones. Winning and losing are secondary to the star players: the children argue passionately over the goals scored by superstars like Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi and Harry Kane.

Seven-year-old Aluo, a first-grader with lightning-fast footwork, idolizes France’s Mbappé. His cousin, Yang Xiaojun, a skinny third-grader, became a die-hard Gareth Bale fan after watching a clip of the Welshman’s legendary bicycle kick.

When they score on this mountain pitch, the kids leap into the air, spinning to land in Cristiano Ronaldo’s iconic, arms-down “Siu” celebration.

For these children, soccer is bright spot in childhood marked by economic hardship. Local data shows rural per capita income in Daliangshan is around just 12,700 yuan ($1,770) a year. To make a living, parents migrate to factories in the southern Guangdong province, Wuhan in the central Hubei province, and the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, returning only once a year for the traditional Yi New Year.

Raised by aging grandparents in households with multiple siblings, these “left-behind” children have few outlets for their energy. A piece of candy or a lucky draw at the school gate used to be the highlight of their week. Now, soccer offers them friendship, structure and a window to the outside world.

To keep them invested, Lama implemented a reward system. Players earn four points for every practice they attend, which they can exchange for free gear. That is how Hu Feifei, one of the girls who recently joined the squad, earned her jersey, socks and boots.

Hu remembers when the pitch was nothing but sand dumped over uneven soil. When it rained, they played in puddles and went home with scraped knees, but they were happy. Today, thanks to a corporate sponsor moved by the team’s story, they play on an artificial turf pitch that Lama proudly claims is “better than the ones in the county town.”

The sponsor discovered them because of Lama, who is no stranger to the spotlight. But his viral fame is a chapter of his life tinged with both pride and heartbreak.

Lama’s obsession began in middle school when a friend gifted him a Neymar Barcelona jersey. The self-described rebellious teen found his anchor in soccer. To play, he transferred to a vocational school with a pitch.

To master the game, he did the unthinkable and dropped out, hiked to an altitude of 2,000 meters, and built a wooden hut on a flat peak. There, with no electricity and relying on a wood fire to cook, he trained alone for days at a time. His goal was to become a professional soccer player within five years.

He documented his solitary, high-altitude drills on short-video platforms. The stark contrast between the primitive, breathtaking environment and the boy’s fluid footwork captivated the internet. He amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, drawing the attention of FIFA on the eve of the 2022 Qatar World Cup. At his peak, he was earning up to 6,000 yuan a month from his videos.

But soon this felt wrong, money was not why he played soccer. “It felt like I was using soccer to make a profit,” Lama says. “It betrayed my original love for the game.”

However, his online presence earned him a spot in professional tryouts. It was here that Lama’s dream collided with reality. “My technique was too poor, I couldn’t understand the tactics, and my receiving and passing were all wrong,” he said.

In May 2023, he finally earned a spot with Jingchuan Wenhui, a fourth-tier club in the Chinese Champions League. Stepping onto the pitch, the cheers of the fans made the experience feel unreal.

It lasted exactly 45 minutes. Half a match that Lama doesn’t dare to rewatch. “My muscles were constantly tense, and I felt I performed too poorly,” he said.

The experience made clarified the insurmountable chasm between himself and real professional players, he said he could “never keep up with the rhythm and physical confrontation.”

The failure was a brutal watershed moment. But instead of continuing to chase trials across the country, Lama packed his bags and looked back to the dirt fields of Ze’e Village.

Today, he serves as an unpaid, unofficial soccer coach for two local primary schools. He runs training sessions five days a week and spends his weekends driving his minivan across the mountains to ferry kids to and from practice.

The transition from viral star to grassroots coach hasn’t been easy. The internet money has dried up, and his public welfare coaching model is financially unsustainable. He is considering charging a modest annual fee of 1,200 yuan for new recruits this fall, but he agonizes over whether the cost will price out the very kids who need the game most. He regularly visits skeptical parents, trying to convince them that soccer isn’t a distraction, but a vital tool for development.

“I want these children to start changing from this generation,” Lama said. “I want them to learn manners and be driven.”

In a region where educational resources are sparse and academic struggles are common, Lama sees soccer as a safety net. His vision is already bearing fruit: four of his sixth-graders recently passed a specialized sports exam, securing them spots in a superior middle school in the county town.

Eventually, Lama plans to build a fully registered professional club. He has already chosen the name: Leke, the Yi word for plowshare.

It is a fitting moniker for a young man breaking tough ground. “I don’t even have a first team yet,” Lama said, looking out over the mist-covered pitch. “I’ve only just lifted my foot to take the first step, and it hasn’t even landed yet.”

This piece was originally published by Caixin Global. It is republished here with permission.

Reporter: Zheng Haipeng.

(Header image: Players from Jijia Primary School pose for a group photo, imitating the signature moves of their favorite soccer stars, Ze’e Village, Sichuan province, June 2026. Zheng Haipeng/Caixin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Ex-Zamboanga del Norte governor Rosalina Jalosjos dies
World.content:
'She will be remembered as a loving and compassionate leader whose presence carried a quiet strength and whose service left a lasting place in the story of our city and our province,' the Dapitan City Government says

Former Zamboanga del Norte governor Rosalina “Nene” Jalosjos died on Friday, August 14, two weeks after the passing of his brother and political kingpin Romeo Jalosjos.

The Dapitan City Government confirmed this through an official statement posted on its official Facebook page. She was 79.

“We remember Ma’am Nene not only for the positions she held and the years she devoted to public service, but for the gentleness, warmth, and genuine care with which she led,” the city government stated.

Rosalina Jalosjos began her political career as a Dapitan councilor in 2010 before winning the mayoralty in 2013 against Agapito Cardino, who had only been sworn in as mayor months earlier after then-vice mayor Patrick Bajamunde-Chan vacated the post.

After serving three full terms, she ran and won as governor of Zamboanga del Norte in the 2022 elections.

Before assuming the post, Rosalina had protested former governor Roberto Uy’s move to donate millions’ worth of medical equipment to Dipolog City and other local governments due to its foreseen impact on the province’s main referral hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During her gubernatorial term, Jalosjos advocated for culture and the environment when she vowed to expand aid for the marginalized Subanen tribe, and ordered the suspension of massive quarrying in Zamboanga del Norte.

In the 2025 elections, Jalosjos sought mayorship in Dipolog City under the Aggrupation of Parties for Prosperity, but lost to Uy. It was the same year the Jalosjos clan suffered major losses in the province.

“To many Dapitanons, she will be remembered as a loving and compassionate leader whose presence carried a quiet strength and whose service left a lasting place in the story of our city and our province,” the statement added.

Details of the former governor’s wake have yet to be announced. – Rappler.com

Kean Bagaipo is a Mover and student journalist based in Dumaguete City.

World.title: Kazakh Voters Increasingly Seek Concrete Policy Solutions, Experts Say
World.content:
ASTANA — Healthcare, education and social protection are emerging as key areas of competition in Kazakhstan’s election campaign, with experts saying voters are increasingly looking beyond broad promises to how seven political parties intend to deliver measurable improvements in quality of life.

Those issues were at the center of an Aug. 14 meeting of the Sarap Expert Club in Astana, where researchers, healthcare and education specialists and human-capital experts examined how social concerns are shaping party platforms and voter expectations ahead of the election.

The election to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral Parliament, is scheduled for Aug. 23. Seven political parties are set to compete, with 545 candidates registered for the race. Campaigning will end at midnight on Aug. 21, followed by a campaign silence day on Aug. 22. More than 12.6 million people are eligible to vote on Aug. 23. As of Aug. 13, the Central Election Commission had accredited 656 observers representing foreign states and international organizations.

Experts said the parties largely agree on the problems across healthcare, education, employment and social protection but increasingly differ over who should provide the solutions, how they should be financed and how their effectiveness should be measured.

Zhuldyzai Iskakova, head of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development, which organized the Sarap meeting, said the televised debates helped make those differences more visible to voters. Three nationally televised debates have already aired live on Qazaqstan TV, Channel 7 and Jibek Joly, while the final debate is scheduled for Aug. 19 on 24KZ.

The first two debates drew a combined audience of around two million viewers, according to experts at the meeting.

“They examined their programs in detail and challenged one another,” Iskakova said. “There is a common perception that the parties are broadly similar and that it is difficult to understand what distinguishes them. In reality, there are fundamental differences between them.”

From social promises to competing solutions

Zhanar Sankhayeva, head of the Department of Political Research at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, said political parties are placing greater emphasis on social protection, healthcare and education in their election programs.

“Healthcare is among the top three issues of greatest concern to citizens, while education ranks among the top six priorities affecting people’s everyday lives,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the substance of party platforms could play an important role in voters’ decisions. She cited a survey by the Institute of Public Policy in which 44.4% of respondents identified parties’ initiatives, policy proposals and campaign promises as one of the important factors influencing their choice.

The expert said public expectations in the social sphere are also evolving. While earlier demands focused largely on expanding access to education and healthcare, voters are increasingly concerned with the quality of the services they receive.

“I would describe the current competition between parties in the social sphere as a transition from a competition of social promises to a competition of concrete models for solving social problems,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the election campaign is now entering a “more mature phase.”

“Voters are also moving from a general interest in the election toward forming specific political preferences,” she said.

Long-term priorities

According to Nazarbayev University Vice President Gulmira Qanay, the quality of people’s lives is a clear indicator of how effective or ineffective state policies are. Health, education, safety, professional opportunities and confidence in the future are among the main factors shaping quality of life.

She highlighted the constitutional emphasis on developing human capital, science and education, which should be an important part of the agenda for the future members of the Kurultai.

“We can see major transformations taking place around the world. If we look at the achievements of leading countries over the past 50 years and examine how they reached their current level of development, much of what we see today is the result of investments made in science, education, medicine and the social sphere,” said Qanay.

However, she also stressed that improvements in quality of life require long-term investment rather than measures tied only to an election cycle.

“These are not achievements that appear in a day or two. (…) That is something future members of the Kurultai should also keep in mind,” she added.

After saying that government policy should ultimately be judged by whether it improves people’s quality of life, Qanay said the same principle should apply to higher education, with universities assessed less by formal credentials and more by what graduates are able to do afterward.

Qanay said Kazakhstan should place greater emphasis on developing intellectual capital and designing education policy around research, evidence and measurable outcomes, particularly as digitalization and artificial intelligence transform the skills and standards expected of universities and the wider education system.

Healthcare challenges

Healthcare illustrates the gap that can emerge between policy ambitions and the everyday delivery of public services. Bakytzhan Tazhibay, chair of the AQNIET Kazakhstan Sectoral Trade Union of Healthcare and Public Service Workers and a pediatric urologist, said his review of all seven party platforms showed broad agreement on the sector’s principal challenges.

These include unequal access to quality care between major cities and remote villages, a lack of transparency in the mandatory social health insurance system, shortages of medical personnel and the bureaucratic burden placed on healthcare workers.

“Any reform will remain on paper if we forget about the people responsible for putting it into practice,” Tazhibay said. “At the center of the healthcare system are doctors, nurses, paramedics and other medical workers.”

He identified staff shortages and professional burnout as direct threats to the quality and safety of patient care. Although healthcare salaries have increased, he said, many doctors and nurses still work more than one full-time position to provide an adequate income for their families. This problem is particularly acute outside major cities.

He described elections as a “moment of truth for society.”

“This is the time when the country’s course of development is set, determining what our social policies, labor laws, family support, and healthcare system will look like for years to come,” he added.

Tazhibay called for healthcare expenditure equivalent to at least 5%–6% of gross domestic product, more stable base salaries, workloads consistent with professional standards and greater public and trade-union oversight of the social health insurance system.

World.title: From Grain to Value Chains: Kazakhstan Seeks to Transform Its Agricultural Export Model
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has nearly doubled its agricultural exports over the past five years, reaching $7 billion in 2025 from $3.8 billion, according to an analysis published by the World Financial Review. The growth has strengthened Kazakhstan’s role as a food supplier to Central Asia and beyond. Still, it raises a broader question about the country’s agricultural future: can rising export volumes translate into a higher-value agri-food economy?

According to the World Financial Review, Kazakhstan’s growing agricultural capacity and location between major Eurasian markets are creating new opportunities for the country to play a larger role in regional food security. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization project that international trade will become increasingly important to global food systems, with around 22% of calories consumed worldwide expected to cross international borders by 2034.

For Kazakhstan, which borders or has close transport links to rapidly growing markets in Central Asia, China, the Caucasus and beyond, this creates an economic advantage. The country can supply regions with growing food demand while using its agricultural surplus to expand exports.

Kazakhstan’s agricultural products are already exported to more than 72 countries. Grain and flour remain among its most important exports, particularly to neighboring markets. Over the first 11 months of the latest marketing season, exports of grain and flour reached 13.5 million tons, according to figures cited in the World Financial Review.

Shipments increased particularly sharply to regional markets. Exports to Afghanistan rose by 59% to 2.2 million tons, while supplies to Uzbekistan increased by 37% to 5.6 million tons. Exports to the Kyrgyz Republic reached 504,000 tons, up around 40%, while shipments to Turkmenistan rose 34% to 210,000 tons.

These figures underline Kazakhstan’s importance as a regional supplier. But they also reveal the limits of an export model based primarily on increasing volumes of agricultural commodities.

From exporting more to creating more value

The more significant shift may now be taking place in food processing. According to official data, agricultural exports reached $7 billion in 2025, up 37% year-on-year. More than half of this amount, around $3.6 billion, came from processed agricultural products, whose exports grew by 35% compared with the previous year. The figures suggest that Kazakhstan is beginning to capture a larger share of the value generated from its agricultural production.

Vice Minister of Agriculture Yerbol Taszhurekov said processing is becoming one of the main drivers of growth in Kazakhstan’s agro-industrial complex. Speaking at a March 5 briefing at the Central Communications Service, he said the country’s strategy is not simply to increase agricultural output but to retain more of the economic value generated by it within Kazakhstan.

“Our strategic task is not only to increase the production of agricultural raw materials but also to ensure their processing within the country, including deep processing that creates products with high added value. Processing forms new production chains, creates jobs in the regions and strengthens Kazakhstan’s export potential,” Taszhurekov said.

But not all processing represents the same level of economic transformation. Turning wheat into flour is already a step beyond exporting raw grain. Deep processing, however, can create products such as starch, gluten, amino acids, syrups, vitamins and bioethanol, connecting agriculture to more complex industrial supply chains.

This distinction may become increasingly important for Kazakhstan. The country’s long-term agricultural strategy is therefore not simply about producing more grain, but about moving further along the value chain. The government aims to increase the share of processed agricultural products to 70%. New deep-processing facilities planned by 2028 are expected to have a combined capacity of 5.8 million tons per year and attract around 1.9 trillion tenge (US$3.9 billion) in investment.

Changing the fields to change the export model

The transformation is also evident in what Kazakhstan produces. In recent years, the area under wheat cultivation has declined by nearly 900,000 hectares. In comparison, oilseed acreage has increased by more than one million hectares and land used for pulse crops has expanded by 275,000 hectares, according to the World Financial Review.

This is more than a change in crop statistics. A broader crop mix creates a wider raw-material base for domestic processing industries. Oilseeds, for example, can support vegetable oil production, while pulses and grain can feed into increasingly sophisticated food and industrial processing. Kazakhstan produced a record 4.8 million tons of oilseeds in 2025, while food production rose 8.1% to 3.9 trillion tenge (US$8 billion).

The shift suggests that Kazakhstan’s agricultural diversification is becoming increasingly connected to its industrial policy. Diversification in the fields is intended to support diversification in factories, which in turn could change the composition of exports.
