World.title: EU annual report: ‘serious problems’ in Azerbaijan and ‘serious restrictions’ on fundamental freedoms
World.content:
European Union annual report

The EU says that the human rights and democracy situation in Azerbaijan in 2025 continued to be marked by “serious problems”. It highlighted restrictions on civil society and media freedom, concerns about the independence of the judiciary, and limited progress on structural reforms.

The overall situation in governance remained restrictive. This is according to the European Union’s Annual Report on Human Rights and Democracy in the World for 2025.

The report says legislative, administrative and judicial mechanisms “seriously restrict” the exercise of fundamental freedoms.

At the same time, the assessment notes progress in several areas. These include the criminalisation of child marriage, new measures to promote gender equality, and efforts to combat corruption.

The EU’s assessment of Azerbaijan in 2025 is critical but balanced.

Civil society under pressure

In 2025, civil society organisations continued to operate under restrictive conditions.

The EU notes that the 2017 Law on Non-Governmental Organisations remains in force. Registration, reporting and grant approval requirements continue to restrict the activities of independent organisations.

Local organisations reported persistent administrative pressure and increased scrutiny.

The departure of several UN agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme and UNICEF, also affected their operating environment. This reduced opportunities for international monitoring and assistance.

The EU says it continues to support civil society, independent media and human rights defenders, including through human rights monitoring and legal assistance programmes for vulnerable groups.

Concerns over the judiciary and the rule of law

According to the EU, problems related to the rule of law and judicial independence persist.

The assessment says courts lack sufficient independence when handling politically sensitive cases.

The report cites judgments by the European Court of Human Rights as an important indicator of the problems that remain.

In 2025, the ECHR issued 39 judgments in cases concerning Azerbaijan and found violations in 38 of them. Most cases involved the right to a fair trial, deprivation of liberty, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

The report also notes that Azerbaijan’s failure to implement ECHR judgments has affected the country’s relations with the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

Electoral system remains unchanged

The EU notes that Azerbaijan’s electoral system underwent no changes in 2025.

The country did not carry out major reforms aimed at implementing the long-standing recommendations of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

The report identifies the lack of progress in this area as one of the persistent challenges to Azerbaijan’s democratic development.

Progress in some areas

The EU report also notes a number of legislative changes.

In July 2025, Azerbaijan criminalised child marriage.

The authorities approved a National Action Plan on Gender Equality for 2026–2028 and amended the Law on Combating Corruption.

The amendments include provisions on whistleblower protection and corruption risk management.

At the same time, the EU notes that the implementation of these measures remains uneven.

Dialogue continues, reforms remain limited

Throughout 2025, the EU maintained regular contacts with the Azerbaijani authorities.

These included meetings with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the Ombudsman and the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations.

The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Tourists among those evacuated from Croatia as wildfires stretch across Europe
World.content:
A wildfire engulfed homes in a picturesque Croatian resort overnight, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of "very extreme" wildfire conditions stretched across the continent.

Hundreds more were evacuated from a beach resort in northern Greece and from a village in southwest France, while a major grass fire engulfed houses in England, officials said.

England's Stourbridge saw multiple homes lost after a grass fire began on the hottest day of the year. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Record-breaking heat and drought that scientists link to climate change have created ideal conditions for wildfires across Europe this summer, especially in France, Spain and Greece. The Balkans region has also endured several heatwaves.

Flames turn night sky red

Local residents and tourists described scenes of chaos as they fled in their cars from a fire outside Omis, a scenic town on Croatia's prized Dalmatian coast surrounded by trees and rocky hills.

Mario Vukucis stands next to his brother's burnt-out cafe and bar in Stanici, Croatia. (Reuters: Antonio Bronic)

"The flames were licking both sides of the road. When I got a little further around the bend and looked, I saw flames shooting up from under my hood. The car was on fire!" said local resident Ljubica Uglesic.

Nearly 300 fire fighters were deployed to a blaze in Croatia. (Reuters: Antonio Bronic)

The fire, which turned the night sky red, appeared to have calmed on Friday morning, said Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucakovic.

Authorities found one charred body while, of 40 people treated in the nearby hospital in Split, seven were in a serious condition, the hospital said.

Dinghies help in rescue from Greek seaside town

In northern Greece, people wearing face masks, some clutching children or pets, boarded dinghies and boats in the seaside town of Siviri as the fire devoured a forest and columns of smoke turned the cloudless sky a dark grey.

The coastguard said that more than 300 people had been evacuated by boat from the town, which sits on a peninsula of woodland, olive groves and beaches south of Greece's second city, Thessaloniki.

Those forced to flee found shelter through the Red Cross and tourists were among the evacuees. (Reuters: Alexandros Avramidis)

More than 140 firefighters, nine aircraft and seven helicopters were deployed to battle flames, while fishing vessels took part in the evacuation.

In Britain, Simon Markey was playing golf in Stourbridge, in central England, when he saw a fire start in a field nearby and spread quickly across the golf course despite efforts by firefighters to contain it.

It reached an area of houses, said local resident Paul Nash, whose neighbour's house burned down.

Ten homes were burnt in fires in England, while two fire fighters and a child were taken to hospital. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

"I heard a scream, and all the trees along the railway track were exploding. They weren't just setting fire, they were exploding. So we just grabbed everything and left," Mr Nash said.

In France, authorities evacuated 525 people from the village of Luglon after a wildfire broke out in the southwestern Landes region, not far from an area already devastated by major blazes this summer.

Fires near Bordeaux have remained consistent throughout summer. (AP: Emma Da Silva)

Rescue services in Spain late on Thursday launched an operation to remove the remains of three kings who ruled the Aragón region in the 11th ​century from a monastery threatened by a wildfire.

An even larger fire in Huelva, in southern Spain, has burned 31,000 hectares so far and forced the evacuation of 700 people.

Only 100 kilometres from a region which saw 50,000 hectares fire-damaged last month, the south of France continues to burn. (Reuters: Stephanie Lecocq)

Firefighting planes in Spain have clocked more than 8,200 hours flying time so far this year, exceeding the number of hours flown in 2025, when a record 393,000 hectares of land burned, Spain's Environment Minister Sara Aagesen said on Bluesky.

'Very extreme' wildfire condition across Europe

The European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service warned of "very extreme" conditions across a large area of central and eastern Europe, with additional pockets over southern Britain, Ireland, northern France and southern Sweden, in its outlook for the week to August 19.

By Friday a fire in Germany had affected 300 hectares of land and encroached on residential homes. (Reuters: Timm Reichert)

The average high across Western Europe on Friday was forecast to be 31.2 degrees Celsius (88 degrees Fahrenheit), which is 8 C (14 F) above what was typical from 1961 to 1990, data from the Reuters Climate Monitor showed. The temperature for Europe as a whole was 1.6 C (2.9 F) above the 1961-1990 average, it said.

The hot, dry summer is also taking a heavy toll on agriculture. Relentless heat and drought could halve this year's French maize harvest and reduce European Union production to its smallest in decades, according to analysts.

Reuters

World.title: Deborah Mailman becomes first Indigenous inductee to Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Deborah Mailman is set to become the first Indigenous person to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame.

"This means everything," Mailman, a Bidjara and Maori actor, tells ABC Radio National's Awaye!

"For me and for our mob, this isn't just recognition for me.

"It's recognition for everyone who's gone before me, who changed things for someone like me to be doing the work that I'm doing."

On Sunday Mailman will become the sixth woman to join the list in just over 40 years, following recent inductees Rebecca Gibney (2024) and Magda Szubanski (2025).

"Times are changing, thankfully, but it's 2026," Mailman says.

"To be the first [Indigenous person] — it's long overdue. Not just for me, but for anyone in this industry."

Mailman sees the milestone as a reflection of how Australian TV has changed in the last 10 to 20 years.

"Where the most exciting storytelling is coming from is the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sector," she says.

"It's just getting stronger and stronger … look at the skill that's there, that has been nurtured over a long time, to get to the point where we have so many of our mob doing incredible work."

2026 Logie nominations The annual awards show also introduced a new category honouring Australian sports journalists, named after legendary commentator Bruce McAvaney.

Mailman picked up her most recent Logie in 2024, taking out best lead actress in a drama for playing renegade politician Alex Irving in ABC TV's Total Control.

It was her sixth, following industry and publicly voted wins for shows including Mabo, Redfern Now and Mystery Road.

Speaking to ABC Arts at the Logies that year, she described how it felt to win the award for the show's final season in the year of the failed Voice to Parliament referendum.

"Over the four or so years [of making Total Control], we had a new prime minister, throw a pandemic in the middle of it, and then the country voted no," she said.

"To be part of this production that kept us [Indigenous peoples] in that focus, that kept our narrative strong, that meant everything to me. That meant everything to all of us who are part of it."

A foot in the door

Mailman's first Logie came in 2002 for her first small-screen role as the optimistic and generous Kelly Lewis in share house drama The Secret Life of Us, an award she won again in 2004.

She started her acting career on the stage, which saw her co-write and star in the seminal play The 7 Stages of Grieving in 1994, before she played Nona in director Rachel Perkins's film Radiance in 1998, landing her an AFI Award (now AACTA) for best lead actress.

Three years later she scored her breakthrough TV gig with The Secret Life of Us.

Mailman looks back fondly at making the show, which catapulted its cast, including Gold Logie winner Samuel Johnson and 2026 Logie nominee Claudia Karvan, into the mainstream.

"That experience really gave me my training in front of a camera," Mailman says.

"It introduced me to the art of filmmaking."

Mailman with her Secret Life of Us co-stars, including Claudia Karvan and Joel Edgerton. (ABC iview)

She especially loved how relatable the storylines felt, not just to her and the rest of the cast, but to the audience.

"It was such a big new adventure for me and I just loved every moment of it," Mailman says.

There, at that apartment building in St Kilda, Mailman met lifelong friends and collaborators.

"It was my first real foot into the [screen] industry," she says.

"To be supported in the way that I have been, right from the get-go, has been really important."

Telling First Nations stories

After The Secret Life of Us, Mailman featured as Lorraine in Redfern Now (earning another Logie), as a guest star of sketch series Black Comedy, and in movies including the musicals Bran Nue Dae and The Sapphires.

In 2012 Mailman starred as Lorraine in Redfern Now. Four years later, she picked up the Logie for most outstanding actress. (ABC TV)

More recently she's played Kerry in Mystery Road, Aunty Linda in Indigenous superhero series Cleverman, and a nun in Warwick Thornton's award-winning The New Boy.

Roles like these are just a handful of the Indigenous-led projects Mailman has taken on throughout her career.

"That's where a lot of my work has gravitated towards: working with my own mob and telling stories that matter to me and my family and many communities around the country," she says.

She sees it as a kind of correction after First Nations stories were excluded from Australian screens for many years.

"Our voices weren't there," Mailman says.

"Now to be part of that canon of storytelling that shows the breadth and diversity and dynamic of who we are as people and our culture and what our stories are means everything to me."

Mailman is proud to follow in the footsteps of other Indigenous trailblazers on both screen and stage, including Justine Saunders (The Fringe Dwellers), Kylie Belling (Until the End of the World) and National Black Theatre founders Bob Maza and Gary Foley.

"They were instrumental in providing opportunities that are there for me now," she says.

Mailman also admires other Indigenous community leaders and activists who are not from the performing arts world.

"They're the people I have to thank because they fought the hard fight," she says.

Mailman feels privileged to potentially inspire the next generation of First Nations actors and creatives, alongside her peers and collaborators Perkins and Leah Purcell (The Drover's Wife).

"A whole bunch of us grew up professionally together," Mailman says.

"I'm part of that community and I'm proud of that.

"I'm really proud I'm still doing what I'm doing and that I've been part of this group of artists who've led by example."

Celebrating Blak excellence

Mailman joins the Logies Hall of Fame in a year dominated by Indigenous stories and storytellers.

Half of the nominees for most popular new talent are First Nations actors: 10-year-old Eloise Hart (Mystery Road: Origin, Goolagong), Lila McGuire (Goolagong) and Tamala (Ghosts Australia).

2026 Logies: First Nations excellence With strong representation of Indigenous talent in this year's Logie nominations, actor Lila McGuire says it's a "very important time" and "a gift for young mob".

The same is true for best lead actor in a drama, with Hunter Page-Lochard (Reckless), Mark Coles Smith (Mystery Road: Origin), and Rob Collins (RFDS); and best supporting actor, with Clarence Ryan (Mystery Road: Origin) against Thomas Weatherall, nominated twice (Heartbreak High; The Narrow Road to the Deep North).

Meanwhile, Goolagong is up for best miniseries, Mystery Road: Origin for best drama program, and Miranda Tapsell's Top End Bub for best scripted comedy.

For Mailman, being recognised in the same year as so many Indigenous nominees makes being inducted into the Hall of Fame this year even more special.

"That speaks volumes to me," she says.

" It's so exciting to have that many of our actors be acknowledged in this way, which demonstrates absolutely their excellence in their craft. "

It also means being inducted in front of close friends such as Collins.

"There's going to be mob in the room!" Mailman says.

"It's going to be a real joy to have that energy, to know that everyone else is being celebrated along with me.

"It's just a big warm hug."

World.title: Multi-million dollar art recovered after three-minute Italian museum heist
World.content:
Three century-old paintings believed to have been stolen by an organised gang have been recovered, months after the criminals broke into an Italian museum in a three-minute heist.

The fine artworks are the 1919 impressionist painting Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's 1887 Still Life with Cherries, and the 1922 Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.

Authorities said the Cézanne was valued at six million euros ($9.79 million), the Renoir at three million euros ($4.89 million), and the Matisse at 20,000 euros ($32,665).

Fish by Pierre-Auguste Renoir. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

Italy's Carabinieri, the domestic police force, and its cultural heritage protection unit confirmed in a statement on Friday, local time, the paintings were discovered during searched ordered by prosecutors.

The police did not provide details of the searches, but said investigations into the heist were ongoing.

Cup And Plate Of Cherries by Paul Cezanne. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

How Italy's three-minute art museum heist unfolded

The heist at the Italy's Magnani Rocca Foundation, located about 20 kilometres south of Parma in the country's north, took place on the night of March 22, according to police.

Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse. (Reuters: Supplied/Fondazione Magnani Rocca)

Authorities at the time said they believed the masked thieves forced open an entrance door, while local media reported they managed to take the paintings in less than three minutes before escaping across the museum's gardens.

In the days after the heist, Italy's La Repubblica newspaper reported the thieves entered the museum's grounds via an unlit, country access road after sawing three bars off a back gate.

They then forced the building's front door open with a crowbar and accessed the museum's French Room on the upper floor by breaking down its doors, the outlet said.

CCTV from inside the museum shows the masked thieves removing the works of art from the walls of an upper floor room. (Reuters: Supplied/Carabineiri Parma)

The newspaper said an interior alarm startled the group, who then fled and were believed to have lost a fourth painting — the three million euro ($4.9 million) Paysage de Cagnes also by Renoir — during their escape.

Carabinieri officers and private security contractors who arrived at the museum later said they spotted the group on thermal imaging cameras while inside the building, but were unable to stop them fleeing.

The Magnani Rocca Foundation was established by art historian Luigi Mangini in 1977, aimed at promoting cultural activities around art, music and literature.

The security vision also shows the thieves running through an open foyer area to escape through a window. (Supplied: Carabineiri Parma)

The foundation hosts Mr Mangini's collection of art and also includes works by Dürer, Rubens, Van Dyck, Goya and Monet.

Apart from its showcased art, the building is known for its spacious gardens, often roamed by a muster of white peacocks.

Mr Mangini lived in the greenhouse on the villa's grounds until his death in 1984.

Experts stunned by theft of 'recognisable' art

During its investigation of the heist, the Carabinieri's RIS forensic agency and the force's dedicated art recovery squad analysed CCTV footage from the villa on the night of the theft.

Magnani Rocca Foundation museum villa is renowned for its spacious gardens and white peacocks. (Instagram: Francesca Fietta/magnanirocca)

La Repubblica reported in April that authorities believed the gang consisted of up to five people, who police were trying to "height match" as part of identikit efforts.

One source told Reuters they had been surprised at the thieves' choice of works of relatively low value from the museum's permanent collections.

The ⁠lack of commercial insurance in Italy for paintings like those that were stolen is not uncommon, market sources say.

Art historian Silvia Evangelisti told La Repubblica the heist was "a very strange theft".

"These works are so recognisable that it's impossible to imagine the market they could be sold on," she said.

"They could have stolen older works, which Luigi Magnani's precious and refined collection is full of.

"Perhaps they were disturbed by their location on the first floor; they were in a hurry to act so they could escape more quickly."

Italian art expert Claudio Strinati echoed that sentiment.

"Renoir's painting — for example — is very beautiful but, within the context of the foundation as a whole, it isn't among the most important works," he told The Associated Press.

Simone dall'Orto, the mayor of the Traversetolo commune to the south-east of the museum, said the thievery had "dismayed" local residents.

"It affects not only an artistic heritage of extraordinary value, but the very identity of our community," he said.

The crime also followed a series of high-profile heists at major European museums, including the stunning theft in October of French crown jewels and other items worth 88 million euros ($143.7 million) from the Louvre in Paris.

ABC/Wires

World.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down a drone over Latvia
World.content:
A NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, a spokesperson from the alliance says, confirming earlier statements by Latvia's defence ministry and military.

The military alliance has launched an investigation, the spokesperson said on Friday, local time, as concerns grow in Europe over unauthorised drone activity — particularly along the military alliance's eastern flank bordering Russia, whose war in Ukraine grinds on.

Ukraine's drone attacks on Russia could backfire Ukraine is firing drones deep inside Russian territory almost every day since June, but some analysts argue it could give Vladimir Putin an excuse to escalate his war.

It was not immediately clear where the drone shot down over Latvia had come from.

"We can confirm that two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled earlier today in response to a drone over Latvian airspace," a NATO spokesperson said.

"One of the Eurofighters shot down the drone," they added, saying that "two Turkish F-16 fighter jets were also scrambled" and all aircraft "were operating under NATO command".

Earlier on Friday, Latvia's defence ministry wrote on X that NATO "fighter jets have successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle that had entered Latvia as a result of Russian electromagnetic warfare".

Both Russia and Ukraine are relying on heavy use of drones to launch attacks in the four-year conflict.

Latvia, an EU and NATO member state of about 1.9 million inhabitants, shares a border with Russia to the east.

It and other countries along NATO's eastern flank including Romania and Poland have suffered repeated incursions into their airspace.

Russia dismisses Black Sea ceasefire

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks in recent weeks against commercial ships in the Black Sea. (Reuters: Victor Sayenko)

Russia on Friday dismissed the idea of a ceasefire with Ukraine in the Black Sea, saying it saw no grounds for "half-measures" that would offer a respite to the other side.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks in recent weeks against commercial ships in the Black Sea, driving world grain prices higher.

Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks On the outskirts of Russian cities, warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer are being struck by Kyiv's drones, with some analysts saying it could lead to a financial crisis.

In a statement, Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of "brazen acts of terrorism" against shipping, while making no mention of Russia's own attacks.

"We view these attacks as a deliberate policy aimed at destabilising civilian shipping in the Black Sea region to further escalate tensions and prolong the conflict, all with the blatant acquiescence of regional neighbours," Ms Zakharova said.

"At the same time, we see no signs of improvement in the situation and, consequently, no grounds for half-measures that merely grant the Kyiv regime a temporary breathing space."

Ms Zakharova said she was commenting on a statement by Türkiye's foreign minister in a media interview that Ankara had put proposals to both Russia and Ukraine for a moratorium on military operations in the Black Sea.

She said Russia had received no formal proposal from Türkiye.

No peace talks on Ukraine have taken place since February, when the United States went to war with Iran and broke off its efforts to mediate between Moscow and Kyiv.

3 dead and 20 injured in latest attacks on Ukraine

Ukrainian rescuers working to extinguish a fire in a damaged residential building following an air attack in Donetsk. (AFP: Ukrainian Emergency Service)

Russia attacked 12 Ukrainian regions overnight, wounding dozens of people, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

In Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, a Russian glide bomb demolished six floors of a 10-story apartment block, killing one person and wounding 16 others, he said.

North Korea benefits from Russia alliance Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in an attack that killed a Ukrainian family. It could be part of a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Russian jet-powered drones also struck a home in northern Ukraine on Friday, local time, killing a 29-year-old woman and her nine-year-old son, officials said.

A Russian strike in northern Ukraine's Sumy region also wounded four other people, including the dead boy’s father and grandmother, who were hospitalised with severe burns, the regional military administration chief said.

Ukrainian forces, meanwhile, extended their long-range strike campaign against Russian infrastructure, hitting the port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region north of Moscow and starting a brief fire, its governor said.

Ust-Luga is one of Russia's largest oil and gas export terminals located more than 800 kilometres from Ukraine.

It has been a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks this summer, as Kyiv seeks to undermine Russian oil exports that provide Moscow with vital revenue for its war effort.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its air defences on Friday intercepted 553 Ukrainian drones over 18 Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the waters of the Azov and the Black seas.

ABC/wires

World.title: Cory Bernardi condemned for anti-trans slur, labelling protesters 'incels'
World.content:
A social media video from One Nation MP Cory Bernardi in which he uses an anti-trans slur and describes protesters as a "bunch of incels" has been condemned by organisers of yesterday's SA rally against his party.

WARNING: This story contains language that some readers could find offensive.

Hundreds of people, many of them school students, attended Thursday's event outside SA parliament, which was part of nationwide protests against One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson.

Mr Bernardi, who was elected to the Legislative Council at the March state election, appeared on the steps of parliament, where he began filming the event before roaming through the protest.

In a video from the event which he later posted on social media, he repeatedly shouted "it's a tranny", and at one point referred to the protesters as "a bunch of incels".

Sam Ats and Jordan Armstrong were among the organisers of the anti-One Nation protest. (ABC News: Kathryn Bermingham)

One of the organisers of the SA event, Year 11 student Sam Ats, described Mr Bernardi's comments towards the protesters as "appalling".

"Cory Bernardi is a 56-year-old man who is bullying teenagers and high-schoolers, calling them slurs, recording them without their consent to bully and intimidate people who are trying to make their voice heard," the 17-year-old said.

Another organiser, university student Jordan Armstrong, who identifies as a transgender man, also condemned Mr Bernardi's behaviour towards the protesters.

"Calling them slurs and harassing them, it's actually quite embarrassing for him," he said.

"It was pretty pathetic."

Jordan Armstrong described Mr Bernardi's comments as "pathetic". (ABC News: Kathryn Bermingham)

The rally on the steps of South Australia's parliament on North Terrace was one of several protests across the country against One Nation's national leader Pauline Hanson.

Protesters repeatedly chanted "f*** Pauline Hanson".

Asked whether that was inflammatory, Sam Ats responded: "I'd say that saying, 'There's no such thing as a good Muslim' is inflammatory."

Mr Bernardi posted two videos from the event on Instagram, including one in which he described the protesters as an "assortment of weirdos", adding that there were "some 'furries' there".

"I saw some weird-looking chick with pointy elf ears on, uh there was plenty of transvestites and things like that, and they're all chanting for a socialist agenda," he said.

"There were oldies there, and I say oldies, people my age, helping these kids."

Cory Bernardi wandered through the protest while filming on his phone. (Instagram)

In a second video, filmed on the steps of parliament, he described the protesters as "total losers" who "don't want to be at school today" and as "a bunch of incels who are now promoting socialism".

"I'm just going to go down there and say g'day," he said to his phone camera, before roaming through the protest and approaching attendees.

"Why aren't you chanting?" he asked one teenager.

That video was accompanied by Taylor Swift's song I Knew It, I Knew You, which was written for the film Toy Story 5.

The use of the music coincides with controversy in the US, where some of the songs of the pop star, who has been outspoken against conservative politics in recent years, have been removed from social media videos posted by Donald Trump's campaign and the White House.

Corey Bernardi records a video on the steps of Parliament House. (ABC News)

Mr Bernardi was also the subject of chants on Thursday. After he approached young attendees, protesters began chanting "f*** Cory Bernardi".

Mr Bernardi later told media that the protesters "don't know what they're talking about" and described the gathering as "an assortment of incels, unintelligent, unemployable people".

The ABC has contacted Mr Bernardi and One Nation for comment.

World.title: Freo locks up minor premiership after downing Crows in thriller
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Caleb Serong played a starring role as Fremantle snared just the second minor premiership in the club's history with a 24-point win over Adelaide in Perth.

Scores were level early in the final quarter of Friday night's blockbuster following Crows forward Riley Thilthorpe's second goal of the night.

But buoyed by a thundering 55,010-strong crowd, Fremantle did what it has done all season — blowing its rival off the park with a devastating burst.

Michael Frederick started the run when he nailed a tough set shot after being tackled high.

Jye Amiss (centre) kicked 5.1 in the win while Josh Treacy (right) took six contested marks. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Although Josh Treacy, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw missed their shots after that, Amiss bobbed up for his fifth goal of the night by snapping from the goalsquare.

And when Isaiah Dudley dodged and weaved his way through three Crows players before unleashing a successful snap, the margin was 22 points and it was game over.

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox rubbed it in by roughing up an opponent and then pointing to the scoreboard after kicking a goal in the dying minutes of the 16.16 (112) to 13.10 (88) win.

The triumph boosted Fremantle's record to 19-3, securing the club a second minor premiership to go with their 2013 efforts.

It also meant Fremantle will end the home-and-away season with a perfect 12-0 record at Perth Stadium.

Adelaide (14-8) now faces a huge battle to snare a top-four berth, with the loss even leaving them vulnerable to slipping into the dreaded wildcard spots from seventh to 10th.

Amiss finished with 5.1 in a powerful display, Josh Treacy was huge with six contested marks but a wayward 1.4, Dudley kicked three goals, while Serong was influential with 29 disposals, 12 clearances, 536m gained and two goals.

Crows playmaker Izak Rankine racked up a monster 14 disposals in the opening term on the way to 39 possessions, 10 clearances, 717m gained and one goal.

Adelaide star Izak Rankine finished the match with a game-high 39 disposals. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Adelaide had an interesting lead-in to the match, with players forced to evacuate their hotel just hours before bounce down due to a fire alarm going off in their hotel.

Amiss missed an early set shot sitter from 15m out as Adelaide skipped out to a two-goal lead.

But Amiss soon made amends, nailing three other set shots for the term — from 50m, 40m and 35m — to give Fremantle a 13-point edge by quarter time.

Fremantle led by just five points at half-time, and the third quarter was a rollercoaster ride featuring four lead changes and five occasions when the scores were even.

Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce suffered a huge scare when his heavily-strapped left knee hyper-extend during a collision, leaving him hobbled for the next couple of minutes.

The action was fierce and fast, but it was Fremantle who produced more of the memorable moments.

Treacy hurt himself while completing a team-lifting tackle on Max Michalanney.

The Fremantle powerhouse dusted himself off after a few deep breaths and kicked a goal moments later.

Serong nailed a goal from just inside the centre square following a dazzling series of handballs from the Dockers.

And when Brayshaw dribbled one through with the outside of his right boot, Fremantle turned for home with a seven-point edge.

The Dockers kicked five goals to three in a powerful final term to wrap up top spot on the ladder with one round to spare.

World.title: Tasmanian woman charged over alleged 'series' of attempted poisonings
World.content:
A 43-year-old South Launceston woman has been charged over what police allege is a "series of attempted poisonings".

Tasmania Police allege that over a period of months, the woman had delivered "intentionally contaminated drinks to a 47-year-old man on several separate occasions".

"The man did not consume the drinks and was not physically injured," police said on Friday night.

The man and the woman "were known to each other", police said, and "there is no indication that contaminated drinks were sent to any other person".

Police said on Friday they had charged the woman with two counts of attempted unlawfully administering poison with intent to harm.

She has been detained to appear in court.

World.title: Tobacco, firearms, silver, gold seized in joint Victorian, Tasmanian operation
World.content:
Two men have been charged and one arrested after a joint police investigation into the alleged movement of millions of dollars in cash from Tasmania to Victoria.

A 33-year-old from Hoppers Crossing, Victoria, and a 22-year-old from Sorell, Tasmania, appeared in Melbourne Magistrates Court on August 12 following raids involving officers from Australian Federal Police, Tasmania Police, Victoria Police, and Australian Border Force.

Both men were charged with knowingly deal proceeds of crime and recklessly deal proceeds of crime.

Police say more than $2.5 million worth of tobacco products were seized. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

In a statement, the AFP said it is alleged they facilitated the movement of criminal proceeds in cash from Tasmania and Victoria using hire cars and a commercial passenger and freight vessel.

Both were bailed to reappear in court on December 2, 2026.

A third man, 37, from Hoppers Crossing, was arrested and later released. He is expected to be charged via summons.

Police allege the men facilitated the movement of criminal proceeds in cash from Tasmania and Victoria using hire cars and boats. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

During the investigation — which started with intelligence from the Tasmania Police Crime and Intelligence Command — investigators identified the alleged movement of criminal assets between the states.

Tasmania Joint Organised Crime Taskforce (TAS JOCTF) members "subsequently executed search warrants at properties in Melrose and Sorell in Tasmania on 11 August, 2026", the AFP said.

" Coordinated warrants were executed on the same day in Hoppers Crossing, Victoria, by members of the Victoria Police VIPER Taskforce, which arrested the three men. "

During the search warrants, officers seized more than $2.5 million worth of tobacco product, more than $1 million in cash, 9 kilograms of silver bars (worth more than $30,000) and one ounce of gold (worth more than $4,000), the AFP said.

Police also seized five imitation firearms, including a gel blaster firearm, three registered firearms, a .22 rifle and ammunition, a cash-counting machine and mobile devices, the AFP said.

Police say the investigation started with intelligence provided by Tasmanian police. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

AFP Detective Superintendent Ray Imbriano said the arrests followed "strong collaboration from the AFP's commonwealth and state law enforcement partners".

"This operation would not have been possible without the close cooperation between commonwealth and state law enforcement agencies on both sides of Bass Strait, and I thank all members involved," Superintendent Imbriano said.

The AFP said the men face a maximum sentence of 25 years' imprisonment if convicted.

World.title: Deborah Mailman makes history as first Indigenous person inducted into Logies Hall of Fame
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Sunday night, Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame, as well as only the sixth woman. “I had a moment of almost bursting into tears,” she says. “I couldn’t quite understand it all, to be honest. It took some time for it to land because I was like, ‘Are you sure?’ I had to re-read the email and go, ‘Hang on, what?’ And then when I started thinking [about it], I got really quite emotional about it.” Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame on Sunday night. Jessica Hromas/eyevine/Headpress The award, which began in 1984, recognises “outstanding and continued contribution and enrichment to Australian television culture by an individual, a group of individuals, or a program”. Mailman will be one of three inductees on the night, with the other two revealed during the ceremony. For Mailman – whose breakthrough came in the 1998 film Radiance, followed by roles in the TV series The Secret Life of Us, Redfern Now, Cleverman, Offspring and Total Control, as well as the films Rabbit-Proof Fence, The Sapphires and Bran Nue Dae – the fact she is the first Indigenous person to receive the honour is a source of enormous pride but also conflicted emotion. Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards “This is not being disrespectful ... but it’s a long time coming,” she says. “And I don’t mean that for just for me, but in terms of us as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country, and in this industry, because I’m a beneficiary of the many people who have gone before me and who’ve worked their asses off for someone like me to be a beneficiary and to have these opportunities, so I acknowledge that I’m only here because of the hard work that’s gone before.”



The fact that she is only one of six women to receive the honour – joining Magda Szubanski, Rebecca Gibney, Kerri-Anne Kennerley, Noni Hazlehurst and Ruth Cracknell – is also something Mailman wanted to acknowledge. “I don’t know if there’s any sort of sugarcoating that,” she says. “I mean, it has been an industry built for some time for certain people. But now we’ve seen in the past decade or so, even longer than that, when we look at storytelling in this country and where that excitement has been for some time, and the voices that haven’t been there before, and the representation around so many voices that have never had a foot in the door, that’s what it’s about.” Deborah Mailman with her The Secret Life of Us co-stars (from left) Samuel Johnson, Joel Edgerton, Spencer McLaren and Abi Tucker at the 2002 Logie Awards, at which Mailman won most outstanding actress in a drama series. Getty Images Deborah Mailman with her most outstanding actress Logie in 2004. Paul Harris Deborah Mailman at the 2024 Logie Awards, where she won Best Lead Actress in a Drama for Total Control, with her co-star Rachel Griffiths. Getty Images That Mailman, 54, has become one of the most recognisable and beloved faces on screen is still a surprise to her. Growing up in Mount Isa, she only took to acting when faced with the alternative: business studies. “I didn’t choose it to become an actor,” she says, laughing. “I just thought, ‘Yeah, I didn’t want to do that, so I’ll try this [drama].’ And I just had two really great teachers throughout high school that saw something or supported me, and I just loved drama. I wasn’t an academic, I was average at best, and … I was very shy and that helped with my confidence.”



Related Article ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage In many ways, Mailman’s life can be measured in firsts: her first screen role, in Radiance, landed her the Australian Film Institute award for best actress in a leading role, making her the first Indigenous woman to do so; her first TV role in The Secret Life of Us, in which she played student Kelly Lewis, landed her Logies for outstanding actress in a drama series in 2002 and 2004. She has won six Logies in total, including for the TV film Mabo, the ABC dramas Redfern Now, Mystery Road, Total Control and the Nine shark drama Bite Club. “I still pinch myself that I’m still in this industry – and I’m still in love with it,” she says. “It’s a hard industry to be a part of, and when I signed up at 17 years of age, I had no idea what this was going to look like for me. And the fact that I’m still here and still getting great opportunities, and getting really good work, that’s not lost for me.” Deborah Mailman, pictured with Rachel Maza, in Radiance, the film for which she made history as the first Aboriginal actress to win the Australian Film Institute Award for best actress in a leading role. She still gets approached the most by fans of The Secret Life of Us, and Play School, and in many ways still considers herself to be a “shy kid”, so it’s no great surprise to hear that she is “really, really, really nervous” about the prospect of standing on stage on Sunday, with all eyes turned in her direction. “This is doing my head in,” she says. “Having been at these events before, you’re part of a production, you’ve got your co-workers, your colleagues around you, and you’re celebrating together. This is a very different feeling, and, yeah, I’m really, really, really nervous, but I’m also trying to just enjoy what this is about as well.” Maybe she could channel her Total Control character, the fearless senator Alex Irving, and just get up there and let them have it?

World.title: Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win
World.content:
So that is that.

With three-and-a-half rounds of football still remaining, the top eight has all but been decided.

Loading

This is a rivalry often celebrated on a Good Friday, but for Canterbury this is a very black one indeed. With everything to play for, Cameron Ciraldo’s team didn’t register a point until Enari Tuala went over in the 63rd minute. By then, it was too little, too late.

In defeating Canterbury, Souths have effectively ended their season and extended their own. While there may be some permutation that would allow the Bulldogs to scrape into the play-offs, so poor is their for-and-against that you can effectively put a line through them.

Asked if he was still hopeful of qualifying for the post-season, Ciraldo replied: “Hope’s not a strategy.

“All we can control is how we play next Saturday night. That’s all we can worry about now, we can’t worry about anything else.”

In climbing, at least temporarily, above Newcastle into sixth spot, the Rabbitohs have almost certainly booked their first finals appearance since 2022.

David Fifita scores against Canterbury. Getty Images

Thursday night’s Roosters-Panthers clash – the best game of the year to date – was a defensive masterclass. Inspired by what they had witnessed just 24 hours earlier, Souths showed similar resolve on their line.

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton seemed try-bound early, only for Jack Wighton to somehow contort his body under the ball to make a save. Jethro Rinakama was also bound for glory, only for Cameron Murray to produce an equalling stunning stop. It is a fair turnaround for a side that conceded over 29 points per game since Round 18.

“They are vital, they make a difference in a game,” Souths coach Wayne Bennett said about the desperation on the goal-line.

“Stopping them on the tryline from getting the ball down, everyone gets confidence from that … It’s a state of mind. They can do it, they don’t always want to do it.

“They are learning how to win, these guys, what works for them and what doesn’t. Today they applied it for 80 minutes and got a great result.”

The best defensive stop of the night, however, belonged to Crichton. His decision to invade the space of referee Ashley Klein proved a try-saving one.

Under the pump for much of the opening quarter, the Rabbitohs were rewarded for not cracking. David Fifita, the best on ground, pounced on a Cody Walker grubber to open the scoring. Only moments earlier, a similar grubber from Lachlan Galvin went dead-in-goal.

Loading

Fifita and Crichton, meanwhile, kept finding each other. The Maroons forward ran straight over the top of his opponent in the eighth minute, the collision of the night. Crichton, to his credit, didn’t back down and had a few personal wins of his own, like the penalty he milked from the back-rower late in the opening half.

Walker also had a hand in the second try, yet another example of the ball singing along that lethal left edge. If there is a better job in rugby league than being Alex Johnston, we are yet to find it.

Canterbury needed to start the second half well. Souths kicked off and the ball – and the Bulldogs’ finals prospects – slipped through Bailey Hayward’s hands.

It’s a good thing this didn’t come down to goal-kicking. Bud Sullivan kicked just the seventh goal of his career, and then appeared to injure his groin in attempting an eighth. A decade after making his NRL debut, it was left to Matt Dufty to stand over the tee for the first time. Late in the game, there was an opportunity to extend the lead beyond two converted tries with a penalty goal. Bereft of options, they tapped and scored. It will be an area of concern for the tighter, more important games that lay ahead.

World.title: Strict bail conditions for Setka after being charged for a third time
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka made menacing posts on social media about a former CFMEU administrator, suggesting he take “anti-c--- tablets”, police allege. The 61-year-old was arrested on Friday morning and faced the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court later in the evening, where prosecutors applied to have Setka’s existing bail revoked. Loading During his subsequent application for bail, the court heard that on Monday, Setka had taken to Instagram to share nine images directed at senior figures of the CFMEU. “Images posted depicted the following: an image of Murray Furlong, the general manager of the Federal Commission, two memes with a couple sitting at a park and the title saying ‘say goodbye to being a c---’, and a smaller medication image labelled ‘anti-c---’ tablets,” the investigating police officer told the court.



The court also heard two images of Mark Irving, the former administrator of the CFMEU, and an image of Matthew McGowan, the current assistant administrator and head of the Victorian branch, were posted by Setka. Further images depicted Elizabeth Lukin, a consultant within the construction industry, and McGowan’s wife, as well as other union figures. Setka was on Friday morning charged with using a telecommunications device to menace, using a telecommunications device to offend and two charges of committing an indictable offence while on bail. The former union boss was first arrested in November and charged with seven counts of using a carriage service to menace, harass and offend the union’s government-appointed administrator, Mark Irving, KC. He was charged a second time, in February, over allegations he issued a threat on Christmas Day to an official from the Albanese government-backed administration that took control of the CFMEU in 2024. The court on Friday heard about the alleged offending that prompted Setka’s first arrest in November last year, with emails sent from his account allegedly telling the administrator that he would “come to the CFMEU office whenever he pleases”.



“[Setka] told the administrator to go f--- their mothers with Nick McKenzie,” the investigating officer said, referring to The Age’s senior investigative reporter. “The accused signed off the email saying that if the administrator leaks any more information that he will fix it himself.” The court heard that following his arrest on Friday morning, Setka “made admissions to posting on social media, and made admissions that it came from his account”. “When the accused was asked about if the social media posts would offend the recipients, he said if that hurts their feelings, he ‘wouldn’t give two f---s and that’s their problem’.” The court heard Setka would pose an unacceptable risk of endangering the safety and welfare of other people, and will “continue to make social media posts”.



“We’re not just talking about that isolated post. We’re looking at a pattern of behaviour from the accused,” he said. John Setka is facing further charges. Victoria Police Defence lawyer Lee Ristivojevic, for Setka, told the court the prosecution’s case was “weak”. “It’s submitted that the nature of the allegations, of the charges, that if he was to be found guilty, he’s not likely to receive a term of imprisonment for the offences,” she said. “We say that it is not a serious example of the offence.” Ristivojevic said Setka had “what I’d described as a positive bail history in terms of court orders”, and that it was “not suggested he’s breached any conditions of bail”. She further submitted that a compelling reason to release Setka on bail was that he provides essential care for his elderly mother.



Related Article Updated

Building Bad Setka charged with harassing a CFMEU administrator Magistrate Nicole Spicer ultimately granted Setka’s bail application, noting that none of the alleged victims had sought personal safety intervention orders. “I do consider that the risk can be brought to an acceptable level by the imposition of conditions targeted to make clear that the particular behaviour that you have allegedly engaged in in making social media commentary of a personal and allegedly harassing nature simply cannot occur whilst you are subject to the grant of bail,” Spicer said. She imposed bail conditions that Setka “not threaten or harass any employee or representative of the CFMEU administrator, or any person named in criminal charges” against him. She further ordered him not to “make posts or comments on any social media platform which are threatening, intimidating or use obscene language directed towards or about such individuals”. Police established Operation Hawk in mid-2024, in response to this masthead’s Building Bad series, which exposed criminal behaviour and corruption in the CFMEU. World.title: Fozball hits unwanted 33-year record in bizarrely boring loss to Dolphins
World.content:
Manly 0 Dolphins 22 SportNRLNRL 2026 Fozball hits unwanted 33-year record in bizarrely boring loss to Dolphins Dan Walsh August 14, 2026 — 8:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

At various points in 2026, Manly have been one of the most exhilarating attacking sides in the NRL. The Dolphins still are, and are finals-bound for the first time in their history as a result. So at half-time in Friday’s clash at 4 Pines Park, you could only ask, what on earth had happened? Loading The same questions remained at full-time too, along with how Selwyn Cobbo defied the laws of man and nature to ground a 57th-minute try in the corner while wearing heavy contact from Clayton Faulalo and Reuben Garrick. From an 8-0 half-time lead, the Dolphins closed out the grittiest of grinding wins with 31 errors in total. But their 22-0 victory margin is really the only take-away in a contest that barely got out of first gear, and never threatened to find second or third.



Manly’s finals hopes, already circling the drain, slipped straight down it when Jamayne Isaako provided another rare highlight – latching onto an intercept and setting up an 85-metre try to NSW Origin flyer Jack Bostock. Loading The locals summed up Manly’s slide into ignominy best. When Lehi Hopoate was denied a late try for putting a hand into touch, fans made an early exit – neatly wrapping up a campaign under Kieran Foran that had once promised so much. ‘Fozball’ is officially done for the season, and Manly were held to zero on home soil for the first time since 1993. “It hurts for sure. We’re a proud club and we certainly have really high hopes for ourselves as a footy team,” Foran said, with Manly’s slew of injured middle forwards, along with sidelined captain Tom Trbojevic, looming large over the past six weeks.



“We understand the expectation of playing in this jersey and playing at this club, and it’s disappointing to be held to nil ... but we’ll grow from this. There are reasons for why it’s been tough and I haven’t liked to use any of those as an excuse.” Until the Dolphins’ backline stars shone brightly enough to seal a win that keeps them in touch with the top four, this Friday night affair was most notable for nothing much happening. Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf, of course, saw a fourth consecutive win for his side differently and was understandably chuffed with keeping Manly scoreless. “Our defence was outstanding,” Woolf said. “Obviously, to keep them to zero, that was great for us, and we showed some great desperation at times. At the start of the game we had a couple of errors that put us under pressure, and to make as many tackles as we did and hold up like we did, I was really proud of that.”



A pair of sin-bins for Manly speedster Tolu Koula (28th minute) and Dolphins back-rower Connelly Lemuelu (35th minute) for professional fouls hardly opened up a 12-on-12 shoot-out. Instead, the visitors’ safety-first footy and home side’s shot confidence held firm. Manly spent much of the first 20 minutes camped on the Dolphins’ tryline. They never threatened to cross it though as passes went to ground and over the sideline. Manly lock Jake Trbojevic. Getty Images After holding firm in defence, the Dolphins offered little in attack themselves before finally crossing the Brookvale Rubicon into Manly’s half in the 25th minute. Even then, their first attacking crack at the Sea Eagles line amounted to only a penalty goal after a Jason Saab high tackle.



Related Article Canterbury 6 South Sydney 22

NRL 2026 Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win When they next came calling, Jeremy Marshall-King snuck out of dummy-half and caught Koula offside, with Kodi Nikorima finally skinning the shortened defence for the opening try. Hopes of a brighter second half were put on ice when Manly’s Jake Simpkins fumbled a ball a metre into the air from dummy-half before regathering, and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow misjudged a kick take by roughly 10 metres. And as much as anything, those two bemusing moments, from two of the game’s more enterprising attacking teams, said it all.

On Sunday night, Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame, as well as only the sixth woman. “I had a moment of almost bursting into tears,” she says. “I couldn’t quite understand it all, to be honest. It took some time for it to land because I was like, ‘Are you sure?’ I had to re-read the email and go, ‘Hang on, what?’ And then when I started thinking [about it], I got really quite emotional about it.” Deborah Mailman will become the first person of First Nations descent to be inducted into the Logie Awards Hall of Fame on Sunday night. Jessica Hromas/eyevine/Headpress The award, which began in 1984, recognises “outstanding and continued contribution and enrichment to Australian television culture by an individual, a group of individuals, or a program”. Mailman will be one of three inductees on the night, with the other two revealed during the ceremony. For Mailman – whose breakthrough came in the 1998 film Radiance, followed by roles in the TV series The Secret Life of Us, Redfern Now, Cleverman, Offspring and Total Control, as well as the films Rabbit-Proof Fence, The Sapphires and Bran Nue Dae – the fact she is the first Indigenous person to receive the honour is a source of enormous pride but also conflicted emotion. Related Article Logies Full list of nominees at the 2026 Logie Awards “This is not being disrespectful ... but it’s a long time coming,” she says. “And I don’t mean that for just for me, but in terms of us as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country, and in this industry, because I’m a beneficiary of the many people who have gone before me and who’ve worked their asses off for someone like me to be a beneficiary and to have these opportunities, so I acknowledge that I’m only here because of the hard work that’s gone before.”



The fact that she is only one of six women to receive the honour – joining Magda Szubanski, Rebecca Gibney, Kerri-Anne Kennerley, Noni Hazlehurst and Ruth Cracknell – is also something Mailman wanted to acknowledge. “I don’t know if there’s any sort of sugarcoating that,” she says. “I mean, it has been an industry built for some time for certain people. But now we’ve seen in the past decade or so, even longer than that, when we look at storytelling in this country and where that excitement has been for some time, and the voices that haven’t been there before, and the representation around so many voices that have never had a foot in the door, that’s what it’s about.” Deborah Mailman with her The Secret Life of Us co-stars (from left) Samuel Johnson, Joel Edgerton, Spencer McLaren and Abi Tucker at the 2002 Logie Awards, at which Mailman won most outstanding actress in a drama series. Getty Images Deborah Mailman with her most outstanding actress Logie in 2004. Paul Harris Deborah Mailman at the 2024 Logie Awards, where she won Best Lead Actress in a Drama for Total Control, with her co-star Rachel Griffiths. Getty Images That Mailman, 54, has become one of the most recognisable and beloved faces on screen is still a surprise to her. Growing up in Mount Isa, she only took to acting when faced with the alternative: business studies. “I didn’t choose it to become an actor,” she says, laughing. “I just thought, ‘Yeah, I didn’t want to do that, so I’ll try this [drama].’ And I just had two really great teachers throughout high school that saw something or supported me, and I just loved drama. I wasn’t an academic, I was average at best, and … I was very shy and that helped with my confidence.”



Related Article ★★★★

Review Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage In many ways, Mailman’s life can be measured in firsts: her first screen role, in Radiance, landed her the Australian Film Institute award for best actress in a leading role, making her the first Indigenous woman to do so; her first TV role in The Secret Life of Us, in which she played student Kelly Lewis, landed her Logies for outstanding actress in a drama series in 2002 and 2004. She has won six Logies in total, including for the TV film Mabo, the ABC dramas Redfern Now, Mystery Road, Total Control and the Nine shark drama Bite Club. “I still pinch myself that I’m still in this industry – and I’m still in love with it,” she says. “It’s a hard industry to be a part of, and when I signed up at 17 years of age, I had no idea what this was going to look like for me. And the fact that I’m still here and still getting great opportunities, and getting really good work, that’s not lost for me.” Deborah Mailman, pictured with Rachel Maza, in Radiance, the film for which she made history as the first Aboriginal actress to win the Australian Film Institute Award for best actress in a leading role. She still gets approached the most by fans of The Secret Life of Us, and Play School, and in many ways still considers herself to be a “shy kid”, so it’s no great surprise to hear that she is “really, really, really nervous” about the prospect of standing on stage on Sunday, with all eyes turned in her direction. “This is doing my head in,” she says. “Having been at these events before, you’re part of a production, you’ve got your co-workers, your colleagues around you, and you’re celebrating together. This is a very different feeling, and, yeah, I’m really, really, really nervous, but I’m also trying to just enjoy what this is about as well.” Maybe she could channel her Total Control character, the fearless senator Alex Irving, and just get up there and let them have it?

World.title: Rabbitohs sink Bulldogs’ finals chances with dominant win
World.content:
So that is that.

With three-and-a-half rounds of football still remaining, the top eight has all but been decided.

Loading

This is a rivalry often celebrated on a Good Friday, but for Canterbury this is a very black one indeed. With everything to play for, Cameron Ciraldo’s team didn’t register a point until Enari Tuala went over in the 63rd minute. By then, it was too little, too late.

In defeating Canterbury, Souths have effectively ended their season and extended their own. While there may be some permutation that would allow the Bulldogs to scrape into the play-offs, so poor is their for-and-against that you can effectively put a line through them.

Asked if he was still hopeful of qualifying for the post-season, Ciraldo replied: “Hope’s not a strategy.

“All we can control is how we play next Saturday night. That’s all we can worry about now, we can’t worry about anything else.”

In climbing, at least temporarily, above Newcastle into sixth spot, the Rabbitohs have almost certainly booked their first finals appearance since 2022.

David Fifita scores against Canterbury. Getty Images

Thursday night’s Roosters-Panthers clash – the best game of the year to date – was a defensive masterclass. Inspired by what they had witnessed just 24 hours earlier, Souths showed similar resolve on their line.

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton seemed try-bound early, only for Jack Wighton to somehow contort his body under the ball to make a save. Jethro Rinakama was also bound for glory, only for Cameron Murray to produce an equalling stunning stop. It is a fair turnaround for a side that conceded over 29 points per game since Round 18.

“They are vital, they make a difference in a game,” Souths coach Wayne Bennett said about the desperation on the goal-line.

“Stopping them on the tryline from getting the ball down, everyone gets confidence from that … It’s a state of mind. They can do it, they don’t always want to do it.

“They are learning how to win, these guys, what works for them and what doesn’t. Today they applied it for 80 minutes and got a great result.”

The best defensive stop of the night, however, belonged to Crichton. His decision to invade the space of referee Ashley Klein proved a try-saving one.

Under the pump for much of the opening quarter, the Rabbitohs were rewarded for not cracking. David Fifita, the best on ground, pounced on a Cody Walker grubber to open the scoring. Only moments earlier, a similar grubber from Lachlan Galvin went dead-in-goal.

Loading

Fifita and Crichton, meanwhile, kept finding each other. The Maroons forward ran straight over the top of his opponent in the eighth minute, the collision of the night. Crichton, to his credit, didn’t back down and had a few personal wins of his own, like the penalty he milked from the back-rower late in the opening half.

Walker also had a hand in the second try, yet another example of the ball singing along that lethal left edge. If there is a better job in rugby league than being Alex Johnston, we are yet to find it.

Canterbury needed to start the second half well. Souths kicked off and the ball – and the Bulldogs’ finals prospects – slipped through Bailey Hayward’s hands.

It’s a good thing this didn’t come down to goal-kicking. Bud Sullivan kicked just the seventh goal of his career, and then appeared to injure his groin in attempting an eighth. A decade after making his NRL debut, it was left to Matt Dufty to stand over the tee for the first time. Late in the game, there was an opportunity to extend the lead beyond two converted tries with a penalty goal. Bereft of options, they tapped and scored. It will be an area of concern for the tighter, more important games that lay ahead.
